_ TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTHWICH PABLIA.IIIOTARY DIVIBION O CHBeIHIB.B. GENTLEM EN, You took me into your service last December as an appren- tiCe. I wiin to remain in that service as a journeyman. I ask no higher wages, but only a renewal of your confidence hnd a continuarre of your kindness. Two years ego. Iriahinen living in Ireland were, for the lirst time, put on an equallty with you in respect of the power to send men to Parliament to represent their opinions and their feelings; Last yea.- they returned to Parliament 85 men. out of a total of 1,5, pledged and iletermined to demand at your hands a restoration of their ancieut right to a Parliament of their Own in Dublia, and Great Britain elected a large majority of Men anxious to do battle for the well-being of the people against the privileges of a alma. The statement has been made that the Irish proposals would lkeVer have been submitted for constderation, if lar, Gladstone had been returded t 3 piwer with a sufficiently large Liberal Vote to support him agent the vote of the Irish party.

Let truth prevail. Mr. Gladstone in the November of Lest year thus warned his Countrymen "If sinh a matter comes forward at the outset Ol the proceet:inge of the new Parliament as I have described, /tamely, a demand made constitutienally by the vast majority Of the represen'atives of Ireland, for the concessi es of large , local powers of self-gevernmeet, aocompanied with the ad- Minion that the unity of the Empire is not to be impaired. the 'es„ Magnitede of that subject will sweep into the shade for the Xtte.nente all those subjects of ordinary legislation on which I, Or on which ethets, have addressed you, and the satisfactory Settlement of teat subject, which goes down to the very roots and foundations of our whole civil and political constitution. Will become the first duty of Parlament." When Parliament met, the leaders of the Tory party, dis- appointed in their hopes of supp,rt from the new eleetere, do- elated once more for the old bed policy of government by • force, and were ousted 'mom offiee. Mr. Gladstone, Prime 'Minister for the third time, then Sailed upon the llotoe of Commons to satisfy the natioual as- pirations of the Irish peop'e, and to declare for government by Cement of the g ive,ned. f A yollB of the House of Commons rejected Mr. Gladstone's lk.oposal ; and the manhood of the three kingdoms is novi Called upon for a decision. I am confident that the verdict Will be given in favour of a generous and a trustful Irish Depend upon this, that when Ireland [shall once be governed bys Legislature chosen by her own people, intent upon devel- oping the resources of the laud and fostering the prosperity of the nation. IL ishmen, with their homes and the fruits of their labour secure, will make their native island a prosperous, a happy, and a progressive portion of the British Empire, and SOntentedly will stay in their own land. The Protestant religion. which the majority of us held so sear. has for many a day gone by been associated in the ' minds of the Ireth people the world over, with a long and sad 'Fiery cf oppression and wrong-doinie. You, whose highest eopirstions and holient thoughts have been ever inspired by its teachings, know full well that it rests upon the charity which believeth all things and hepeth all things, and that every day U urges you to do mato others as you would they should do unto you. Upon you it now lies, as a solemn duty, to re- deem the clasraeter of that religion before the eyes of these People. The psrformance of this duty will bring its own blessing. You will steady the Irish leaders with the weight of respon- sibility. You evil: add another to the magnificent grout) of self-governing communities which form at once the strength lad the ornsment of the Br ti-h Empire. You will Pet free the Imperial Parliament to grapple with the great problems of legislation which await solution. Again I say, that while holding myself at liberty to. look beyond the proeramme set forth by our venerated leader. Mr. Gladstone, I avow myself. now as heretofore, a num snp- Porter and a devoted follower of him who. more than all livieg Statesmen, is entitled to our affection and our gratitude. I remain, Gentlemen, Your faithfnl servant, JOHN TOMLINSON BRUNNER. Winnington Old Hall,,Northwieh, June IaSS,

GENTLEMEN. Mr. Gladstone has determined to (Assnlve Parliament because it will not let him have his own way.

_ He elaborated a plan for (as he thought) the better govern • ment of Ireland. but Parliament did not concur, and dee iced to pass the Bills whereupon he has decided to dismiss the representatives so lately chosen by the country, and he asks for another election, that he may see what will then be said to his Bill. Though this is troublesome and expensive, and puts a stop' to business yet it must be gone through. because he is within his Con titutional rights in thus asking. it is cow for the country to decide whether they will elect again those who are opposed to Mr. Gladstone's scheme. He is its sole author—it is entirely the emanatiou of his own brain—but, when he announced the scheme to his colleagues they shrank from it with dismay; the shiest and the best of them gave up their offices rather' than countenance measu es which they saw were fraught with mischief for England, and with disaster for Ireland. Mr. Gladstone's oldest friends, his truest friends, found themselves forcerl to separate from him on this matter. His first lieutenant—Mr. Chamberlain—pronounced his determined opposition to the working of the Bill; Lord Hartington found laimself obliged to go against his leader; so oid the clear- minded Sir Heory James, and Mr. °when ; also Mr. Trevel- yan, than wuom there exists no snore noble-minded patriot ; Lord Belborne, late lord Chancellor, whose high personal character and distinguished legal attainments carry such weight, declared that Mr. Gladstone's scheme 'A Li nothing short of political madness; Mr. Bright felt bound to oppose this extraordinary Bill, and voted against it. Mr. Gladstone's scheme has two parts—the one which has just been rejected by Parliament and another, which he says is co-relative, namely the Irish Land Purchase Bill. It may be desirable to buy out the Irish landlords. I think not; but as the proposal has been made, it is natural to inquire "tat whose cost?" Mr. Gladstone says the Irish tenants are. In the long run, to be the payers; but, as at present, they have not money in hand for the transactien, he proposes a stop-gap I shall be found, in the shape of some corporate body, who shall pledge its credit to borrow the money. Mr. Gladstone proposes this stop-gap shall be the British taxpayer. He suggested a loan of a hundred and thirteen minims star- ling; tut, when we were started at so large a sum he reduced the proposition to fifty millions, namely, ten millions, in the first year, twenty millions in the second year, twenty millions In the third year, and actually he added the nation should then pause to consider the result of the experiment: What ad ex- periment! An experiment, at the cost of fifty millions, to see whether Mr. Gladstone is capable of leading us wrong against our better judgment. Is that statesmanship? Is a great country thus to be hoodwinked and cajoled? Mr. Gladstone explaised that the Br.tirh taxpayer is not to bts called upon to pay the half-yearly interest of th;s vast sum if the Irish tenants will pay their rents. If? indeed But if they won't pay their rents how are we to snake them pay? Some people don'tlknow a tad debt when they see it; but you will recognize that you will made a huge bad debt if you allow yourselves and your sucseasors to be bound to ray, for ever, half-yearly interest on the vast sum for which Mr. Gladstone desires to make you liable. We were informed ay Mr. Chamberlain that when the scheme was first disclosed to the Cabinet the sum named was One Hundred and Twenty Milliciers, he thougist it would re- quire more than One Hundred and Fifty Millions. Certainly It is a fact Oat, not many yeass ago, Idr. Gladstone estimated the value of land in Ireland at between Three Hundred and Four Hundred Millions. You would lose your mony if you consented to this scheme; but that is not the worst of it for you will perceive that in the making of that loss quarrels would most surely arise. The opportunities allorded to men for quarrel are many, but of all subjects there is none more fertile for strife than bickering about money. There could be no sorer way of making a quar- rel between England and Ireland than by creating two distinct Legislatures, with the probabil•ty of a money dispute. Mr. Gladstone asks you to accept this tremendous* liabil- ity ; but wiry? Only because the Irish refuse to pay their rents.

Let us have nothing to do with this hair•brained scheme which really has not common sense; we ought not to be asked to advance our money in this way; tut above all let us avoid that civil war which would be rendered inevitable. We are a rich nation, and we may be able to afford to make a bad debt: even to the extent of the hundred millions indi- cated ; but, rich and powesful as we are, we cannot afford to run the far greater risk which is latent in Mr. Gladstone's Bill. We cannot aft, rd to be forced into that against which I now warn you—we cannot afford to have to fight against our Irish fellow-countrymen. What is wanted in Ireland is what we have in Eng'and and Scotland—a dutiful obedience to law—And no Government is worthy of the name unless it can cause law and order to be maintained. When you sent me to Parliament, one of the objects we mutually bad in view was the furtherarce of such legislation (call it Hcme Rule, if you Phe) as could be applied to all parts of the United /I ingdorn. with intention to devolve, prudently, on local boards the control of local affairs, relieving thereby the work of the Imperial Parliament—but being distinctly under its supremacy.

There is ni reason for giving more of this to Ireland than to England or Scot"aud. Let our sister Kingdom have her full share of this legislation, but let her also be law-atiding, as we are, and so become content aid prosperous. Mr. Gladstone's wild scheme has been rejected by the strong common sense of the House of Comrgons, to which you sent me a short time ago. If you again so gbnour me, I shall repeat my vote on this matter ; and you will ever find that in all matters I shall always do my inmost to serve you faithiutly and well.
I am, Yours truly, WILLIAM C. BROOKS. Barlow Hall, Manchester' June 17th, IEB6.

THE ORGAN-BLOWER. (By DR. OLIVER WENDELL HOLMES.) The following is given as an example of the apparently careless, yet deeply practical, character of the poetry 6.'? our American visitor : Devoutest of my Sunday friends, The patient organ-blower bends; I see his figure sink and rise - (Forgive me, Heaven, my wandering eyes!) A moment lost, the next' half seen, His head above the scanty screen, , Still measuring out his deep salaams, Through quavering hymns and p inting psalms. No priest that prays la aded stile To save a rich man's mortgaged soul, , No sister, fresh from holy vows, So humbly stoops, so meekly bows; His large obeisance puts to shame The proudest genuflecting dame, Whose Easter bonnet low descends With all the grace devotionlends. Oh, brother, with the supple spine, Bow much we owe those bows of thine! Without thine arm to lend the breeze How vain the fingers on the keys! Tho' all unmatched the player's skill, These thousand throats were dull and still; Another's art may shape the tone, The breath that fills it is thine own. Six days the silent Memnon waits Behind his temple's folded gates; But when the seventh day's sunshine falls 'Through rainbowed windows on the walls, He breathes, he sings, he shouts, he fills The quivering air with rapturous thrills; The roof resounds, the pillars shake, And all the slumbering echoes wake. The preacher from the Bible text With weary words my soul has vexed— Some stranger fumbling far astray To find the lesson for the day. He tells us truths too plainly true, And reads the service all askew; Why, why the—mischief can't lie look Beforehand in the service book? But thou, with decent mien Ind face, Art always ready in thy place; Thy strenuous blast, whate'er the tune, As steady as the strong monsoon; Thy only dread a leathery creak Or small residual extra squeak, ' To send along the shadowy aisles A sunlit wave of dimpled smiles. Not all the preaching, oh, my friend, Comes from the Church's pulpit end; Not all that bend the knee and bow Yield service half so true as thou. One simple task performed aright, With slender skill, but all thy might; Where honest, labour does its best, And leaves the Player all the rest. This many-diapasoned maze, . Through which the breath of being strays, Whose music makes our earth divine, Has work for mortal hands like mine. My duty lies before me. No! The lever there. Take hold and blow, And He whose hand is on the keys Will play the tune as He shall please.

- -- -- When are watches easily stolen ?—When they are off their guard. Hasty words often rankle in the wound which injury inflicts; and soft words assuage it. Forgiving cures, and forgetting takes away the scar. It is doing some service to humanity to amuse inno- cently; and they know very little society who think we can bear to be always employed, either in duties or meditations, without any relaxation. The following is an epitaph in a churchyard in Clonmel "Oh, cruel Death! why were you so unkind To take him first and leave me here behind? 'Twere better to have taken both or neither, Which would have been more satisfactory to the survivor." scene—Edinburgh Exhibition.—Elderly Dame (look- ing at the figure of Fame over the grand hall) : "An' wha's yon gran' leddy they've gotten up yonder, John ?" —John: "Oh, yen's Madame Fame !"—Elderly Dame (interestingly): "An' what's she famed for ?"—John : " Blawin' her am n trumpet, to be shure !" Every man desires success, and the strength of his desire is shown in the earnestness of his efforts; the difference lies in the objects in which lie desires to suc- ceed. Earnestness is good, success is good; what we have to watch is that we are earnest in a worthy cause; then our success will be justly a matter of rejoicing. "You look so happy that I suppose you have been to the dentist and had that aching tooth drawn," said a man to a friend with a swollen jaw. "It isn't that that makes me look happy. The tooth aches worse than ever; but I don't feel it." "How's that?" "Well, I feel so jolly because I have just been to the dentist, and he was out !" HARD TO PLEASE.—" Never fear, my dear," remarked the wife to her impecunious husband; "never fear, I still love you." "I know that," he replied, "but that doesn't help matters much." "I'll trust you always," she exclaimed. "Yes, my dear," lie replied, with a Migh that came from his heart, "that's all very fine, but, un- fortunately, you are not the grocer." A German composer was conductin, one of his over- tures. As the horns played too loud, he told them re- peatedly to play more softly; and more softly they played each time. At the fourth repetition, with a knowine, wink at each other, they put their instruments to their lips but did not blow at all. The conductor nodded approvingly :—" Very good indeed! Now, one shade softer, and you'll have it." A healthy sensitiveness accepts the pain which it must bear as a wholesome medicine, not dwelling upon its bitter taste, not npbraiding those who hand' it, not re- garding it as a permanent evil, but simply using it for self-improvement. At the same time it gladly welcomes all the pleasant tidings which are thus brought to know- ledge. It is as keen to feel the good as the evil, and finds it in much larger proportion. Men who are drunk with ambition for wealth, or fame, or position, and are straining every nerve in business or politics, or any other all-absorbing object, neglecting everything else in life, and pressing swiftly forward to ruined health and an early grave, are less the victims of excitement than of one-sidedness. Could they but be excited in other directions the whole tenor of their lives would be altered. It is their torpidity to the many claims of life that paves the way to the ultra and fatal i devotion to one. _

Two young city ladies in the country were standing by the side of 'a :deep ditch, which they didn't know how to cross. They appealed to a boy who was coming along the road for help, whreupon he pointed behind them with a startled air and yelled "Snakes!" The two young ladies crossed the ditch at a single bound. The Laird of Balnamoon, riding past a high, steep bank, stopped opposite a hole in it, and said, "John, I saw a brock gang in there." "Did ye?" said John; " wull ye haud my horse, sir ?" " Certainly," said the Laird, and away rushed John for a spade After digging for half an hour, he came back nigh speechless te the , Laird, who had regarded him musingly. "I canna find him, sir," said John. "'Deed," said the Laird, very coolly, "I wad ha' wondered if ve had, for it's ten years sin' saw him gang in there." "Ali, Farmer Robinson," said his fair city guest, "how quietly you live out here in the country; you are not disturbed by society quarrels, or political excite- ment,". or labour quarrels, but all is comfortable and pleasant." "Yes, miss, I 'spose it looks so to you. But there's the hottest society quarrel over who's going to sing alto in the choir next year, an' the's politics: Ben Johnson swears I shan't be selectman again • and as for labour troubles, my hired man struck yesterday because I wanted him to milk the cows before breakfast. Oh, we have our little seasons of enjoyment as well as you city folks." A joke is a mystery to some people. Once-in a certain law court the proceedings were delayed by the failure of a witness named Sarah Mony to arrive. After waiting a, long time for Sarah, the Judge concluded to wait no longer, and, wishing to crack his little joke, remarked, "This:Court will adjourn without Sarah Mony." Every- body laughed except one man, who sat in solemn medi- tation for five minutes, and then burst into a hearty guffaw, exclaiming. "I see it—l see it !" When he went home he tried to tell the joke to his wife. "There was a witness named Mary Mony who didn't come," said he; "and so the Court said, We'll adjourn without Mary Mony.'" "I don't see any point in that," said his wife. "I know it," said he. "I 'didn't at first; but you will in about five minutes." ! CONSCIENCE I—An Indian merchant took an elephant to a fair. No sooner had he arrived than he noticed a European, who, without saying a word, walked round and round the elephant, examining it attentively on all sides. The merchant addressed several questions to him without eliciting a reply. An intending purchaser ap- peared on the scene, and the merchant turned eagerly to the European and whispered in his ear, "Don't say a word till I have sold the elephant, and I will make you a hand- some present." The stranger nodded assent, and remained mute as before. When the bargain was concluded and the money paid, tile merchant handed over ten per cent. of the purchase-money, and said to the mysterious per- sonage, "Now you can speak; I want you to explain how you came to notice the blemish in the left leg of my elephant, which I thought I had managed entirely to conceal ?" "A blemish'!" replied the silent one. "I discovered nothing: it is the first time I ever saw an elephant in my life, and I examined it out of sheer curiosity." MARRIAGE CEREMONIAL OF GEORGE lll.—Unforeseen difficulty occurred in settling the form of ceremonial to be obseived at the marriage of George 111. with the Prin- cess Charlotte. Dr. Birch, then librarian of the British Museum, was appealed to, and he reported that there was no precedent of a royal marriage according to the , form of the English Church. Henry VIII. was married, to everyone of his wives according to the ritual of the Church of Rome. His daughter Mary was married to Philip of Spain, at Winchester, by Bishop Gardiner, Cran- mer being then in prison. Edward VI. and Elizabeth both died unmarried. James I. was married to the Prin- cess of Denmark, some years before he came to England, by the Presbyterian minister of Leith; Charles L was married by proxy at Paris to the Princess Henrietta. Charless queen, refusing the offices of the English Church was merely taken by the hand, in the presence chamber at Portsmouth, the King saying the words of, matrimony in the Prayer Book, "I, Charles, take thee, Catherine, &c. The Queen expressed her consent, and Dr. Sheldon, Bishop of London, declared them man and wife. The first marriage of James 11., then Duke of York, to the daughter of Lord Chancellor Clarendon, was privately performed by Dr. Crowther, the duke's chap- lain, at Worcester House, September 3rd, 1660. The second marriage to the Princess of Modena, was per- formed at Dover on the day of her landing by Dr. Crewe, then Bishop of Oxford. George I. and George 11. were married before they came to the throne. THE YOUNG PRINCES IN BARBADOES.—From St. John's we drove down through the slopes of the undercliff to Codrington College, passing many still more flimsy and rickety negro-huts. On our arriving at the entrance of the long avenue of cocoa-nut palms which leads up to the college, there was an enthusiastic gathering of negro women, men, and children to see "Queen Victoria's pic- caninnies." They clustered round the first carriage that arrived, which was a waggonette containing mids, whom they took for us, and frantically embraced every part they could lay their hands on—the stops, door, splash- board, kissing these and even the wheels and over- whelming the occupants with blessings and salutations of joy and delight. When we came a little after, the first burst of efikotion had been let off, but still enough remained to give us a hearty welcome. The stalwart Barbadian negro is better satisfied with himself and more independent than any other. He may have be- longed originally, in Africa, to some higher race, for there ere as great differences of race among negroes as among European nations. The true Barbadian born looks down en all other negroes as beings of an inferior grade. They are almost the only negroes who will work. The island is so thickly populated that if they did not they would starve. In consequence labour is cheap, and the whole island looks like a well-kept garden. Many Bims migrate to other islands as carpenters, smiths, &c. We took two Barbadian negro carpenters on board the Bacchante with us during the whole of our cruise in the West Indies. They were employed on inlaying the combing (of the after-hatchway on the quarterdeck with various coloured woods; they did it very well, and worked steadily, giving no trouble whatsoever.—The Cruiqe of H..lf.S. Bacchante. By Prince Albert Vector .and Prince George of Wales, PRINCELY SEAFARERS "CROSSING THE LlNE."—After divisions Neptune hailed the ship, and came on board the portside : we crossed the line at 10 a.m., so he and Amphitrite stayed with us till the dinner hour, during which time the ship's company were employed in mak- ing his acquaintance. A bluejacket, named Goodfellow (ciptain of the quarter-deck), made a sturdy, thickset, and hairy King of the Sea and acted the part uncom- moray well. He and his shy little " Amphitritty " (Bar- ton, boatswain's yeoman) came aft with their attendants, where they were met by the captain and those of the officers who had crossed before, and received from them tribute in shape of sardines, pots of jam, pipes, pickles, and "cake for the bears to eat." Then the two took their seats side by side on an extemporised throne over the engine-room hatch-way. Meanwhile the lower stun- stail had been rigged up in the starboard gangway so as to form a large tank, which had been filled with sea- ) water. The contents were constantly renewed so as to keep the depth of the water about five feet. At the after end of the tank a platform of gratings about six feet above the deck, and on a level with the hammock net- tings, and with a ladder up to it, had been erected, and on this stood " the shavers," under the first lieuten- ant's, superintendence. Doctor Gideon Delemege was the only one of the ward-room to be shaved, but all the gun-room (exCept Murray and Moore) and about 230 of the crew were operated on. These were all sent between decks and brought up one by one blindfolded, and presented to his Majesty with a few words from the senior member of their mess, descriptive of the character they each bore in the ship. Neptune then, after exchanging a few observations with his new acquaintance, gave directions as to which of the four various sided razors was to be employed. They passed on, and, mounting the ladder, sat down in a chair on the platform for the operation. "The barber" was accom- panied by "the doctoriwith pills" in readiness, and his bttendant with "smelling salts," in case anyone should require his assistance, which was given quite gratui- tously, and freely proffered to all. This was all over in half a minute, when they found themselves covered with soapsuds, tipped over backwards off the platform into the water in the sail, through which they were passed by the six " bears " (all first-class petty oirtcers), getting snore or less ducked on their passage out. Everything went off with the utmost good humour, and it was most refreshing having the steam hose played over us as the temperature, both of the air and water, was 78deg. We all had great fun in slushing and squirting each other with these, turning a hose now on one officer or man, .and now on another, as we ran about, in more or less light attire, all over the deck and climbed up in the rigging. There was ducking in all its forms and under every modification of splashing and immersion; there was the duck courteous, the duck oblique, the duck direct, the duck upright, the duck downright, the shower duck, and the duck and drake. The gambols and sky-larking were concluded by noon, and the usual ship routine resuined.7-/bid. The MORNING AD} ERTISER of Febrnary 22nd, 1886, has the following:—" Messrs. COX & CO., 41. SPEECHES BY MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, J.P., MR. C. 31. PERCY, MR. E. TROW, &c. On Saturday evening a mass meeting of work- ing-men was held in the Public Hall in support of Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., the Liberal candidate for the borough. The gathering was One of work- ing-men in every respect, having been pi omoted by a self-constituted committee under the presidency of Mr. T. Flood. In its result the meeting proved, in a most. unmistakeable manner, that Mr. Cros- field's candidature has evoked an anusual amount of enthusiastic support amongst the working f.,.lasses of the town. It was announced that the doors of tho hall would be opened at half-past six o'clock, but almost an hour before that time a large number of people eager to obtain vats had assembled in Rylands-street, and very soon after the doors were opened the large hall was filled to overflowing. The long period ot waiting was whiled away by the hearty singing of political songs, and cheering for popular leaders. The chair was taken by Mr. T. Flood, who was supported by a crowded platform, amongst those present beinc, Mr. C. M. Percy. (Liberal candidate for Wigan), Mr. E. Prow (secre- tary of the Amalgamated Association of Iron Workers and Steel Workers), Messrs. William Stirrup, J. The CHAIRMAN read an apology from Mr. M. Chambers, who was to have taken the chair, and who wrote saying that circumstances rendered it impossible to be present. Proceeding, lie said that if there was anything at which he felt no-I.a it was the attempt that the opponents of home Rule were making to make the struggle one of race, instead of politics. Their opponents, they knew, fought a losing battle, and were sensible of it, for they knew that the Liberal party had been the party of pro- gress, freedom of conscience, and of liberty. (Cheers.) From what he knew of the history of this country, and of his own native land, he knew that the Irish leaders were able to loOk with confidence upon the leaders of the Liberal party. He denied that any measure for the alleviation of distressed Ireland had ever been introduced by the Tory party, and there was not eirpon the statute book that day a measure that they had passed for the good of that country. (Cheers.) It had been said that they passed the Catholic Emancipation Act, but they did not do that until they were forced by outside agitation. He was not an advocate for separati9n from the Crown, for a man would be a traitor Who would advocate that. But the land that gave him birth had been misgoverned for eighty years. Thirty-eight land bills had. been introduced since 1800, and out of that number only two had been successfully carried. On the other hand 86 coercion acts had been successfully passed. Was that, he asked, legislation for the alleviation of the distress of Ireland.? ("No.") It was not, and that conviction had been brought home to the minds of legislators, and the timeihad come when something must be done to settle this question. (Cheers.) He contended that the Irish were socially and morally by no means the inferiors of the people of the mother country, and said that Irishmen in all parts of the world had gained great distinction they had shown bravery on English battle- fields, and had shone equally as statesmen. (Cheers.) With regard to the industries of Ireland, he said, who was there that knew the industrial history of that country that could deny the fact that at one time Ireland was teeming with a population of eight millions, and that the provinces of Leinster, Ulster, and Munster were thriving hives of industry. (Hear, hear.) He would ask them as honest men if they could say that it was honest to restrict the freedom of their fellow creatures? If the people of Ireland had a chance of living in Ireland they would live there. Thousands of his fellow country- men to-day would not be in unfair competition with Englishmen if they had the opportunity of staying at home. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) But when randlords drew 6f millions of capital out of the country in the form of rent and stifled the industry of the country, they might depend upon it that Irishmen would have to seek fresh fields and pas- tures ndw. (Loud cheers.) Mr. I. BIDDLE proposed—" That this meeting of Warring- ton working-men desires to express its unabated confidence in the Right Honourable William Ewart Gladstone—(loud cheers)—thanks him for the noble effsrts he is making to promote peace and prosperity to Ireland, and pledges itself to render him every possible lawful support." (Cheers, ' and a voice: "We will do it.") Well, he asked them to do it, and would they do their part? (" Yes," and cheers.) That question of politics was government by the people and for the people—(cheers)--and not for the aristocracy, not for the sinecurists, and not for the--he was going to say aristocratic paupers. (Laughter and cheers.) That meet- ing seemed to be in favour of Mr. Gladstone going on with the measure he had in hand—(applause)—and the question for them to decide, as far as they possibly could, was which of the leaders should take the matter in hand? (Loud cries of "Gladstone.") It was reported that one of the candidates the other night said he wanted to treat Ireland sympathetically, humanely, and even lovingly. (" Oh, oh.") Many of those present would no doubt have seen the "Lady with the Ring of Iron" and he would ask what form was the "love " to take. It etruck him (Mr. Biddle) that it was:of the form of the ring of irong—(A voice : " Twenty years' coercion ")—a ring of iron of twenty years firm Government, which was the term for coercion. He thought they were prepared to say that was not English, it was not humane and the " love " was all the worse for being "love." (Cheers.) Mr. Gladstone's policy had al ways been for general advancement, for doing away with" monopolies, fo.l bringing the men of England to think of their real position as men, and as parts of a great whole, and that every man was an individual, and did not run in groups as the hares, while 'their Government ought to be on the principles of honesty, fair play, and justice all round. (Cheers.) He claimed that that was not a religious coestion, and if the matter was right it must prevail. If they looked at the two leaders, there could be no question that for the general welfare of all in the country, and the general welfare of the world at large, the most fit and pro- per person to lead them in the country was the Right Hon. William Ewart Gladstone. (Loud cheers.) Mr. WlLLiest WlLiarr, in seconding the resolution, said

he had great pleasure in doing so, because he believed Mr. Ciladstone's motive in promoting the Home Rule Bill was simply and purely to do that which was right. (Cheers.) He contended it was their bounden duty as Englishmen to do their duty to Ireland. That week, on a platform in War- rington, Sir (inert Greenell himself—(hisses)-- said he would rule Ireland not with coercion, but with kindness and with sympathy, but he (Willett) thought that if Mr. Glad- stone's measure was passed it weuld not only bring peace and prosperity to Ireland, but it would also give them an opportunity of getting some of the great and growing evils redressed under which they now laboured. (Cheers.) As Englishmen they had their difficulties to encounter. They were over-burdened with taxation, and he hoped and trusted that Mr. Gladstone would have the sympathy of every constituency throughout the length and breadth of the land, and if the working people did their duty he had not the least doubt he would be re- turned by a triumphant majority. (Cries of "He will," and cheers.) There had been a 'great deal of talk about Mr. John Bright, for whom he had every reepect, but, as a working-man, he was positive Mr. Bright's conduct had lately been inconsistent with his conduct years ago. (Hear, hear.) From the year 1847 John Bright had advo- cated Home Rule in his speeches in England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales. (Applause.) He (Mr. Willett) be- lieved Mr. Gladstone was going to carry his measure suc- cessfully. They had been charged with setting up one man, but they believed in the old Liberal watchword, not only religious freedom, but civil freedorn,and they wanted to give that liberty to 'lreland. (Oteers.) The Government bad been charged with wanting to separate this country from Ireland, but there was nothing in it —it was not so. (Applause.) The Tories had never advecated anything, and did not in- tend to do, except coercion, and coercion never ruled men kindly ; they never took to it, and never would. (Cheers.) When the measure was passed all the honour and glory that could be heaped en Mr. Gladstone's head would be merited for what he had doiae. His work was gigantic, his best friends had deserted han, but he was very glad to say that the working-men had not. ,(Cheers.) They were the backbone and the sinew of the country, and they had a right to be .heard. They had got the franchise and they should exercise it, and give back to the giver the benefit of what he had given to them—the franchise. (Cheers.) Mr. ED. Thaw, on rising to support the resolution, Was received with cheers. He said in the first place he heel very great pleasure in supporting the resolution, because he believed that it was one of the grandest efforts that had ever been put forth by the Grand Old Man—(loud cheers) to grant justice to Ireland. He perfectly agreed with his friend in the audience when he said that Ireland had been oppressed by both Liberal and Tory, but the Liberals had seen their error, and the Grand Old Man had found out that their treatment of Ireland had been the wrong treatment. They had been applying the wrong medicine to cure the disease. He had now probed the disease to the bottom, and had found out what was the remedy, and like an honest man he says he is prepared to say that his past treatment had been a mistake and he would remedy it by granting justice and proper treatment. (Cheers.) He waked, if Englishmen had been under the dominion of a foreign power and treated as Ireland had been, would they have sat down any inure quietly than Ireland had done? (*. No.") In the second place he supported the resolution because everybody said a change was wanted. There was not a Tory or Whig from John 0' Groat's to Land's End who ventured to deny that a change was wanted. Lord Cs.rnarvon some time since believed in it, and he believed in it to-day. (Ap- plause.) Lord Randolph Churchill—(prolonged hisses and groans)—though he might deny it, was the medium through which the chequet were imported into various con- stituencies to pay expenses where the Irish voted for the Tory candidates. Everyone wanted a change, and who was it that they, as working-menovanted to bring about the change? ("Gladstone," and cheers.). He did not think either Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Goschen' Lord Hartingten, or Mr. Caine, were competent to take the reins of Govern- ment, and the issue was narrowed down to a point—it was two men' and it would be decided by the result of the elections during the next ten or twelve days—Gladstone or Salisbury (" Gladstone." and cheers.) He liked to hear them shout "Gladstone" as the man they wished to bring about the change, and they must so decide it at the ballot box. (Cheers.) They said " Gladstone," and he as a work- ngman said "Not Salishury.". (Laughter and cheers.) He believed in emigration, but it was in sending Salisbury and all his crew out of the country. He was prepared to give the Churchill family the full value of all they had stolen from the people—(langhter and cheers)—he was pre- pared to pay the full value of their perpetual pensions, to send their goods and chattels, families and themselves, out of the country, and give them land to settle on, if they would leave the people to enjoy their liberty at home. Mr. Gladstone was above class interests and self-interest, and was the friend of the masses of this country. (Cheers.) The speaker then made reference to the attitude taken up by Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain at the present crisis. What objections, he staked, were urged against giving Ireland Home Rule? That England mistrusted the Irish people. (Cries of " No.") They were afraid that the Catholics would interfere with the Protestants. ("No.") He was only telling tbem what some people said. It was said that if a Home Rule Bill were passed, a Land Bill would have to be pissed, and that a lot of taxes would have to be paid to purchase the land of Ireland. but would it not be mora in accordance with the dictates of their conscience If they were to pay a tax rather than to keep up such an enorm- ous military expenditure in Ireland? He had no doubt about the Irish. He had had as much to do with Irishmen both here and in Ireland as most men, and he always found them ready to hold their own. If any one of them was suffering because of the lack of work, let him re- member that when the Irishman stepped foot on English soil he was their equal, and made as much or more headway than themselves, and he thrust them out of employment. But while he remained on the other aide of the Channel, he did not have fairplay. and Irishmen had, as their chairman said, been driven in millions from the country; and they had been driven into England to glut their labaur market. Mr. Trow ridiculed the assertions that the passing of the Government Bill would lead to separatien, and said that every Irishman who had common sense knew that the very success of Home Rule depended upon their being able to rely upon England for support. Why, you patriotic Tories, you Unionists; you cowards! (Prolonged cheers.) He re- peated the word "coward," and he would prove that they were cowares. A little island with a little over five millions of inhabitants, three-fourths of whom professed a different religion to the other fonrth, azainat a country with 30 millions of people, yet they said there was a fear of separa- tion if they granted Home Role. (Laughter, and hear, bear.) He was in favour of Home Rule because in England they wanted reforms in the land laws and the labour laws. They wanted the working-men—the backbone and sinew of this country—batter represented in the House of Commons than it is. (Cheers.) They wanted justice and fairplay and liberty, and so long as every English working-men re- corded his vote in favour of a Tory and against Home Rule, so long was he preventing justice be- ing administered to himself. (Cheers.) They wanted reform in the land laws, but Ireland blocked the way. (Hear, hear.) They wanted reform in their labour laws, but Ireland blocked the way. As long as Irishmen were in the House of Commons they would be in a position to pre- vent these reforms. (Hear, hear ) They, are the governing power, and they would govern them in England in spite of what they might say, and they would never be able to go- vern themselves until they had satisfied Ireland. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He would therefore ask them seriously at the next election to coneider the matter of the vote they were going to record, to consider the question of giving justice to men who were equally able to take care of themselves as they were and remove the chains of their slavery which would be the means of drawing them away from the labour markets of England. (Cheers.) Let them remember that Home Rule was not the hydra- headed monster some people wanted to make out. In Eng- land they were acting worse than Russia, which allowed Home Rule to Finland, and although they sometimes spoke against Germany, yet Bavaria was an integral part of Ger- many and had a king of its own and made its own laws. Norway and Sweden were united, although they each had parliaments of their own, and the same was the case with regard to Austria and Hungary. (Cheers.) Mr. TM", also referred to our self-governing colonies, and added that we would be told next that the Imperial supremacy was lost because the Isle of Man had Home Rule. (Loud laughter.) He was in. favour, he said, of a union of sympathy and a union with Ireland of living hearts; a union with Ireland in defence of their and our rights, which would be brought about by giving that country the justice we enjoyed our- selves. (Loud cheers.) The position they were in was that they had wrongs to be righted, grievances to be re- dressed, and on the morning of the poll every man should decide :

This day shall simple manhood try The power of gold and land, The wide world has no wealth to buy The power in my right hand. While there's one right t 4 claim my vote. One wrong to sweep away. One horny hand and ragged coat. A man's a man to-day.
(Cheers.)
The resolution was carried unanimously, and with ac. clamation.

The CHAIRMAN, at this juncture, made some reference to Mr. R. W. Murray, who had been on a Tory platform in Warrington, and Waco had fought in the past in defence of slavery. ("Shame.") Mr. Jolts BROMLEY rose to propose the next resolution. Before doing so he paid that that great meeting was drawn together by the cause of freedom and justice. The Tories were saying that we had governed Ireland for something like 700 years, but they did not say how. It almost made one's hair stand on end to read of Irish past history. (" Shame.") That 700 years' rule had been a failure, and they had a great cause to fight for in giving liberty to Ire- land. As long as the Irish members remained at West- minster and obstructed business needful legislation for Eng- land, which was much required, would of necessity be neg- lected. He then proposed "That, having read the address of Mr. John Crosfield, in which ho pledges himself, if re- turned to Parliament, to support Mr. Gladstone's proposal for the Government of Ireland, this meeting desires to ex- press its hearty approval of the same, and pledges itself to use every lawful effort to secure his triumphant election." (Cheers.) Mr. H. WIIITMAM seconded the resolution. He said that the English and Irish electors met together that night to further the cause of Ireland, and they proposed to do so by sending Air. John Croefleld to Parliament, with the view ,

that he would support Mr. Gladstone. Seven or eight years ago he (the speaker) was in favour of Home Rule, and he felt that the sooner it was gained the sooner the English working-men would be able to devote a little more attention to their own intereste. (Cheers.) He was surprised that a constitnency comprising the num- ber of working-men that Warrington did, should ever send a Conservative to represent it. (Cheers.) He desired Home Rule for his own sake as much as for the sc.ke of the Irishman. They could scarcely go into any works without seeing the Irish competing with the English in the labour market, and the Irish agricultural labourer came to England to earn money to pay the rent for land in Ireland that never earned the rent for itself. But the Home Rule question was not the only one with him. He wanted con- sideration to be given to the questions of' the land laws, "royalties," and railways. Reform in that direction had been opposed by the Conservative party, and, he asked, would Sir Gilbert Greenall, if returned, side with the working- men representatives sent to Parliament?. (Cries of "No.") At this point of Mr. Whitham's speech, the candi late and Mr. F. A. Roberts came on the platform and were most enthusiastically received. Proceeding, Mr. Whithana said that he should like Mr. John Croefield to express an opinion upon the question of "royalties" and railways, and say how far he was prepared to go with the working-men members of Parliament. (Cheers.) He should also like the Conservatives to put a similar question to their candidate, and also get a definite reply from him. He then made reference toe a speech of the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton with regard to Mr. Peter Rylands, and coneluded by heartily seconding the resolution. (Cheers.) Mr. C. M PzucY. who was well received, supported the resolution. He said that during the last election campaign, when he appeared at Warrington, he was somewhat worn- out himself, and the cause that he was fighting proved also to be somewhat worn-out when the election day came. (Laughter.) Although they in Warrhagton had an excel- lent and honourable candidate then, who would have been a very worthy representative of that constituency, and who would be the very worthy member for the -city of Lincoln Mr. William Crosfield (cheers) who fought and lost as he (Mr. Percy) had done, they did not sit down and cry like the Ulster Protestants. (Laughter and cheers.) They did not ask for protection for miporities, but simply recruited their strength, for they knew the day was not far distant when the battle had to be fought again, and they should win. (Cheers.) He expressed himself fond of a bard battle, and said that last year he was defeated by a majority of 500, but had this year undertaken to wipe out a majority of nearly 1,000. (Cheers.) They would either bring down the Tory stronghold in his town, or toes' would so track the wall that it would fall in natural course. (Cheers.) He said that they were bound to confine them- selves to one question, but the Liberal party was never so strong as when fighting upon one great question. In 1865 they fought on one great question, and in Warrington they won; in 1874 they fought upon several issues and were de- feated ; npsn a great question they were successful in 1.880; and in 1885, when every half dozen people bad a. separate programme, they suffered another defeat in Warrington. This time they were united again under the leadership of the greatest man that ever lived. (Cheers.) Tories and Liberals alike believed that the Home Rule question must in some way or other be settled, and out of 103 Irish members in Parliament 86 were unanimous in favour of Home Rule. He himself had always held the doctrine that a nation Lad a right to manage its own affairs, and he held that the Irish nation had a right to govern themselves in purely Irish matters. So far from having a tendeAcy to separation, he believed that this measure of justice to Ireland would wipe out the recollection of centuries of injustice and tyranny—(cheers)—and would remove from the neinds of the Irish people in Ireland the bitterness and hatred against England, would make' England more united at home, stronger abroad, and enable the two peoples to live together in terms of brotherly love and affection. A great reason why he wished this question to b 3 settled was because until it was no legislation could be accomplished for England. He believed that 86 determined men in Parliament could pre- vent legislation, and, until their Irish national demands were met, they were perfectly justified in doing so. (Cheers.) One of the speakers had mentioned royalties. Royalties, he said, to the tune of something like five mil- lion sterling, were paid to mine owners, and that a.nount did not represent a.eingle farthing contributed to the local rates of any district, and meant a loss of about one million of money per year to such rates. When they compared mining royalties in England with the countries on the continent, the comparison was somewhat startling. In England, for every ton of coal raised an amount varying from 6d to is a ton had to be paid to the owner of the land, which lowered wages, but in France, and Germany, and Belgium the ironstone be- longed to the people and the royalty never exceeded five per cent of the profits. (Hear, hear.) It had been stated that thousands of tons of foreign iron was underselling English iron in English markets, and at the same time hundreds of English ironworkers were walking the streets in enforced idleness. (" Shame.") The real remedy for that state of things was to remove the fetters off Cho home industry—(cheers)---and reduce these royalties. He urged that an investigation should be made into these matters. As mining laws were now constituted, not one ounce of coal could be taken until a fixed amount was paid, and, he said that there was one firm in that county that failed and threw hundreds out of empleyment, and yet they had paid £llO,OOO for coal they had never got, which remained the property of the mine owner, who was work- ing it to-day. (" Shame.") There was in the county of Lancaster another firm that had £300,000 upen its h*oks of overpaid mine rents. Such a condition of things was ruinous. When the Irish business was settled they would, he believed, have such a glorious series of liberal measures as would introduce a new era, and he hoped that to aid to bring about that they would remove the stigma that rested upon the escutcheon. of Warrington, by turning out the Tory representative —(cheers)—and putting in a man who by his reputation in that town, his connection with it, by his very life and his- tory, was the best representative for Warrington. (Re- newed cheers.) Mr. Percy then made a further reference to Ireland, remarking that the whole history of the Catholics in Ireland showed that they had no religions bigotry, were not actuated by religious animosity, and were simply actuated by patriotism. (Cheers.) He hoped, and thought, that the great measure of ?Tome Rule would be passed. He believed that unless Ireland was ruled in the way that was provided in the present measure, or sinless the same principles were granted to the Irish nation, there were terrible days in store. They could not suppress the aspirations of an entire nation. They were determined in Ireland to have a Parliament of their own, and be believed there would be a revolution in that country unless her demands were considered. When they thought how there was note battle this country had fought hut that the Irish and the English soldier had fought side by side, and how Irishmen ane Englishmen had been so intimately con- nected, they would all wish to preserve and intensify those friendly relations. He believed that the Irish were prepared on their part to forget and forgive, and that the passing of the measure would be the means of building up in the hearts of the Irish people an increased and increasing love to the English people. (Cheers.) The resolution was then put and carried amidst cheers, which were agaia and again renewed. Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD was received with enthusias- tic cheering, and the singing of "For he's a jolly good fellow." He said: Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I feel that I have not words to express the pleasure that it gives me to be with you to-night. (Hear, hear.) This is one of the most magnificient meet- ings—and I have seen a great many—that I ever saw in this hall. (Cheers.) I thank you heartily for the kind reception you have given to me, and, as I said the other night, I have the feeling in my breast that I have your sympathy and that you have mine. (Cheers.) Well, now, the first thing I will do will be to answer Mr. Whitham. (Hear, hear.) I condemn these "royalties"—(cheers)--Land I will stand shoulder to shoulder with Mr. Percy in the House of Commons—(hear, hear, and cheers)-- because ;we are both going there—(laughter, and loud cheers)—and we will see if we cannot do some- thing to get rid of an injustice like that which is pressing upon one of the most important industries of this kingdom. (Hear, hear.) As regards the railway rates, I am very much dissatisfied with the present condition of things. I will willingly and earnestly support any bill brought into the House of Commons which shall deal with railway. rates, and make them more equal throughout the king- dom. (Cheers.) I hope that that answer is sufficient for my friend Mr. Whitham. (Hear, hear.) But a deputation is coming to me, I expect, on Monday, and I shall be very glad indeed to meet those gen- tlemen and tell them my opinions upon that or upon anything else. (Cheers.) /am not afraid of my opinions. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) I have been used to speak the truth, and I tell my friend Dr. Mackie—(hissing and laughter, and a Voice, "He's as bad as Lord Randolph Churchill," and " Knobstick shop ")—I tell him that in future he had better be a little more careful when he attacks me and my speeches, and he had better not accuse' me of foul language when I speak the truth. (Hear, hear) I spoke the very words that Lord Salisbury used, and I defy Dr. Mackie to deny it. (Cheers.) I want no beating 'about the 'bush. He goes round .and round, and he tries to blind the Tory audience with a lot of gland words and long sen- tences, but he does not dare to deny the words of Lord Salisbury I quoted, and yet he says that I made afoul attaa. I repeat it, gentlemen. (Cheers.) Lord Salisbury did say that his remedy for Ireland was 20 , years of repression and the banishment —.he called 'lt removal (laughter) —of a million of 'lrishmen out of the land of their birth —(" shame ") —at a cost of fifty millions of money. As somebody has said here to- night, if Lord Salisbury and the Tory lords were to go out of the country themselves we could manage very well without them. (Loud cheers.) But we want Irishmen to live in their own country, peace- ful, prosperous, and contented, and that is what Mr. Gladstone is going to effect. (Cheers.) Well then, I shall wait of Dr.Mackie. I challenge Dr. Mackie in this hall and from this platform to say plainly, did I speak the truth or did I not. (" Yes," and cheers, and a Voice; Re says he is neutral in politico,'

div.p: Loud laughter.) We know what neutral in poli- tics means. (Hear, hear.) • It is what John Bright said of an American, "he is slantingdicular—(loud laughter)—and he always leans the wrong way.'' (Renewed laughter.) Well, there has been imported into Warrington this week another gentleman. My friend, Mr. R. W. Murray—(hisses, and a voice "Tit-bits '') 7-comes here to help to turn me out. (" He cannot," and-" He has turned himself out.") He comes here to help to put Sir Gilbert Greenall in for Warrington. (Hisses.) Well, we know some- thing about my friend Mr. Murray. When Mr. Murray was in Warrington, when he lived herel, he did precious little for the Liberal party. He would hardly lift his little fincter to assist us; and as treasurer of the Liberal Association, -never received one shilling from that man. (" Shame.") There is a gentleman rolling, in wealth, a far richer man than I am, and he never gave me one shilling to help us in fighting the Liberal .battles. (Hear, hear.) And what are his antecedents? He fought as a soldier in the Confederate army in the States.. .He fought for slavery against freedom. . (Cheers.) I repeat it; remember this, gentlemen, on the day of election, he fought for slavery against freedom. Is that the man that is to come here and • tell you that you are not to vote for me, and that you are to vote for Sir Gilbert Greenall ? (" No.") gentlemen he is fighting against liberty now. (Hear, hear.). We are.fighting the battle of freedom; we are going to free the Irish nation from tyranny, and we are going to unite Ire- land and Great Britain in a union stronger and closer than ever it has been in the memory of man. (Cheers.) I love my Irish fellow-countrymen, and I want to gain their love and affection. Wawill bind them to us in bonds of love and affection and chains , that shall never be broken. (Hear, hear.) The Irish I nation has a large and a good heartin it, and if the Irish nation is properly treated it will be a help and a strength to England that she has never had before. (Cheers.) Mr. Murray says in his Speech that if I would promise to vote against my great leader, Mr. Gladstone, be tvould- promise not to come to War- rington: (" Oh, oh," and laughter.)' He must think himself a very great • man. (Laughter.) Why', I would not promise to vote against Mr. Gladstone for ten hundred thousand Mr. Murrays. (Pro- tracted cheering.) I do not fearf gentlemen, if they bring every Ulster man that there is. (Hear, hear.) They may bring every jack mail of them into Warrington if they like. I -stand, as I said the other night, upon a rock, and it is immovable. I am your candidate, and I will be your representative. • (Loud cheers.) Ido not want to occupy too much time—(".,go on ")—but you have no idea of the effect it has upon I a man speakingto an audience like this.. The re- ception that you gave to me, the affection y6u show to me is so great that I feel as if I could speak the whole night to you. (Laughter and cheers.) Well, gentlemen, the Tories are patting my old and tried friend, that venerable patriot, John Bright, on the shoulder. They ought to have patted him on the shoulder long ago. (Hear, hear.) They have slan- dered him, they have called him every name they could think of, they have abused him in the most abominable manner, and now they are trying to put their hand upon his shoulder. I love and I respect John Bright to-day as much as I ever did in my life. (Hear, hear.) There never was a nobler patriot born than John Bright; and let me just .for one minute give you this—it is the only extract I shall read., (Hear, hear, and laughter.) :You have got it on the walls, but for fear any of • you may not have:: seen it I will read you this one passage in' John Bright's own words on April 2nd, 1819 :—" The Ulster men' have stood in the way , of improvements in the franchise, in the Church, and in the land question. They hive purchased Protestant as- cendency, and the price paid for it is the ruin and degradation of their couutfy." (Hear, hear.) Gentle-. men, I went to meet our great leader at the War- rington station—(loud cheers)—and it did my heart good, and it did good to the heart of every man that was there to see the fine spirit and pluck of our great leader. (Hear, hear.) He lifts his head undaunted and unafraid, and his eye is as bright as I e'er saw it in my life. (Hear, hear.) We have got the grandest leader that any party in this country ever had, and it will be a scandalous shame if we, the men of Lancashire, do not rise as one man and carry every Liberal member in Lanca- shire to support our great and glorious leader in the next Parliament. (Prolonged cheers.) Mr. CROSFIELD then moved a vote of thanks to Mr. c'Percy,. "the future member for Wigan " (cheers)—andto Mr. Trow, who had come all the way from pfulington to speak to them that night. The vote of thanks *as cordially passed, and in responding, Mr. Percy moved a similar vote to the Chairman, which was also heartily accorded. The meeting, ,one of great enthusiasm throughout, then terminated.

div.head: LOCAL DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: LOCAL DIVORCE CASE.

On Monday, Sir Janos llannen and a common jury had before them the case of Marsden v. Marsden and Deeley, in which John Marsden, an iron merchant at Liverpool, sought a divorce by reason of the adultery of his wife with the co respondent, Wm. Deeley. There was practically no denial, and the only question for the jury was the assessment of damages. The marriage took place in December, 1877, after which the parties cohabited at Thornfield, near Huyton. Petitioner, who for many years had been a member of the Kirkdale Burial Board, made the anquaintance of the co-respondent on his being added to the body some few years back, and last year was at Mr. Mars- den's to tea, when be made the acquaintance of the respon- dent. Last year, whilst on a visit to Sonthport, respondent told petitioner that she had met his friend Deeley, and after that she was absent all one day, and refused to explain where she had been to. In April the petitioner was stav- ing at the Bath Hotel, and observing that Deelev was "prowling about," he spoke to his wife on the subject, and caused his solicitor to send a letter to the co-respondent. Subsequently he asked his wife not to see Deeley again, when she wrote on a piece of paper that Deeley loved her and that she loved him, and she therefore declined to do as he asked her. Information afterwards came to his know- ledge that his wife, with Deeley, had been to the Tipping Arms at Bold, and to the Farmer's Arms, near Huyton, under circumstances leaving no doubt as to their guilt, and he separated from his wife. Subsequently he found a num- ber of letters which had been written by the co-respondent to his wife, commencing "Dear, darling Annie," and ending, "Your devoted William," "My own darling Annie," and "Your own dear darling, affectionate husband, William.".._. After formal evidence in proof of the petitioner's case, the jury assessed the damages it f5OO, and his lordship pro- nounced a decree nisi with costs.

" George was too happy to think anything strange just then, and he signed the paper with a trembling hand and a bursting heart. Then she laid her ear against his middle vest button, and they were very, very happy. "Tell me, darling," said George, after a long delicious silence, "why did you want me to sign that paper? Do you not repose implicit confidence in I my love for you?" " Ah, yes," she sighed, with infinite content, "indeed I do! But, George dear, I have be en befooled so many times ' " 1

NOTES BY THE WAY. Amid a scene of excitement at Lord's on SaturdaY• the Australians gained a victory over Middlesex by one wick% The match was full of interest and was the hardest strugg"" the Australians have had during their present tour. On Tuesday the cricket at Lord's was quite without terest, the defeat of the M.C.C. being certain. The chili' was No weak in batting to make anything of a fight, all', before half-past four the game was over, Cambridge winhin" by an innings and 44 suns. On Tuesday afternoon at Chichester the Australians beat by eight wickets the team selected by Lord March. The play lasted only two, hours and A half, and in that time 0. teen wickets fell for 122 rues. Lancashire on Wednesday finished a match with Oxford University, winning by nine wickets. The cnly interest ill the game was whether the University men would says the innings defeat. They bitted very steadily, but when eveo wickets were down for 160 the probabilities seemed againl them. Arnall-Thompson, however, by plucky hitting, ea"; the innings, and Lancashire had to get 16 runs, which Cos one wicket. be' At Moreton-in-the-Marsh on Wednesday, in the match s tween Gloucestershire and!Notts, Shrewsbury played a Mg; nificent not-out innings of 227 against Gloucester. He /14„t at the wickets seven hours and three-quarters, and did Ilya give a chance until 120, and at 164 he was badly missed la the long field. His hits were fifteen 4's, twelve S's• thirty-four 2's. The match was, of course, drawn. About an hour's play on Wednesday morning at Shee44d was sufficient to bring the Match between Yorkshire al3 Surrey to a condlusion, Surrey gaining an easy victory hi, seven wickets.

RUSSIA AND TURKEY. CONEIT&NTINOPLIZ, SATURDAY. The Porte has not yet replied to the Russiem note communicated by M. Onou, Councillor to the Rus3ian Embassy, complaining of the vio- lation, by Prince Alenander, of the Organic Statute of East- ern Ronmelia. The note, after enumerating all the various instances in which the statute has been violatA, insists that it is the duty of the Porte to protest against these ac- tions on the part of his Highness. In diplomatic circles the note is regarded as a fresh proof of Russia's intention to Overturn -Prince.Alexander. FRANCE. LYONS, SATURDAY.—AI. Lockroy, Minister of Commerce, Who is stayinc here, to-day received the members of the Chamber of Commerce, and, in addressing them, declared himself 'a strong advocate of Free Trade, at the same time admitting that he was bound by the sentiments of the majority of the Chamber, which was in favour of Pro- tection. ',NISM IN SPAIN.

REPUBLIC A_ em MADRID, SUNDAY. A considerable sensation has been Caused in political circles, and much displeasure in Court and Catholic circles, by the declaration which a Republican deputy, Senor Ascarate, drew from Senor Segasta in the de- bate on the Address yesterday. The Prime Minister said if he found himself some day in presence of a Republican ma- jority in Parliament which legally signified its intention of altering the form of Government he would submit to the decision of the national sovereignty manifested by its repre- sentatives. The Ministerial majority and the Republicans loudly cheered Senor Sa.gasta's bold utterances. THE WEST COAST OF AFRICA.—THE WHITES BOYCOTTED. CAMEROONS, MAY 23.—Aftairs are in a very unsatisfac- tory state here. The natives have boycotted all the whites, and refuse to trade with them or supply them with any food. No white man can buy a fowl or a bullock, and the natives have barred the way to the fresh water, so that the 'whites have to depend upon rain for all the water they re- quire. Large numbers of the factories up the river are closed, and the traders are sending their working staffs home. The natives aro determined that the German Governrcent shall derive no advantage from the port. They are paying up all the debts they owe to the white traders, but are doing no fresh business. THE UNITED STATES. CHICAGO, SUNDAY.—Further details of the strike on the Lake Shore Railroad state that the strikers, assisted by a riotous mob, obstructed the freight traffic during the whole of yesterday. Only one small freight train succeeded in reaching a point 20 miles south of Chicago. The strikers throw cars across the railroad and pursue trains with the engines they have captured. Two policemen and five of the rioters were wounded yesterday, and about 30 arrests were made.

BELGIUM. WEDNESDA.Y.—The strike among miners in this district again threatens to become general. This morning work ceased at s2veral of the pits at Paturages, Quaregon,, and Wasmes. The men remain quiet. GERMANY. Bnlturr, WEDNESDAY. —This morning's newspapers con- firm the reported expulsion from this city of Herr Singa, the Social Democrat and member of the R3lchstag. He must leave by noon on Saturday next. THE NETHERLANDS. TIIE 'HAGUE, WEDNESDAY.—M. DOrnei9. Niewenhuis, the Socialist leader, who .en the 10th hist was convicted of having used insulting language towards the King and was condemned to ens year's solitary confinement, to-day de- clared his intention of appealing against the sentence.

TRIPLE MITADER.—David Jeanson, sm of a master builder, was charged at Llandaff, on Monday, with ths attempted murder of John Gavin, Thomas Kellow' and George Mille. About ten o'clock on Saturday night the three men were crossing a field near the new cemetery, when they observed the prisoner seated on the grass with a young woman. Mills and his companions went behind the hedge, _and the prisoner and the young woman then arose and pro- ceeded to walk across the field. Mills told him there was no footpath there, and ordered them back. The prisoner thereupon drew a revolver and fired several shots at the men, Gavin being struck in the head, Mills in the hip, and Kel- low in the thigh. The injured men were conveyed to the Infirmary. Gavin is in a critical state, and his depositions have been taken. The prisoner was remanded.
