THE WAAL PROCLAMATIONS. On Saturday afternoon, the eleventh Parliament, in the fiftieth year of her Majesty's reign, was dissolved by Royal proclamation, and at the same time a new Parliament was by Royal command summoned by writs to assemble at Westminster on Thursday. August the sth next. The Queen had the necessary Priv3r Council for the final sanction of the dissolution at Windsor Castle at three o'clock on Satur- day afternoon, and Earl Spencer (Lord Preeideet of the Council), Lord Rosebery (Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs), and Earl Sydney, with Mr. Lenn.ox Peel (Clerk of the Council) in attendance, travelled, on Satur- day afternoon, at one o'clock, by special train from Paddington. There was a considerable gather- ing of people on the platform at Windsor, but nothing in the shape of a demonstration took place on the departure of the Ministers to attend the Council. After luncheon at the Castle the Council was held, and shortly after three o'clock her Majesty signed the Royal pi oclamation dissolv- ing her eleventh Parliament and commanded the assembly of the twelfth Parliament of her reign. The moment this was done a telegram was despached with all speed to the Privy Council Office in Whitehall, and thence was con- eyed to Mr. Muir Mackenzie, at the Crown Office, West- minster. Upon the receipt of this telegram the Crown Office instantly issued the Royal Proclamations, which had been prepared for some time, and were ready to be de- spatched, and which were published in a supplement to the "London Gazette "of Saturday evening. The " Gazette " also contained an Order in Council dissolving the Convoca- tions of Canterbury and York. A Royal proclamation is likewise issued for the election of sixteen peers of Scotland at Holyrood House on July 20th. Orders in Council are published for the issue of writs for elections for a new Par- liament to assemble on August sth, and for electiog new members of Convocations. The writs for the election of the new Parliament are made returnable on Thursday, the sth August, but it is probable that unless the country should pronounce an advet se judg- ment on Mr. Gladstone'a Government, Parliament will be prorogued from that date until October. The writs were despatched at four o'clock on Satard ty afternoon front the Crown Office. Those for the metropolis by sne.cial messen- gers to be delivered by hand, and those for the country to the post office by special messengers. As regards Ireland a separate telegram was despatched after the Council at Windsor to the Lord Chancellor at Dublin Castle, and similar steps to those in London were taken for the publica- tion of Her Majesty's commands.

• MI GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO MAN- CHESTER. Mr. Gladstone passd a good night at the residence of Mr. William Agnew, Summer Hill, Pendleton, and on Saturday morning was in good health, but had not recovered his voice. About noon a deputation from the Liberals of Salford waited upon him, and presented an address to him on the lawn. The Pre- mier left Manchester for Liverpool at four o'clock. Mr. Gladstone and his party left Mr. Agnew's resi- dence about a quarter to three o'clock and drove through the principal streets of Salford, being re- ceived with great enthusiasm by large crowds. Driving to the Manchester Town Hall, he thanked the Mayor for the manner in which the arrangements for his -visit had been carried out, and then drove to the Exchange Station. MR. GLADSTONE IN LIVERPOOL Mr. Gladstone addressed a meeting in Ilengler's Circus, Liverpool, on Monday afternoon. He re- ceived a most enthusiastic welcome from a vast and most influential audience. Mr. R. D. Holt, chair- man of the Liberal Association, presided. Mr. J. LOVELL read an address to Mr. Gladstone from 24 Liberal Associations in Liverpool and the neighbourhood. The address referred to the past labours of the Premier, and expressed strong hopes that he would be able to crown them by giving to Ireland a measure fraught with peace and con-

tentment. Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to the address, and re- ferring to the various means by which the contest they were now engaged in was carried on, said the factor upon which he chiefly relied for victory was argument, and lie had been constantly surprised by the Nteakness of the arguments .advanced by the opponents of the Government measures. He held in his hand a copy of the manifesto of the "Paper Unionists," in which it was stated that the local Irish were about to be thrust out of their allegiance to Parliament. On the contrary the whole Irish people were going to remain in its allegiance to the i Crown, n its allegiance to the Imperial Parlia- ment, at whose hands it asked, and was prepared thankfully to receive, the gift of a legislative body -sitting under statutory authority for the control of properly and exclusively Irish affairs. (Cheers.) It was also stated in the paper he was referring to that the Land Purchase Bill would involve anex- pendrture of millions of public money, but be Was prepared to throw that bill up if any such pro- visions were to be found therein. To spend money was one thing, to invest it was quite another, and he should have thought that some of the gentlemen who had Signed that paper, with Lord Derby at the head of them, knew pretty well the difference be- tween spenfl.ing and investing. (Laughter and cheers.) T. his was a question' of Ib.e wealthier _a g,wa classesionlsi theld nation b t t the venough ms e she oge f hset wealthieroofnunity td d classesf ,ae termination to overbear constitutionally at the polls the resistance of these classes? Lord Randolph Churchill had, he Was told, had a good deal to say about him, though he had not been careful to inform* himself of has opinions. His own opinion of him i was that f they could cut out of him about one- half the qualities he possessed they might make ; from the other half a valuable and distinguished public servant. (Loud laughter and cheers.)- Well, Lord Randolph Churchill had said " Governments , will do wrong, Parliament's will do wrong, classes I will do wrong, society will do wreng, and the Pall Mall clubs always do wrong, but the people do not go wrong ;" so they sass. -„,what Randolph's opinion was as to the sympathies of . the .masses. He was aboiA to make a threefold appeal to the English people, not to Liberals alone. He (Mr. Gladstone) appealed to their prudence, to their courage, and to their sense of honour. First, to their prudence. Had , they considered the present condition of Parliament? ' Manya mail had at heart some question closely asso- ciated with his interests in life, and many a man had perhaps still more nearly at heart many a question closely connected with the welfare of the country. Were they satisfied with the capacity which Parlia- ment had lately shown for dealing with these ques- tions? (" No, no.") Hitherto the Irish Nationalists had had no backing. Would that be so now ?("No.") Ireland was, in fact, mistress of the situation, and would continue to be so until we consented to some arrangement dictated by policy and Justice and humanity. So much for the appeal to prudence. Then he 'would appeal' to the courage of the Eng- lish nation. There had been placed before them again and again an imaginary danger, that if they gave to Ireland a. great boon the Irish were such a set of fools as not to receive it in their own inter- ests in a Proper manner; and further, the Irish were supposed to be such .a set of monsters as to make the gift simply the basis of hostile operations against England. Suppose it came to hostilities, how were the `two countries situated? 11.-eland had population of five millions, poor. Without public establishments, without any .army or a navy, and without any title or any power under the proposed bill .to create an army or a navy. Stich were the formidable antagdnists which England had We to contend with. And bow did England stand ? had a population of thirty millions, constantly in- creasing, well knit together, with a powerful army, an all powerful army, and a people to which they were about to add a strength it had never had before—the strength of a just cause. (Cheers.) Then he would appeal to the honour of England. It had been a Matter of pain much more than surprise to him that in this controversy on the side of their opponents the honour of England was never maintained. He had heard enough of honour in his lifetime to make a i man sick, if it were possible, of the very word, but t had always been honour pleaded as an excuse for bloodshed. - Was there no honour save that which caused the sword to be unsheathed? When he opened- the question in the House of Commons he said very little about. the Act of Union for two reasons. First of all, because, looking at the facts, i whatever that act might have been in ts beginning, he did not think it could safely or wisely be blotted out of the Statute Book, but chiefly because he ,did not wish to expose to the world Our shame. But the opposition to the bills had compelled him to unveil the truth, and so far as he could judge, he grieved to say in the presence of distinguished Irishmen that he knew of no blacker or fou4er chapter in the his- tory of man than the making, of that Union. Cheers.) The Union was followed by a long cata- logue of bad consequences, broken promises, the passing, of bad laws, restrained liberties, and the shameful ;postponement of relief of crying griev- ances. We had hitherto given to force that which had been denied to justice, but it was high time we should think of the question of honour and Set about the sacred and overpowering duty of effacing—if efface it we could—that terrible stain -which the acts of England had left upon her fame. • (Cheers.) He would ask the Tories to remember that the bill .was not a Radical measure. They were not invent- ing- something new which was the device of Radi- calism, but doing that which the Conservatives were always boasting that they were doing's-restoring

div.head: 'THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 3, 1886.
div.p: 'THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 3, 1886.

that which was old. (Laughter and cheers.) He entreated them—the people a this country—to be- think themselves of the position in which they stood—to look back upon the history of the past, and forward into the prospects .of the future—to determine that it should no longer, be said of En' land, as it was now habitually said throughout the civilised world—that Ireland was the Poland of 'England. Let them determine not to have a Poland any longer. We had had it long enough, and now let them listen to prudence, to courage, and, speak- ing the words of the poet, Ring out the old, ring in the new. ring out the notes and the memory of discord, ring in the blessed reign and time of peace. (Cheers.)
THE ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Thomas Wade; aft.r attending a meeting in support of thn Liberal candidate for Colchester, on Monday nigbt, fell tiown dead immediately be reached home. He had been very

excited. Mr. Gladstone, notwithstanding his recent exertions, is quite well. He attended early service at Hawarden Church, and during the remainder of Tuesday rested. The date of his return to London is uncertain. Mr. Gladstone has addressed a letter to Sir Robert Peel in support of his candidature for Inverness Burghs. Sir Robert left a safe seat at Blackburn because of his accept- ance of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule policy. The Gladstonian election fund, which is being raised at the National Liberal Club, now amounts to over £2,000, and on Monday the committee decided to make grams in aid of the expenses of a number of Parliamentary candidates. A correspondent haying sent to Lord R. Churchill a copy of a statement by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, that hie lordship's manifesto was packed from top to bottom with falsehoods, Lerd Randolph replies that in his opinion no words of Mr. Herbert Gladstone are worth the notice of any one. Some amusement has been caused by the appearance, in two of the divi• ions of Edinburgh, of two candidates, bear- ing the historic name of Wallace. Both also bear the , Cbristian name of Robert, both are barristers-at•law from London, and both are vehement supporters of Mr. Glad-

stone. On Saturday evening Mr. R. H. Grindley. for several years editor of the "Liverpool Albion," and for the last three years editor of the "Birmingham Daily Gazette," sud- denly expired on the platform of a Conservative meeting in Birmingham, where be had concluded a speech a few minutes before. At the fortnightly meeting of the Irish National League, in Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. Harrineton announced that the receipts since the last meeting amounted to £6,185 for the Parliamentary fund, and a telegram had been received stat- ing that an additional £12,000 had been placed to their credit by their friends in the United States Mr. Chamberlain, writing to a Walsall Congregational minister, says it is a great pleasure to him to have the sup- port of Nonconformists at a time like the present, when the hasty and ill-considered proposals of the Government have endangered the supremacy of Parliament, which in this country is a guarantee of our civil and religious liberties. On Monday night, when Mr. W. Redmond, the Parnellite candidate for ?North Fermanagh, was returning from a meet- ing at Tempo, with his friends, an attack was made by Orangemen. The Nationalists, who occupied a drag, had the worst of the fight which ensued, until the police arrived and made a number of arrests. Disturbances were renewed subsequently, and many of the rioters were infured. , The address of the Protestant Home Rule Association was issued on Friday. The authors say :—lt is not our desire to separate ourselves from our Catholic fellow countrymen. We ask countenance and support in order to counteract the [gross misrepresentation which alleges that the Protestants of [ Ireland are unanimously opposed to the Irish policy of Mr. [ Gladstone. We reject with scorn the calumny that the lives and liberties of Protestant Irishmen would be im- perilled by the restoration of an Irish Parliament. The Council of the Metropolitan Radical Association have issued an address to all Radical electors, in which they say: —0 The great question before you at this crisis is whether Ireland shall manage her own affairs. For centuries she has been robbed, insulted, and oppressed by the British ruling claasee. Will you, the democracy of Great Britain, i aid the democracy of Ireland, or once more hand over that ' unhappy country to political bandits, whose only policy is systematic coercion? That is the question before you, and wa appeal to you for a wise and just answer. At the meetieg of the Southwark branch of the Irish National League, held on Sunday night, a deputation at- tended on behalf of Cardinal Manning and read the follow- ing statement :—" Archbishop's House, Westtninster, June H.—Reverend arid dear Father,—l am desired by the Arch- bishop to inform you that the use of his name in Mr. Dar- ling's handbills, classing his Eminence with the opponents of Home Rule, is contrary to the truth. His Eminence has already always avoided mixine, in politics by reason of the office that be bears, but this mischievous misstatement com- pels him to put it in your power to say that while preserv- ing the integrity of the Empire and the sovereignty of the Imperial Parliament, be has always been in favour of giving to Ireland the power of administering its own local affairs as d'stirct from the affairs of the Empire. You may make , any use yo ri think fit of this letter.—Believe me, yours very I faithfully, JAMES GUIRON, Assistant Secretary to the Rey. W. Fleming, Hackney." OPPOSITION TO LORD HARTINGTON. Mr. R. C. Richards, president of the National Reform Union, cotton manufacturer, of Kirkham, and chemical manufacturer, of St. Helens, was an- nounced to addrees a Liberal meeting at Damp, on Monday evening, with a view of becoming a candidate for the Rossendale division in opposition to Lord Hartington. The announcement created considerable excitement in the division, as it was understood that his lordehip was to have a walk over. On Monday night a meeting of Liberal electors was held at Bacup. The following resolution was carried, with only one dissentient, in a very crowded meeting : " This meeting of the Liberal electers of Bacup desires to express its hearty approval of the proposals with regard to Ireland. It protests against Lord Hartington being returned to Parliament as the representative for Rossendale, seeing that his views are entirely opposed to the opinions of the large majority of Rossendale Liberals. It also expresses its determination to secure support Red return a candidate, if possible. who will assist Mr. Gladstone in the solution of the Irish difficulty." A resolution declaring Mr. Richards a ' fit and proper person to represent the division was carried with a like 'result. Mr. Richards, however, afteryeircs with- drew his candidature. On Wednesday night, at a crowded meetieg of Rossendale Liberals at Reistenstall much indignation was expressed at the sudden withdrawal from the constituency of Mr. Richards, who is announced RS the second Gladstonian can- didate for Bolton. It was stated that Mr. Thomas Newbig- ging, civil engineer, of Manchester, and a native of Rossen- dale, had definitely promised to oppose Lord Hartington, and a resolution in Mr. Newbigging's favour was carried with enthusiasm wills only four dissentients. Mr. Michael Devitt will address a meeting on his behalf at Rewtenstall early next week.

MR GLADSTONE AND THE LATE TORY CABINET. The followirg corresponaence bearing on the over- tures made be, Mr. Gladstone to the Salisbury Cabinet touchine the Irish question has been furnished for publi- cation : "Deer Mr. B slfour,—lt is intimated by Mr. Labouchere in the enclosed paragraph that while a member of the Salis- bury Government you laid before the Government, as from Mr. Gledstone. propositione for the non-partisan support to be given by Mr. Gladstone to measuree for the settlement of the Irish question, and that it was on the rejection of these propositions by the Salisbury Cabinet that Mr. Gladstone felt bound tn press his own Irish Home Rule measures. May I ask if this is correct?--Yery truly yours, W. lire', EERT —June 23rd." "Dear Mr. Hurlbert.—Stated in that way, I should say the assertion was misleading. On the 20th of December, 1385, Mr. Gladetone wrote me a letter in which he expressed a desire that the Irish question should be dealt with by the then existing Government, intimating that in that case his desire would be to treat any proposal they might make in the same epic it in which he had treated their action in Af- ghanistan and the Balkan Peninsula, reserving to himself, however, all necessaty freedom. There was nothing in that letter to indicate what scheme he was prepared to support, and the words used, taken by themselves, and without the commentary supplied by Mr. Herbert Gladstone's indiscre- tions, woulia have covered a policy of ;coercion as well as a policy of Home Rule. It should be recollected that the only indications publicly given of Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy at that time were contained in his Midlothian speeches, and that in the course of these speeches he took occasion to ask the country to give him an overwhelming Liberal mejority, in order that he might himself have a free hand in dealing with the Irish problem. It is curious to note that while one of the accusations made against the Conservative party is that, for the sake of office they were• prepared to coquet with the Parnellites, and themselyes to take up the question of Home Rule, their unhesitating rejection of Mr. Gladstone's overtures conclusively proves that office to be held on the tenure of carrying out the Irish policy, hinted at by Mr. Gladstone, had no attractions for them. One would also like to know why Mr. Gladstone. if he bad made up his mind on Home Rule, did not boldly raise that issue on the Queen'* Speech, and turn the Go- vernment out on it (if be could), rather than snatch a divi- sion on a subordinate question with which Lord Salisbury's Government were :solemnly pledged to deal.—Very truly yours, A. J. BALFOrri —June 23rd." Mr. Gladstone has addressed the following to Mr. Bright —"I regret to read this morning your published statement in a letter to Mr. Ryland*, that a Year ago all Liberals held his opinione on the Irish question. Without losing a mo- ment, I bee you either riublicly to except me from this as- sertion, or give proofs of what you say. Never since Home Rule eves started, 15 years ago, have I once condemned it in principle, or held in any way, the opinions of Mr. Rylaeds, which, to speak frankly, I think absurd." SPEECHES. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, at Bristol, on Saturday, said that in our colonies no stateman's name was received with greater dislike—he might almest say execration—than that of Mr. Gladstone, whose policy tended to the disintegration of the Empire. Sir George 0. Treyelyan Commenced his candidature for the Border But ghs on Monday evening at"Galashiels. He wanted to settle the relations between Great Britain and , Ireland on other grounds besides those which would only I conciliate Mr. Parnell. The fact was, the Government ought

never to have introduced such a colossal measure, and he could not by any means support it. Mr. Jacob Bright addressed a meeting of the members of the Hulme Irieh National League Club on Saturday even- ing. He said the English and the Irish had too long occu- pied separate camps. Theobjects of sagacious and honest Irishmen were the same as those of sagacious and honest Englishmen. He believed they would henceforth work to- gether, and he might prophesy that in the future nothing would keep them separate as tilt y had been. Lord R. Cnurchill, in an address to his supporters in South Paddington on Saturday night, undertook to defend his extraordinary election address, which, he said, contained one supreme merit, and one alone, that from end to end there was not a sentence or a line or a word which was not gospel truth. The reason why Mr. Gladstone had brought forward his present remedy for Irelapd's ills was that he needed the support of the 85 Irish members in order that his Govern- ment might be retained in Downing-street. Mr. Herbert Gladstone stopped at Exeter on Saturday afternoon, on his way to St. Austell, and spoke in support of the candidature of Mr. Johnson.—At the St. Austell meeting. held in support of Mr. Borlase, Mr. Herbert Glad- stone said there were possible dangers in the Premier's policy, but dangers were inevitable to any great measure. Ireland would not become prosperous and contented at once, but it would pave the way to prosperity by giving leer a settlement and freedom from the agitation which had so long cursed her. Mr. John Morley addressed a meeting at New- castle on Saturday, and said the proposition laid down by Mr. John Bright, that no Parliament could be more power- I ful or so great in Ireland as the united Parliament sitting at Westminster. though it sounded plausible, would not bear investigation. How was it that two bills of consider- able importance coming from the people of Ireland and ap- proved by the great majority of England and Scotch mem- bers, had been praztically thrown out by the House of Lords ? He referred to the Labourers' Cottages Bill, and the bill to provide compensation to tenants for trees planted by themselves. The Land Purchase Bill was part of the machinery of the Government plan, and like the other bill, was open to modification. Lord Randolph Churchill visited Manchester on Wednes- day and addressed two meetings. the first in the Hulme Town Hall, the second in the Free Trade Hall. To the Hulme meeting, which was held in the after- noon, he drove in an open carriage from the railway station, where he arrived at three o'clock. At the station, and along the line of route, which had been marked out for his lord- ship, a large number of persons bad assembled, and by them he was loudly cheered. Occasionally hooting mingled with the cheering. In the afternoon speech Lord Randolph urged. that the difficulty of the Irish question at the present day was essentially a Parliamentary difficulty, to the origin of which he directed particular attention. The evening proceedings were most enthusiastic. The Free Trade Hell, Manchester,was crowded to excess, and his lordship spoke for more than an hour. In his speech he took up several points raised in speeches of Mr. Gladstone. He touched also upon the question of Irish Aimee, spoke of the almost unparalleld political combination which now obtained, and urged that political weight and political dignity depended to i large extent Upon political consistency, and that no- thing had occurred during the last six months to lead the country to reverse the adverse verdict then pronounced upon Mr. Gladstone's policy. Mr. Parnell addressed a crowded and enthusiastic meeting at the St. James's Hall, Manchester, on Tuesday evening, held tender the auspices of the Manchester Liberal Club. Mr. Jacob Bright was in the chair. In the course of his address Mr. Parnell, after answering some of the objections raised to Home Buie for Ireland, referred at some length to his interview with Lord Carnarvon and to Lord Salisbury's account of the traosaction. He maintained that his own version of the interview was accurate in every respect, and said that his accuracy could be confirmed by Mr. Justin M'Carthy, to whom both himself and Lord Carnarvon com- municated their general impressions. He re-asserted that as the result of that interview the Land Purehase Act of the late Govemment was passed, and that all the circum- stances of the case bore out the truth of his assertions. Mr. Parnell went on to say that Mr. Wilfred Blunt was specially recommended to him by Lord R. Churchill as a Conservative Home Ruler. Mr. Blunt invited him by letter to meet Lord R. Churchill at his country house. That in- vitation he declined, because he intended, if he had any dealings with the leaders of the Conservative party, to have them with honourable men. Mr. Michael Devitt also ad- dressed the meeting, and a resolution was passed expressing confidence in Mr. Gladstone, and ceiling on all Liberals to support the six Liberal candidates for Manchester at the poll. Lord Hartington, on Saturday evening, addressed a large meeting of Unionists in the Town Hall, Paisley. He said it was a fact that the Liberal party was now divided, but his faith and trust was that it would yet preserve strength and vitality, and bold the affections and confidence of the people at large, so that when its services were most required for the interests of the country they would be submitted, and present as bold and strong a front to the country as the party had ever done in the Past The Prime Minister was never tired of telling us that the union between Great I Britain and Ireland was brought about by force and fraud. If this new eonstitution was imposed upon the Protestants of Ulster, it wculd be imposed not by fraud but by force. The whole policy of the Government seemed to him to be founded upon a policy of despair. The Marquis of Hartington visited Sheffield on Monday, for the purpose of taking part in a Unionist demonstration in support of the candidature of Mr. F. W. Maude for the Attercliffe Division of the boreugh.—The noble Marquis was received, with cheers, followed by hostile demonstra- tions. He said it was requisite to consider, not only what the majority of the Irish people might happen to want, but what in our hearts and consciences we believed would be for the real prosperity and interests of he Irish people. If we gave to Ireland Parliamentary government, there would be a. Parliamentary opposition, and what better Cry could an Op- position to Mr. Parnell's Government have than that of complete independence, of the abolition of tribute, and the abolition of what they would describe as the degrading restrictions which Mr. Parnell now accepted? Mr. Parnell, speaking in support of the candidature of Mr. Conybeare on Saturday evening at Plymouth, rejoiced that the democracies of Scotland and England had joined hands. Lord Carnarvon had agreed with him (Mr. Parnell) on the main lines upon which a statutory Parliament might be given to Ireland. Mr. Parnell concluded: Lord Cameroon has stated that he spoke to me unofficially. Well, he has been asked by Mr. Gladstone to give his version of what he said to me, and what he eaid to Lord Salisbury afterwards. This request has been made by Mr. Gladstone not once but twice, and the British public are entitled to have an answer. (Cheers.) I have given my version of a portion of what took place at the interview ; let Lord Carnarvon give his. (Applause.) He says that he spoke to me unofficially. I want to know how much of what I said to him he com- municated to the Cabinet. Lord Cameroon, as the result of that interview, and as the result of what passed between us, gave me earnest of his official capacity during that in- terview- and very good earnest, too; he gave me five millions of money. (Applause and interruptions.) I say he gave me earnest of his official capacgy at the interview. (In- terruptions, caused by youths singing "Rule Britannia," which was met with cheers for Parnell.) Ah ! these gen- tlemen are afraid of hearing the truth. (Loud cheers.) He gave me earnest, not for myself, but for Irish landlorde, in the shape of five millions sterling, money of the British taxpayers, paid within a -seek after that interview. At my request, made at that interview, and at my strong re- commendation, he passed the Land Purchase Act, that would not otherwise have been passed, giving five millions of money to the Irish landlords. (Cheers.) Was that an official act or not—(loud cries of "Yes ")—arising out of that interview? (Cheers.)

RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN IRELAND. FIVE PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED. A Belfast correspondent, telegraphing on Weines• day afternoon, says: " A serious accident occurred this afternoon on the Great Northern Railway, near Portadown. Five persons were killed and many seriously injured, one of the former bein g a lady and the other a gentleman. It is feared that some of the injured cannot recover. The cause of the accident has not been definitely ascertained." Telegraphing in the evening the correspondent adds: The aceident was far more serious than was at first reported, four persons having been killed and six- teen severely injured. Some of the latter are not ex- pected to recover. The accident occurred about two miles below Portadown, at a spot where the line runs alongside a deep ditch. It is believed that the great heat of the past two days had caused the rails to ex • , pand, and on the 2-30 p.m. train from Portadown to I Dublin reaching that place the engine left the track I and dashed into the ditch, dragging with it the whole train save the guard's van, which from some unex- plained cause became detached, its occupant escaping unhurt, while the engine driver and stoker were pitched headlong into a meadow on the other side of the ditch, and were also uninjured. The two car- riages next the engine were telescoped and completely wrecked, and of the passengers four were killed out- right and sixteen others were injured, some, as already stated, beyond hope of recovery. Half a dozen medical men were quickly on the spot and did their best. The scenes were heartrending in the extreme. Several of the injured were sent to Belfast, among them being Police- sergeant Boaner, both legs broken ; Mrs Boaner, legs broken, and severely bruised; Bliss Henry (of Derry), one leg broken; and a man (name not known) apparently in a dying condition. Two gangers and the driver of the train which ran off the lino were on Thursday remanded at Portadown on the charge of manslaughter. It is stated that 270 " aleepers " had been found to be totally unpacked, ana tnat 41 of these were apparently rotten. An inquest was held at Portadown on Thursday on the bodies of the dead, and a verdict was retuned in accordance with the facts already published.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- men Davies and Pickmere, Mr. John Fairclough. DISTURBANCE IN THE MAREET.—DanieI Crosby was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Market- place, on Saturday afternoon, and with assaulting P.C. Chantler, in Market-street. —Prisoner was very violent, and kicked Mr. Place, the market inspector, who gave him into custody. He was carried to the police station, and kicked officer Chantler on the way. It was his 48th appearance for various offences, and Chief Constable Hunt said that he knew him to be a very violent character while under the influence of drink.—The magistrates sent him to prison for a month.--Edward Crosby was charged with being drunk and disorderly in the Market-place, on Saturday, and with assaulting Reuben Tims, a bailiff, who was assisting the police.—Prisoner, whose conduct was described as very vio- lent, was said to be the brother of prisoner Daniel Crosby-- There were a number of previous convictions against him, and he was committed to prison for a month. DRUNKENNESS.—The following were dealt with for drunkenness :—George Marsh, in Whittle-street, on Satur- day, fined 5s and costs; Cornelius Nolan, in Lower Bank- street, on Saturday, ordered to pay 2s costs; Timothy Blabar, in James-streef, on Saturday night, fined 5s and costs; James Sullivan, in Bridge-street, dismissed on promis- ing to leave the town; John Mannion and Patrick Mannion, in Bridge-street, on the 21st-ult, fined ss, including costs, each • M tria Shields, in Orford-lane, on the 24th ult., dis- miss:el on promising not to offend again. BREACH OF THE PEACE —Two men named Webb and I Miller were charged with committing a breach of the peace I by fighting in Fennell-street, on the 19th ult.' and were bound over to be of good behaviour for six months. THEFr OF CROCKERY.—Three boys named Garritty, Kelly, and Rafferty, a girl named Ann McCoan, and a young woman named Margaret Burns, were charged with stealing a quantity of plates and dishes that were formerly used by a horticultural and floral society, and that had been stored in ; premises on friar's-gate —The Bench only recorded ; Victim

• TllMAY.—Before Councillor C. Broadbent and Mr. R. Garnett. CIIZATING THE R&ILWAY COUPANY.—Joseph McKhty, who said he was a militiaman, was charged with riding on the London and North-Western Railway, from Wigan to Warrington, without a ticket, with intent to defraud the company. He was fined 5s and costs, or seven days' im- prisonment. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclougb.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Thotnas Hinds, who was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Hill-street the preyious night, was fined 53 and costs.—A young woman named Catherine Dogherty, was charged with unlawfully refusing to perform the task of work set to her by the matron of the Warring- ton Workhouse and was sent to prison for 14 days. THURIDAY.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. Assauurs.—Alice Hunt was summoned for assaulting Matthew Hunt, her husband, on the morning of the 39,h ult. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant, and said that it appeared strange that a man should thus summons his wife, but he could not put up with her bad behaviour, which culminated on Wednesday morning with what might have been a very serious assault. The husband said that she ran at him with a knife, and attempted to strike him with a brush. Defendant was ordered to enter into recog- nisances to be of good behaviour for six months, or suffer two months' improvement.—Henry Belzey was sum- moned by his wife, Rachel, for assaulting her. He was bound over, in his own recognisances for three months, and ordered to pay Bs, the costs. Galum LlCENSES.—Licenses to sell frame were granted to J. M. Porter, Buttermarket-street and Market-hall ; Wil- liam Lawless, Corporation-street and Market-hall; and Ann Riley, Sankey-street. THREATS.—Ann Leonard was charged on a summons with using threats to Susannah Lee. The case was dismissed on defendant promising not to offend again, and paying the costs. MAINTENANCE.—Peter Williams was summoned to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for not contributing to the maintenance of his father, under an order made that he should pay 2s per week. Mr. Shearer proved the case. After hearing the statement of the defend- ant the Bench concluded that he was not in a position to pay and cancelled the order.
FRlDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison).

ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—Benkunin Rigby, level-hand puddler, employed at the works of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., living at 49, Aikin-street, was charged with assaulting his wife, Mary Rigby, on the previous day. He was re- manded until to-day (Saturday). A VIOLENT VAGIUNT.—A man named Callan was reman- ded until to-day (Saturday) on a °barge of doing wilful damage at the Workhouse.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TVESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greener.; E. Marson, d Broadbent, R. Pierpoint. H. Neild. A CARELESS DRlVlE.—Richard Hassell, a young man, was charged with having been asleep whilst in charge of two horses at Appleton on the 3rd June, and was fined 5s and costs. SCHOOL CASES.—The following persons were dealt with for not having sent their children regularly to school, viz.: —John Hatton, fined 55 • Win. Gleave, 5s ; James Bostock, ss; Richard liamblW, ss; Charles Deluce, ss; Charles Hignett, adjourned. TRESPASSING.—John Povey, a farm labourer, was charged with having trespassed in search of game on land in the oc- cupation of Thos. Warburton on the 17th June. He pleaded guilty, and it was given in eviaence that he had been seen to take a rabbit from a trap. Defendant stated that he had been employed by Mr. Warburton, but lost that situation owing to this offence. A fine of ss, including costs, was imposed.--Thomas Harrop wee charged with trespassing on land in the occupation of Wm. Bromilow, at Hatton, on ; the 28th May in search of moor hens. It was stated, how- ever, by thenlagistrates' clerk (Mr. Nicholson) that moor hens were not game, and the cap was consequently dis- missed. DRUNDENNESS.—John Culcairn was charged with having been drunk at Grappenhall, and was fined 103 and costs. A DOUBTFUL CASE.—Sarah Webster, a youn e woman, was charged with having stolen £O, belonging to fohn Lee. Appleton, on the 16th June. Mr. A. Browne, of Warring- ton, prosecuted, and Mr. Jenkins defended. It appeared from evidence given that prosecutor was a widower, and that on the sth February defendant went to live with him. She lived about a fortnight with him, but one evening when he returned from his work he found that she had gone, and, he alleged, had taken the money in question with her. In cross-exemination, however, he admitted that he and the defendant had lived immorally together, and ultimately the case was dismissed. VIOLENT CUiTOMERS.—Michael and James Murray, Thomas Maloney, and Roger Maloney were charged with disorderly conduct and refusine; to quit the licensed pre- mises of William Whitlow, at Preston Brook, en the 26th May.—Neither of the Maloneys put in an appearance, and the other two defendants were represented by Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington. It was stated that on the day referred to the four defendants had used instiltiag lenguage to the females in charge of the house, and consequently when Mr. Whitlow and his two sons returned they ejected them from the premises. It was stated that Jas. Murray's leg had been broken in the fray.—A fine of Sc and costs was imposed on James Murray, the other defendant who put in an appearance being discharged.

NEWTON ELECTION. On Saturday morning Sir George Errington was intro- duced to many of the prominent Liberals of St. Helens by Mr. J. B. Leach, and in the afternoon he visited Earles- town, where he received a most enthusiastic welcome. The train by which be journeyed arrived at Earlestown shortly after two o'clock, and there were then many hundreds of persons gathered in the vicinity of the station and its ap- proaches. As the train drew up in the station hearty cheers were given, and these were more lustily repeated as the candidate was received on the platform by Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P. (chairman of the Executive), Mr. G. W. Rawlins (Rainbill), and others. With some difficulty, owing to the many friends pressing around him, be made his way to a carriage which was waiting, and amid pro- longed cheering took his seat therein. As the carriage went

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 3, 1846,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 3, 1846,

.LORD DERI3Y made a thoughtful speech at J-Iverpool on Tuesday in defining the position °f. the Liberal Unionists ; but the weak point q.it----looked at with a view to statesmanship that it points no way out of the difficulty; offers no solution, of the Irish probletn. The ewildered citizen asks what is to be done; ,t1(1 Lord DERBY has no answer to give. All t e can say is that if re At 11.9. b zra.nted "c' TWA. nd this or that terrible thing ifily hap- -15.e- And undoubtedly the granting of a Par- laixtent to Ireland would be a disastrous mea- l'ilre if the Irish, as a people, were as bad as tdord DERBY would make them out to be. But '.Oglishmen do not believe that their brethren 4,cross the channel have inherited "a double ,uose of original sin ;" they are disposed to st as they would be trusted; and, having tied eighty.six years of Coercion with no E°od result, they are about to try what a few lean of Conciliation will do. Lord DERBY 8 quite right in saving that the question is on e. of such moment that it ought not to be troyled by any authority inferior to that of the allot). itself. That is the PRIME MINISTER'S plstification for advising a dissolution of Par- canlent ; he appeals to the nation; and it :18 for the nation to give an answer. Follow- in3the track of Lord SALISBURY, Lord Rltty urges that coercion is another name tOr civilisation,when it means "that men who I,reak the law should be coerced to keep it." lota what law? The ordinary, or the extra- rdinary law? Neither Irishmen nor Eng- Ishmen complain of the operation of the °rdinary law. What Irishmen protest against apd rebel against is the passing of special f'ets of Parliament to give special power to Interfere with the liberty of Irishmen :vhen they seek to embody the national pliiment, and enforce the demand for a 4rliaMent on Irish soil. The avowed 14'licy of the Tory party, as announced in the ouse of Commons on the 26th January last. "the suppression of the National League." tit this could not be done by the ordinary 4.W----the law which is "another name for ivilisation." Lord DERBY knows just as Well As Lord SALISBURY knows that a special Act would require to be passed; and that it ,‘vould be known in history as a Coercion Act. Lord DERBY makes what he seems to think is striking quotation from a speech delivered Y Mr. GLADSTONE in 1871 in opposition to 'ionie Rule; but there is nothing in it at all Peonsistent with the present attitude of the RiME MINISTER. " YOU would expect," Mr. 11.LA,DsTONE urged, •' when it is said that the klperial Parliament is to be broken up, that, the very least, a case should be made out, Ilowingthatthere were great subjects of policy, 4hd great demands necessary, for the welfare ?fs Ireland, which representatives of Ireland ,lisad united to ask, and which the representa- 'lves of England, Scotland, and Wales had tilnited to refuse." Precisely, and these are (the conditions which are pressing upon us '3-day— conditions which show that the case liZs been made out. The granting of a ttatutory Parliament is in the first place a attbject of policy; it is in the second place tlow regarded as for the welfare of Ireland; 4tid in the third place the demand is e "which the representatives of Ire- Land have united to ask, and which the representatives of England, Scotland, 11d Wales have, thus far, united to re- So far from showing that Mr. gLADSTONE has been caught napping, Lord .ERBY unintentionally proves that he is ;vide-awake, and that he was wide-awake and looking ahead sixteen years ago. We are Riad to find that there is one issue on which vq,e are in complete agreement with his lord- He says :,---" It would be unjust and e.ven absurd that Irishmen should vote in the Internal affairs of England and Scotland Vhilst retaining exclusive control over their. °Wn," This is a plain statement of a fact which seems to be ignored by those sun- Porters of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN who plead for the principle of Home Rule for Ireland ;" 4,nd in the same breath urge that there must `,),e no abatement of Irish representation in the English Parliament. For ourselves, .as Ive. have repeatedly declared, we are quite billing that the experiment should be tried ()f. setting up a Parliament in Dublin to deal vith exclusively Irish affairs; but we have a trorig objection to allowing Irish represen , - :°l-tives to have at the same time control in le Parliament at Westminster over English, ".peoteh, and Welsh affairs. Reverting to "-.Ord DERBY'S speech, it is much to be re- gretted that its tone throughout reveals eep distrust of the Irish people; they have, C Practically says, to be held down, or they

will plunder tr,:rid prey upon their fellows. This is the old.:fory doctiine ; but it is worn ext. The teaching of Liberalism is that like begets like; that kindness begets kindness it is already bringing forth good fruit-, and it promises to bring forth a hundred fold wir?,n justice is done to Ireland by giving her authority to manage her own affairs, in her own way, in a Parliament .on College Green

IN the Northwich Division the campaign goes briskly forward; but Mr. BRUNNER has nothing to fear if the Liberals do not relax their efforts through under-rating the strength of the enemy. Mr. ROBERT VERDIN means to win, if he can, as the champion of the Conservatives. He does not profess, of course, to champion the Conservative cause, hut he is none the less fighting their battle. In his Address, which will be found in another column, he describes himself as a "Liberal Unionist," and adds "My Liberal prin- ciples are well known to you all, but all other considerations and objects are in my opinion subservient to, and altogether overshadowed by, the one great issue now before the country, namely, the supremacy of the Eng- lish Parliament, the maintenance of the Unien between Great Britain and Ireland, and the pot :ction of the Irish Loyalists." So far as all this is concerned, it is ;:ust what Mr. BRUNNER himself might .ay. The Eng- lish Parliament must necessarily be supreme since it retains the right to take away, if need be, whatever powers it may confer on a subordinate body. ,Mr. GLADSTONE'S pro- posed legislation is essentially of a kind to maintain the "..fnion. What is being nv: in- tained at present is Disunion, which all good and sensible men wish to bring to an end. As to the so-called Loyalists of Ireland, it will be time enough to talk of protecting them when there is any evidence of their being in danger. If they do come to grief, it will be through their own fool sh and disloyal conduct. Mr. VERDIN .seeks to play on the fears of British workmen when he says that if the PRIME MINISTER'S pro- posals are carried out the wealth and capital invested in Ireland will leave that country, stagnation of trade will follow, by which the labour market in England will be overwhelmed, to the great and serious detriment of our working classes." But, as he offers no better argument for his statement than " I believe," it is not likely that it will carry conviction with it. What if the Home Rule Bill should, as it promises to do, prove acceptable to the Irish peopld? Will anyone who has the least knowledge of the Irish character deny that it would be the means of causing frihrPfAl ;'.cturn to their native land? As a people, they are passionately attached to the land of their birth ; give them self-government, and the likelihood is that there will be a rapid influx alike of popula- tion and of capital; and thus be the means of relieving rather than increasing the congestion in the labour market of this country.

SIR GEORGE ERRINGTON is making a capital fight in the Newton Division. He has been everywhere received with such enthusiasm since his arrival that there is a arowing confidence that he will be at the head! of the poll on Thursday next. It is greatly to the credit of Liberals who do not agree with the religious opinions of the Liberal can- didate that they have abstained from raising an issue which is foreign to the great ques- tion which is before the country. Hitherto a Roman Catholic, however eminent, or I however great his abilities, has had little chance of being returned to Parliament by an English constituency. But we are rising above these sectarian feuds. Mr. GLAD- STONE'S noble patriotism and thrilling elo- quence have done much within the past few I months to make Englishmen and Irish- men—Protestants and Roman Catholics— I feel that they are brethren, and that it is time th it they came together to do each other good. At the last electibn, Irish and Catholic electors were beguiled into voting for Tory candidates, in the belief that a Tory Government was about to do something for them. And so it really seemed, when they commenced a policy of coercion T The elec- tors were deceived by fair promises, which would have been followed by a foul perform- ance, if the SALISBURY Government, with the threats of repression in their mouths, had not been driven from power. Sir GEORGE ERRING- TON is not amongst those who would seek to suppress the aspirations of the Irish people. He will not, like Sir RICHARD CROSS, vote against Home Rule. On the contrary, he is pledged to support the policy of Mr. GLAD- STONE; and he comes before the constitu- ency with a recommendation from the PRIME MINISTER, which should act as a stimulant to I every Liberal elector in the Division. We need I hardly say that, while Sir GEORGE is a sound I and consistent Liberal, he is not an extreme man. He has not at all times been able to , ' see his way to act with the Irish Nationalists, ' but he stands side by side with them now; and that there may be no further misunder- standing Mr. T. P. O'CONNOR, with the authority of Mr. PARNELL, has written a letter which will be found in another column in which he states that, in the opinion of the Executive of the National League, Sir GEO. ERRINGTON "ought to receive every Irish vote in the Newton Division of Lancashire.' We sincerely hope that this will b so, and if it be accompanied, as we trust it will, by the vote of every English Liberal in the Divi- sion, he will be returned to Parliament by a large majority.

IN. the Widnes, Division Monday next has been fixed for the nomination, and the poll- ing for Friday next. The Liberal candi- date has therefore close on another week before him to make use of in improving his acquaint- ance with the electors. We are glad to know that he is not letting the grass grow under his feet, and that the prospects of his return —which were good from the first—are brighter every day. The Tory candidate, Mr. T. C. EDWARDS-MOSS, knowing that after his vote against Home Rule he can- not hope to have the support of the Irish electors, is posing as a Unionist. He pro- fesses to appeal for "the active support of all Unionists, to whatever political party they may belong ;" but he takes care not to in- sert his appeal in the columns of a Liberal newspaper. He will take as much as he can I get from Liberal voters, but they may .be , quite sure he will give nothing in return. He " worked the oracle" pretty well last November in bidding for the Irish votr; ; but he now makes a dead-set against Ireland. with a view to trading on the feelings of those who have a prejudice against the Irish race. He may catch ,alew votes, but a few only, by "jumping Jim Crow." Mr. BIRRELL /is on his track, and will have no difficulty in exposing the weakness of his positiGn. The Irish electors have weighed him in the , balance, and found him wanting. He will ' not get their votes on Friday next, and will know what it is to be at the bottom of the poll.

"TOUCH AND GO."

The nominations for the Newton Division are on Monday, and the polling will take place on Thursday. Which "Sir " shall it be—Sir George Errington or Sir Richard Cross ? It is not often that English and Irish Roman Catholics have an .opportunity of voting for a member of their own faith-. Let them be 'true to themselves, and vote for Sir George. Sir Richard Cross voted against the Home Rule Bill. Is not that enough ?

During the last week or two a statement has been extensively circulated, that Col. McCor- quodale intended to vote for Sir R. Cross, at the forthcoming election. The Colonel set the matter beyond all doubt by the following telegram, received on Saturday, from Wales, by Sir G. Errington's agent (Alr. F. Broad- bridge):—" It never has been my intention to vote for the Conservative candidate." This is one counterfeit nailed down. What next, and next?

The Address of Mr. William C. Brooks, which is characteristic, will be found on our front Page- He frankly admits that Mr. Gladstone is within his constitutional right in appealing to the country, and reters to Mr. Trevelyan as " a noble patriot." The .seceders from the Liberal party are getting "good characters " just now from the Tories. It is to be hoped they will preserve what is said of them. These wors of prais.e will be useful some twelve or eighteen months hence —when the Conservatives are "at their old lunes again ;" that is denouncing the seceders as too bad to burn.

It doesn't look as if Mr. PETER RYLANDS was going to be member for Burnley in the next Parliament. Atone of his ward meet- ings, on Saturday night, there were not more than 30 persons in attendance, while there were one hundred times as many present the same evening at the demonstration in sup- port of Mr. Greenwood, the Gladstonian candidate. But perhaps the Tories will vote for Mr. Rylands if they will not go to hear him ; we shall see.

Lord Hartington is to be opposed at Ros- sendaie. INIr. R. C. Richards, who first took up the cudgels, has since become one of the Liberal candidates for. Bolton ,and at the eleventh hour Mr. Thomas'Newbigging has entered the lists, He is a native of Rossen. but engaged as a civil engineer in Man- chester. Let us hope he will be able to "spring a mine" upon Lord Hartington, for if his lordship is returned to Parliament he will be the greatest stumbling block in the way of Home Rule.

Mr. Holbrook Gaskell has intimated that, as a Liberal Unionist, he will vote for the Tory candidate for the Widnes Division. But what confidence can he have in the Toties on the Home Rule question now that he knows—it is not a matter of doubt—hat Lord Carnarvon, the Irish Viceroy af the late Tory Government, took sweet counsel with Mr. Parnell on the question of Home Rule, and that too with the knowledge of Lord ,Salisbury?

How quietly, how softly, Lold Salisbury lets out the fact that he did know that, some- how or other, some sort of an understand- ing- was come to between Lord Carnarvon and Mr. Parnell on the Irish question. But it is well to remember that he did not confess the truth until Mr. Gladstone. had shamed him to it.

• Last year, a rumour got abroad that Lord Salisbury himself had been closeted with the leader of the Irish Nationalist. But. it was promptly contradicted. 'What! the head of the Tory party in communication with the chief of what Lord Randolph Churchill called "the legion of foui fiends ! " Thc: thing was preposterous—Lord Salisbury didn't even know Mr. ifarnell. How pretty it looked—that denial, and how charming it looks to-day, when it is known that Mr. Par- nell was closeted, not with Lord Salisbury, but with his right hand man Lord Carnarvon, the Tory Lord Lieutenant of Ire- land.
Lord Randolph Churchill is being pun- ished as he deserves. He is being hit with epigrams. Here is an old one which has been turned to good account against him at a London meeting :

By a friend of Lord-Randolph's 'twas lately averred The electors would find him as good as his word. "As good as his word," did you say. Gracious me! What a dreadful young man then Lord Randolph must be!

Another epigram—an original one—ap- pears in the "Manchester Examiner and Times" of Thursday, and is as follows:— Darwin! you err when you so rashly say That Man succeeds to Ape in Nature's plan. The order here is just the other way, For Churchill follows up the "Grand Old manl"

Mr. Parnell has evidently the utmost con- tempt for Lord Randolph Churchill. He spoke of him at Manchester, on Wednesday, as a " grovelling creature," the " gutter. sparrow of Tory politics," and as "a contempti- ble political Welsher." And it is due to Mr. Parnell to say that this opinion is not newly formed; he refused to meet his lordship at the house of Mr. Wiltred Blunt when invited to do so; he was determined, if he had any dealings with Tory leaders, to have them with honourable men.

A THIEF THROUGH DRINK AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday, at Runcorn Police Court, George Jones, apparently a tramp, was charged with stealing a shirt ane nine pairs of stockings the property of Samuel Dobsoo, draper and corn dealer, Bridge street. About eight o'clock on Saturday night, hear- ing that the prisoner had stolen some stockings, Dobson went in pursuit of the prlsoaer on the canal bank and cap- tured him. He had nine pairs of stockings in his possss• Rion. The prisoner offered to pay Virl for the shirt which had not been recovered. The prieoner, who wee. "in drink," was given into the custody of P.C. Potts. The pri- soner's plea was that he was drunk and slid net know what he was doing. He was Committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. WIDNES ZION SUNDAY SCII3OL.—Th3 aneiversary ser- mons of this school were preached on Sunday last by Mr. James Bramwell, of Liverpool. Special hymns and anthems were sung by the children and choir, the soloists being Mfrs Harrison, Misses E. and A. Betney, and Mrs. Joseph lietney. ABSCONDING SAILORS AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday, Karl Hansen and Creston Sorersm, Norwegian sailors on board the brig "Vesta," new lying in Runcorn Docks, were charged with absconding from that vessel. About eleven o'clock on Monday Eight P.C. Dale was in Percival's Lane, when he saw the prisoners running across a field near the Decks. Upon seeing him they threw the bundles they were carrying away,but tke officer succeeded in effecting . the capture of the men. The captain of the Verna " wished the men to be kept in custody until the vessel sailed on Friday, but the Bench said that their only I course was to discharge the men, and allow the captain the aid of the pol.ce to get them on board. The men, who could not speak English, were therefore discharged. ACCIDENT TO A WEDDING PARTY AT WIDNES.—An ac- cident, which was fortunately unattended by at y serious consequences. occurred to a wedding party at Diann on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. and Mrs. Peter HID, nee Miss Taylor, daughter of Mr. John Taylor, wholesale confec- tioner, Widnes and Waterloo-roads, whose nuptials had that morning been celebrated at St. Luke's Church, Farnworth, accompanied by a number of friends, were proceeding in a conveyance towards Hale, when the tyre of one of the wheils came off in Ditton-road, and the conveyance turned over into a ditch, and precipitated its occupants to the ground. No one, however, was seriously injured, and the trap was dragged out of the ditch. Mr. Taylor brought the conveyance back to Widnes, and the rest of the party proceeded on their way. . TIIE DILKE CASE..—In the Court of Anneal. on Wednes- day, before Lords Justices Cotton, Lindley, and Lopee, the appeals of Mrs. Crawford and Sir C. Dillen against the de- cision of the President of the Divorce Court, who refused to allow them to appear as parties when the intervention of the Queen's Proctor was heard, came on for hearing. With- out calling upon Dr. Phillirnore, representine the Queen's Procter, the Court dismissed the appeals of Sir C. Nike and Mrs. Crawford. With regard to Sir C.Dilke, Vie Court held that as he had not availed himself of the opportunity of giving evidence at the trial, it would be wrong to allow bim to do so now. With regard to Mrs. Crawford, she was not a party to the intervention of the Queen's Proctor. The Court refused leave to appeal to the House of Lords.—ln the Divorce Court. on Wednesday, an application was made on behalf of the Queen's Proctor that the Crawford case be heard before a special jury. The application was opposed by the petitioner on the ground that owing to public speeches in self-defence by Sir C. Dilke, an impartial jury could not be obtained. Sir James Hannen thought that an unprejudiced jury might be obtained, and therefore directed that the case be tried by special jury, also that Mrs. Craw- ford be Impugned for the 16th July. OBTAINING MONEY BY FRAUD AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Peter Fletcher, cf Marshall's Cross, Sutton, was charged with having on the 25th June, at Widnea, obtained alms by friodulent pretences, ti wit, by means of a letter stating that his wife had died during her esanfinement, and left six children.—P.C. Strong about two o'clock on Friday afternoon saw the prisoner going from door to door in Simm's Cross. He asked him what he was doing, and he replied that he was going about with a nee- ging letter. The officer took him to Mr. Johnson's shop and showed a young woman there the letter, which she identified as the one prisoner had shown her. At first pri- soner gave a wrong name, but he afterwards stated that his name was Peter Fletcher, and admitted that the letter was a false one. He was a married man, but bad no children.— Mrs Tebbut, residing in Ann-street, said prisoner went to her shop with the letter produced soliciting alms, and she gave him a shilling.—lnspector Wood stated that prisoner was a lazy fellow, and bad for a long time been going aboret the country soliciting alms in this manner, sometimes represent- ing that his wife was dead, and at another time that his child had died and he had no money to bury it wieb.-..- The prisoner was committed to gaol for two months with hard labour. OBSTRUCTING A RAILWAY hiSPECTOR AT DITTON.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Gerraghty, a young man, residing in Gerrard-street, West Bank, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at Ditten Station on the 26th June, and also with obstructing Robert &son, an official in the service of the London and North- Western Railway Company, at the same time and place.— From the statement of Mr. ?errand, solicitor's department, Lime-street Station, Liverpool, who prosecuted on behalf of the railway company, it appeared that on Saturday nieht the prisoner arrived at Dirton from Widnes by the 9-30 train, holding a ticket, Widoes to Liverpool. He gave his ticket up to the ticket collector on going out of the sta- tion to a public-house, and returned shortly afterwards and demanded his ticket back. The collector told him there was no train to Liverpool, but to satisfy him gave him his ticket. He was not content with this, however, and fol- lowed the collector about the station demanding a shilling, the price of the ticket, and otherwise obstructing him in the discharge of his duties.—Robert Bason corroborated Mr. Ferrand's statement, and Sergeant Coutts and P.C. Worth- ington preyed the offence of drunkenness.—The Bench im- posed a fine of lOs and costs, or 14 days, for the obstruction, and 7s 6d and co-te' or ten days, for the drunkenness. PENKETH WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL.—On Monday evening a very successful tex meeting and enter- tainment was held in the above school, there being present to tea about seventy persons. The tables were presided over by Mesdames Main.ley, Watson, Pickton, Cook, Bestwick, Seed, &c. Active pares in the entertainment were taken by Miss Gar- nett, Miss A. Moses, Mrs. D. Garnett, Misses Pusill, Routledge, Ashton, Seed, Mainley, Griffiths, Baxter, Stanley,. E. Hobson, and Mr. Routledge. The choir also sang selections. The proceeds of the evening were to go in aid of the enlargement of Penketh• elementary schools. PRESENTATION OF ADDRESSES TO SIR WILLIAM CUNLIFFE BROOKS.—A ceremony of an interesting character took place on Saturday, at Glentana, the Deeside residence of Sir William Cunliffe Brooks, Bart. Sir William having a week previously arrived at Glentarnt, on his first visit to that place since the honour of a. barenetage was conferred upon him by the Queen, his Deeside friends and neighbours deter- mined to give substantial expression to their con- gratulations by presenting an address. The same idea was taken up by the inhabitants of the village of Aboyne and its neighbourhood. The traders in Aberdeen who are connected with Glentana by busi- ness relations had some time previously resolved to express their congratulations in a similar manner, and had entrusted to a local urn!, the task of prepar- ing an address worthy of the occasion. Saturday was fixed by Sir William as the day on which he would receive the three addresses, and the deputa- tions met at Glentana in order that the three presentations might be made at the same time. On reaching Sir William's charmingly-picturesque resi- dence, the party were met by the hon, baronet and Lady Brooks, and were welcomed with the utmost cordiality.. Sir William and Lady Brooks kindly conducted the party to several of the most interest- ing places in the immediate neighbourhood of the honse, and afterwards the whole company adjourned to the fine billiard-room, where the, addresses were presented. In acknowledging the presentation, Sir m , Willia referred to the recent in the Altrin- cham Division, as the result of which he was re- turned to Parliament, and remarked that in that contest there were accidental abstentions of both sides. But if they assumed that those who ab- stained would have voted in the same way as at the previous election, the majority for him would have ! been exactly the same as that of his late nephew— ! 752. After the presentation the whole party were entertained in the the magnificent ball-room of I Glentana, where a sumptuous luncheon was served. I —After lunch the members of the party enjoyed ! themselves in visiting some of the many interesting places in the glen, the genial host conducting one detachment. Tea was served about six o'clock, and shortly afterwards the visitors commenced their journey home.
AN ALLEGED BREIGET OF PROMISE AND ITS RESULT. _ _

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. G. L. Davies, Mary Conway, a farm ser- vant, was charged with threatening a man named John Collins, from which he was afraid she would do hint some bodily iojury.—The complainant, who said he lived in Loch-street, stated that on Monday, the 21st inst., he m't the defendant in Norman-road. When near the parson's house she demanded a shilling from him, and upon his re- fusing to give her anything she threatened to knock his brains cot with a stone. The SAMe night she came to his house and made a disturbance, and again threatened him. He was afraid that she would do him some injury. Only that morning she waited for him with a stone as he came out of the house.—The defendant, who was strongly ex- cited, said that the complainant had promised to marry her; but instead of that he had sotterA her family and "smashed up" everything she had. He had givon 116 r two black eyes, and put her into the Workhousc.. She was nearly driven mad by the conduct of the complainant, and if the magistrateg knew how he had behaved to her they would givl him six months.-1 be defendant was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months, in her own surety of £5, and to pay the costs, amounting to lOs 611 —The defendant: I could not pay a shilling. I don't care a ! pin. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: Or seven claw.

CONVICT AT RUNCORN.—James Smith, having the ap- pearance of a labourer, and who is a returnPd convict, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday. charged with stealing a piece of timber four feet long, the property, of the Weaver Trustees. Shortly before moon on the pre- vious day William Whitby, a labourer in the employ of the Trustees, observed the prisoner walking away from the building where the wood is kept, with the piece of timber produced on his back. He waa drunk. The prisoner threw the timber on board the narrow boat "Industry." Hugh Reynolds, a hand on board tbe boat, threw the board upon the quay, and the Prisoner sent it behind some fiats. Shortly afterwards William Nicholas. the carpenter to the Trustees, told the prisoner he had better take the timber back, and be did so. When apprehended by P.C. Dale, the prisoner said he went to ask for the timber, but there not being anyone present, be took it. He was fetching it at the request of Whitby. Whitby denied this statement. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. •

THE MERSEY SALT AND BRINE COMPANY,
LIMITED.

The sixth ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of this company, whose works are at Weston Point, was held. on Tuesday at No. 8, Draper's-gardens, London, the Hon. Ashley G. J. Ponsonoy, cuairman of the company, presiding.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption ef the report, said they had been waiting fer a long time for some- thing to be done. In the first place they had great difficulty in getting the money, and in the second place, when they were making arrangements with Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., who provided the amount for the general purposes of the company,there were considerable delays on the lawyers' side. They had not, however, been idle, but in the mean- time had been pushing on their headway to 218 yards, and they hoped to have a very plentiful supply of brine, because the rocks were descending to flushes or pools. Besides, they were making arrangements for getting brine in another quar- ter; but he did not think it advisable at that moment to state where. He might, however. say that they would lef able to obtain an almost unlimited quantity. Seven pans were ready for working out of the 61. They were making salt , at the present time, and were doing extremely well with the seven pans. The remaining pans would be finished in in about three months. They had got the best materials from the best houses, and great satisfaction was given on all hands. There was no transhipment required, therefore he thought the future of the company stood very high in- deed. Of course they had had difficulties to conteed against, and they were about a year and & half later than they reckoned. It was therefore proposed to issue additional shares, and he had no doubt they would be able to place them amongst their own shareholders.-111r. Robert Ewing seconded the motion.—Mr. Crowle (shareholder) complained of what he termed the heavy expenditure, and thought that five directors would be sufficient to manage such a coin- pany.—The Chairman explained that the directors were taking but a email proportion of their proper fees. The other expenses were absolutely necessary.—The motion was carried unanimously.—The retiring directors, the Hon. Ashley Ponsonby and Mr. James Lawrie, and the auditors havine, been re-elected, the Chairman moved "That there shall be attached 2.500 shares of the unissued capital of the company at such a preferential rate of divideed or other special privileges as the board may determine, and that the board be empowered to issue the said shares, or any part thereof, on ouch terms or such conditions and at such times as they may think fit:"—Mr. H. W. Blake secoeded.—The motion was carried unanimously, and the proceedings ter- minated.

div.head: wrrtNEs FOOTBALL CLUB DINNER.
div.p: wrrtNEs FOOTBALL CLUB DINNER.

The members of the Widnes Football Club held their an- nual dinner at the Central Hotel on Monday evening. There was a good company, and the repast prepared by Mr. Parkes, the proprietor, gave every satiefaction. Dr. McCambridge presided over the after proceedings, and he was supported by Messrs. IL A. Richards, W. E. Oakden, Melvin, J. A. Brown, Price, F. Wright, F. Smith, Ashley, Elerriman, Lecomber, J. Smith, Hingley. and others.—The Chairman proposed the heaith of the " Queen and Royal family" in appropriate terms, and it was honoured with the usual loyal observancies. "Success to the Widnes Football Club" was also proposed bv the Chairman, who said the records making up the past history of the club were of undoubted merit, and promised well for the future career of the club. The match list fcr the next season also augured well for the prospects of the club. He was pleased to know that the team was to play home and home games witn Runcorn next season. (Applause.) The very friendly game which the teams played at lianc•ln at the end of the last season showed the kindly feelings that misted betweet. the two towns. It seemed to him as if they were more than kind on both sides, for Farrell seemed too 'friendly disposed to tackle Hughes, and Hughes to tackle Farrell—(laughter)— they were so good to each other. (Renewed laughter.) Well, Widnes were beaten; but although not the best club , In the district at present, they hoped to be so soon. (Ap- plause.) He asked them to drink success to the club, and coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Brown. (Applause.)-• Mr. Brown suitably responded to the toast, which was well received, and said the next best thing to attaining the prominent position was fighting for it. (Applause.)—Mr. W. E. Oakden gave the toast "The town and trade of Widnes" in an admirable speech, and referred to its staple industry, the manufacture of chemicals. In the com- mercial, as in the political world, there were radical changes. He doubted whether these changes in the chemical trade were good for Widnes. The trade of Widnes had hitherto been conducted upon scientific principles by a process known

as the Leblanc process, invented by a Frenchman; but within recent years there had been introduced the ammonia process which struck at the root of indusry in Widnes ; and there was not the slightest doubt that if the chemical trade of Widnes was to continue it must be carried on under those principles.—Mr. T. Smith,who,e name ,vas associaed with the toast, respoEded, and promised to doable his sui- scripion to the club. (A pp!ause.)—The toast of the " Pre- sidelA and vice-p-iesidents,' given by Mr. Ashall and " The Press," proposed by Mr. Richards, concluded the list. The proceedings were enlivened and rendered more enjoyable by a variety of songs, sentimental and comic, sung by the chairman, and Messrs. J. Wright, Kiddie, Whits, Singleton, Gregory, and J. Smith.

COTTAGE PROPERTY OWNERS AND THEIR RATES.

The followinc, letter was read from Mr. J. Dolby, the dis- trict auditor :—" Gentleintn,—l beg to report that I have completed the audit of the accounts of the Runcorn • nnissioners for the year ended at Lady Day last. With regard • to the. rate levied by the Cotntnissioners, it atnieaied that, in . upwards of 70 instancq3 ccmmissit.ns bad been allowed to owners in respect of houses in their own occupation. As • there is no authority in law for the allowance of commis- sion in such cases, I trust the Commis=ioners will give direction for the rate to be levied and collected from such persons upon the full rateable value according to the valua- tion list in form. I found that the other accounts generaly had been kept and balanced in a satisfactory manner."— Mr. Fisher said Mr. Dolby stated that bygones mast be by- gones, but that in future the Board must not allow toe usual discount to owners who lived in their own }muse.— The Chairman pointed out that since the Bard commenced to compound the rates, the discount had been Jiowed to owners who occupied their own property, and it had never been found out by the Board ex the auditor until this time. —Mr. Shaw explained that there was a redueion cf 25 per. cent made on all property under £lO rateable. This was allowed simply for collection, and that was where the mis- take had been that those pet,re who were owners of pro- party and lived in their own house under £lO rateable value they had been allowed 25 per cent igstead of IV; per cent. —Mr. Fisher said it was not allowed exactly for collection, but was on the understandin?; that they paid for the pro- perty whether it wee empty or not.—Mr. Shaw: There is Ino property owner in this town that pays for empty pro- perty.—Mr. Fisher: But that is the meaning.—Mr. Shaw denied this, awl said the Board might allow 50 per . cent reduction where the owner paid the rates, whether the property was empty or not. Mr. Shaw contended that with 25 par cent discount some 'reasonable time should be fixed when the rates should he paid to the Board. It was a great shame that persons who were getting 25 per cent allowed sheuld not illy their rates before the last month, while others, shopkeepers and large property owners, who only got 12i per cent paid within two months. Ee thought that the rates slit old be paid within three months in order to claim the redaction. (Hear, hear.) —The auditors report was adopted.
