div.head: ALLEGED ASSAULT AT BANK QUAY
div.p: ALLEGED ASSAULT AT BANK QUAY
STATION.

On Monday, at the Warrington Borough Cone, Mr. William Roberts appeared to answer a summons charging him with assaulting P.C. Turner, of the Borough Police, at Bank Quay Station, on the 22nd of June. Taste was a cross•summens against Turner, taken, out by defendant, also for assault. Mr. J. L. ',Whittle (deputy town clerk) pro,eouted on b.•half of the police, and Mr. RidgWay (Ridgway and Wormley) appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Whittle said that he believed Mr. Ridgway, on behalf of his client, was prepared to plead guilty, and to apologise for the of- fence; but Mr. Ridgway replied that he did not plead guilty.—Mr. Whittle said that at all events Mr. Roberts was prepared to express his regret. It was desirable at the present time to avoid all friction in political matters. They were sorry that the case had arisen but felt it their duty to bring the case forward. —i discussion ensued as to the advisability or not of going on with the case, and Mr. Ridgway, who re• marked that he had twelve witnesses on his side, said there were two sides to every case. He wished to say nothing to reflect on the police. He did not say that the police were wrong or right, bat he wished to leave the case en that neither party might regard the result in any way as in the nature of a victory.—Mr. Runt, the chief constable, said the case was a simple one, and had been made it great deal too much of. They had their duty to de without fear, favour, or affection, and if they had erred at all in this cam it bad been a long way on the side of mercy. At this crisis he desired to do his duty with the gree•est possible patience to both parties alike.— Mr. Whittle then explained that on the night of tho day in question Hr. Gladstone passed through Bank Quay Station, and a request was made for the attend- ance of a policeman to assist in maintaining order. Mr. Hunt sent four members of the borough force, Turner being one of the (our. The railway company had given instructions that no one but officials must be admitted to the platferm. There was a crowd of peeple in the booking office all anxious to get through, and amongst them Mr. Roberts. He asked permis- sion to go through, and was refused, and then in-isted or demanded to go, succeeding eventually in forcing his way in. He bad got a short distance down the subway, when a ticket cell/actor took hold of him and told him to go back. He refused, and Constable Turner went te the assistance of the official. The constable took hold of him, but Mr. Roberts would not go back until forcea back, and-then the assault complained of took place. He believed Turner re- sisted Roberts in the fracas, but he need not go fur- ther into the case.—Mr. Ridgway remarked that Mr. Roberts did ask and was refused admittance, and another person asked and was allowed to go through, and as Englishmen liked to see fair play Mr. Roberts was irritated, and made an effort to get in.—Alder- man Davies: Of course the other person was an Irishman. (Laughter.) Mr. Ridgway said Mr. Roberts in the excitement of the naom,:.nt charged No. IS with being drunk. There was a number of people present. and Mr. Roberts regretted making that state- ment, because the officer was not drank. So far from Mr. Roberts or his friends having any desire to inter- fere with the duties of the police, they would much rather assist them. He could honesidv say that his client regretted all that took place that night.—Mr. Whittle and Mr. Ridgway, after further conversation, left the court with Chief Constable Hunt to endeavour . to come to some mutual arrangement.—On their return Mr. Ridgway, on bshalf of Mr. Roberts, ex- pressed regret for the action he took, and said that L the action of the railway company in allowing another

person to go through provtled him in the emtciternent of the time.—Mr. Whittle thereupon iutimated his williagness to willidraw the cas3; and the Mayor (Aldermsn Harrison) remarked that the c.:mrse was justified by the circumstances -4f the case, for Mr. Roberts had made a handsome apology. Sir LllCills O'Trigzer, in Sheridau's "School for .Sc,andai, said " an affront handsomely acklowleiged, bacomes an obli,gation," rind he was inclined to thiak there was a great deal of truth in it. Mr. Roberts would, of eourse, have to pay the costs.—Mr. Ridgway: That has been arranged amongst ourselves.

MEETING IN THE Cr.-!CI7S.

On Tuesday evcning a Conservative meaing was held in the Circus, 6ankey•streel. Mr. Rob,rt Pierpoint presided, and there were also on th,.! platform Captain Reynolds, Cutincillors R. W. Francomb, J. PierpoTnt, and T. Sutton ; Messrs. John White, J. Woorlz, I'. Moor, and H. Greerall. The CHAIRMAN denied that Lord Saiisbury Lad ever pro. posed 20 years' coc:cion for Ireland. Mr. Cros&ld, the Liberal candidate, had reLrred to the speech of Mr. Murra.y, and had said that that gentleman fought with the Conteder. ate army in the Ame:ican civil war, and also called him a secessionist. But if that were so, Mr. Gladslcne, Mr. Croe. field, and all who stood with them wee sec,ssionists. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Mr. BAINES proposed "That this meeting is of opinion that the establishment of a separate Parliament in Dublin, at proposed by Mr. Gladstone, would not only be fraught with disastrous consiquences to the British EmWre, brit would be an injustice to the loyal portion of the popula- tion."

• Mr. Jone; WraTE, in seconding the proposal, said the Conservatives of Warrington had held meetings in all the wards of the borough ; but Mr. Crosti,ld bad only ventured ..to show himself in the North• West Ward. (A Vo:ce : " Tim!: is where he belongs to," and laughter.) ile was confident as to the result of Friday's election, and cou'd tell them this, that the canvass up to the present pine was better than the canvass at the last elec'ion. (Cheers.) He thought it was necessary to mention that, as he was constanzly meet- ing his Radicat frienis, and they seemed to be cock-a-hoep —(laughter)—and wished people to be lid t a beli,ve that they would win in a canter. (Laughter.) He could assure them that there was an increase of three or four to one in their favour, as compared with the canvass at the last elec- tion. (Loud cheers.) He was not saying that simcly for the purpose of Efluencing these present in any way. It was m?rely to show that it augured well for a victory on Friday trxt. (Loud cheers.) At the last election the • number of voters who went to the poll was 4.,010, hut ac- cording to the results of the canvass this year they exoected to poll 4,330 (Load cheers.) If the promises proved right on the last occision, be did net see why they should not de so again, and if they did Sir Gilbert dreenall would be re- turned by is much larger majority. (Cheers.) Mr. Mara having supported toe proposal, it was carried no

• Sir GILBEnT GREENALL, who was cordially received, said be respected Mr. Peter Rylands for his integri7y end straightforwardness, and if he was the candidate for War- rington he should freely and unhesitatingly vote for him. (Cheers.) They knew his (Sir Gilberts) views and his feelings with regard to Ireland. He was no perry, and would be no party, to any scheme that had for his object the diininiehing or the weakening of the strength and the ' endurance of the Union of Ireland. (Cheers.) They might speak as much ae they liked upon the Irish question; but it would rreolve itself into one coaclusion. Were they for the termination of the Union which existed bet wean Great Britain and Ireland, or would they submit to the power of Parnellism in the present day? (Cries of " No.") He was for Ireland being united to Englard—(clieers)—and ttrwlr believed that that Union et,engthened the endurance of both civil and religious privileges. (Hear, hear.) He should be found supporting their views, and should stand- by the integrity of the Empire. (Cheers ) In answer to questions, Sir Gilbert said he was in favour of reducing royalties, and of equal railway rates. (Cheers.) He was notin favour of paying members of Parliament, but if the • majority of ratepayers were in favour of paving tee return- ing officers' expenses, he, as the candidate, could not ob- ject. (Laughter and cheers.) Mr. GBORGE Woons proposed "That this meeting pledges itself to use all legitimate means to return Sir Gilbert Greeuall as the member for the borough at the approaching election." (Cheers.) Mr. Crosdeld's speech from beginning to end was a concatenation of "soap suds bubbles.") (Loud laughter.) In one sentence Mr. Croefield had said, "I will be your member." (Laughter, and a voice: "He won't.") He answered. "You will not, John." (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Crosfield said, "I stand upon a reek," but he (Mr. Woe* replied, "John, you stand open soap suds bubbles." (Laughter.) 1 bey would show him at ten "clock on Friday night that his ftiundation was shaken, and that Sir GilbettGreenall was returned by an overwhelming majority. (Loud cheers.)
s Mr. T. LITTON supported the proposal, which 11.38 carried, and a vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceed- ings to a close.

MEETING OF WORKING-MEN. On Wednesday evening a meeting of Conservative work- ing-men was held in the Public Hal. The chair Was' taken by Mr. John Roberts, and there were also on the platform Sir Gilb4rt Greenall, Captain Reynolds, Mr. G. Woods, Mr. St. Pierpoiot, Mr. Wynne-Jones, and others. There was a full but by no means a crowded attendance. The Ca/aro/AN said he was sorry to see that many Eng- lishmen believed that if the Home ttule Bill were granted it would be the means of every Irishman leaving England and settling down in Ireland. He asked them not to make a mistake. Never would such a thing occur; capital would leave Ireland, and instead of Irishmen leavinz England they would come over in live hundreds where formerly they came in hundreds. (Hear, hear.) They would come in such numbers that they would fight Englishmen for work and bread at the very thresholds of their doors. They were told by their Liberal candidate that he loved Irishmen to the very bottom of his heart, but if he loved Irishmen to the bottom of his heart, why did he did be discharge them after the last election ? (Loud cheers.) If there was any Irishmen there they might de- pend upon it that as soon as the Contest was over they would Bee where the love and affection was. (Hear, bear.)

Mr. GEORGE WOODS moved "That this meeting is of opinion that the establishment of a separwe Parliament in Dublin, as proposed by Mr. Gladstone, would not only be fraught with disastrous consequences to the Briti6h empire, but would be an act of gross injuvice towards the local portion of the Irish population.: (Cheers) Mr. Crosfield. he said, had said that the question they had to decide that election was a question of liberty' He begged to der that statement as haring no foundation in lint. The q! tion was, wore the working men of Warrington coin • to assist in driving in the thin end of the wedge for th memberment of this empire in this jubilee year of the reign of our gracious sovereign. (Loud cheers.) Mr. P. NATLOR seconded, and Mr. G. F. WOOD S" AppOrted the proposal, which was carried.

Ir. A. SIMPSON moved " That this meetin4 nse eVerS7 legitimate means to return Sir G. Greenall as nember for Warrington." (Cheers.) Mr. W. BLOOMFIELD seconded, and Mr. W. Ihoimcs, ana Mr. WYNNE•JONES supported this proposal. The proposal was then carried.

SIR Rs CROSS A'AtONGST UTE MINERS. Sir R. Cross, the Conservative candidate for the Newton Division of South-We,st Lancashire, addressed a large meet- ince of. 'Messrs. R. Evans and Co.'s miners on Thursday even- ing. at Golborne. iir Richard, who was accompenied by Mr. T. 1). Grinake, arrived just in time to catch the men as they left the pits. Sir Richard said it was enly by hard werk that he .had attained to his present position. (;.leer, hear.) Referring to Ireland, be said the rersons who bad followed Mr. Parnell for many years had beta tyrants to the law-abiding citizens, and, in addition to coor4ng and boycottieg them, they had constantly held their lives in jeopardy. He did not cell that liberty, for the same liberty should apply to Ireland as to England anci Scotland. The Conservatives at the last election were not in favour of co- ercion ix Ireland, because the people had first received the franchise, and he considered they ought to have the pr;vi- i&ge of freely exercising it. (" It was to catch the Irish votes," and laughter.) In conclusion, he appealed to them not to hand over two millions of Loyalists to the tyrants of the National League, to put down whom no man had done mere than the present Prime Minister himself. (Slight ap- plause and "Three cheers for Sir George Errington," which, were heartily given.)—The Chairman : I think we ought t.) have a resolution.—Dr. Dobb proposed a vote of thanks to 6ir Richard.—Mr. Yates (manager): I propose no resolu- tion be submitted. You have all beard the address and von can just vote as you please. (Rear, hear.) Sir Richard then drove away amid applause, hooting, and three cheers for HOMO Rule.

Mr. John Bright, who was on Thursday re-elected with- out opposition for the Central Division of Birmiog! am, addressed his constituents in the evening in the Two Hall. A resolution was passed expressing satisfaction at the re- election of Mr. Bright, because of his life-long fidelity to principle, his fearless independence, and the earnest &sire which, throughout the whole of his honourab!e political career, h 3 had constantly manifested to do justice so Ire- land. Mr. Bright, who met with a very cordial reception, said that during toe 29 years he had represented liirint ham he had been alongside but not a follower of the loader of the Liberal party. sion—(cheers)—and what they wanted was enthu- siasm on the part of the English Liberals. (Hear, hear.) No supineness, no apathy. Ile hoped that every Liberal in the town was heartily ashamed of the present state of the repre- sentation. (Laughter.) And if the present state of the representation had been 'brought about by his apathy . and. supineness, he i hoped he was determined on this occasion that that apathy shotild exist no longer. (Cheers.) Now that they had closed the riinks of the Liberal party, the strongest and most: numerous; it Would be utter disgrace if they did not show that next Friday. (Cheers.) The Liberal party came before the pub- lic with strong credentials in the fact of what it had done before—from the emancipation of the .Catholics mere than fifty years ago • down to the passing of the great reform measures of the last Parliament. The • Liberal party 'had supported every great reform measure in the face of the most strenuous opposition of the Tory party. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) It-was not merely in the opposition of the Tory, party, but whenever any great measure was passed in favour of reform they were treated to the most doleful prophecies of ruin and disaster td the country. I(Laughter.) Whenever any measure of progress and reform was passed the spirit of the Prophet Jeremiah came upon the Tories—(renewedlaughter)--a spirit of mourning, and lamentation, and woe. (Much laughter.) Their young men saw visions and the old men dreamt dreams of disaster and ruin. (Laugh- ter.) Why, he himself had seen the sun of England set for ever at least half a dozen times. (Laughter.) It was going to set this time for good, never to rise again. (great laughter.) Prophecies had been ut- tered from that platform during the last ten days of Irish tyranny to the minority, of separation of the kingdom, and the utter ruin of the Empire. These kind of things had been heard over and over again, and he dared say they should hear them hereafter. They (the Liberals) had not only a good cause, but they had a great leader. (Cheers.) There was not an elector in this kingdom who was not better for the life and work of Mr. Gladstone —(cheers)—better materially, better intellectually, better in every way connected with civil, religious, and commercial liberty. (Cheers.) He was fighting this battle for them now with a vigour that was al- most youthful. (Hear, hear.) His eye was not dim, neither was his natural force abated. (Hear, hear.) And surely services such as he had rendered, and was now rendering, deserved from them hearty and resolute support. (Cheers.) They had a good candi- date. (Cheers.) They had known him all his life. He had gone in and out before them from his youth up. He knew his father before him, and he knew that Ihe was a man resolute in regard to Liberalism and 'to freedom. (Cheers.) Mr. Crosfield had rendered very great services to Warrington and to its in- terests—(hear, hear, and cheers)—and while they did not know, and were not likely to know, about his private benevolence, still that had been very , great and very useful to that town. (Cheers.) He was a large employer of labour, and he (the chairman) was told by the workpeople that he was a , a kind and considerate employer.. (Cheers.) This I then was the conclusion ; that they had a good cause, i a great leader, a party with glorious antecedents, and a good candidate. (Loud cheers.) Let them prove themselves worthy of all this. (Hear, hear.)' Let them be determined as far as in them,lay, even at some Sacrifice if nece§sary, to return to Parlia- ment next Friday,a member who was as capable as he was willing to serve them. (Prolonged cheers.) . Mr. GEO. MELLY, who bad a most cordial reception, said when be came Into the room he beard the audience oc- cupied in singing the National. Anthem "God save the I Queen." If they on that platform !Allayed that they were about to disintegrate her Majesty's Empire, if they believed I that, they were traitors in thought, and Caet audience would not be there. (Loud cheers.) But they looked beck upon the teachings of history and asked themselves this question : 11l what did Vele great Empire differ from other Empires of the world that they had been able in peace and happiness, and serenity, to celebrate the jubilee of that noble, of that loving, widow, wife, and sovereign. (Cheers.) While every other crowned head, without a eingle exception in the length and breadth of Europe, had had during the last 50 or 60 years to seek some haven, in hotels near Charing Cross or some place of refuge, like Claremont, which Her Majesty the Queen had placed at their •disposal—why was it that there had not been one drop of blood sh,d in civil ,strife during all these years, and that they cauld all meet together that night be they Tories or Liberals, Redicels or Irish Nationalists, and sing " Goa save the Queen." (t beers.) It was be- cause during the last 200 years, since William and Queen liery came to rule over us,our statesmen had seen the rieht moment to make concessions to the people—(hear, , haar)—and that of their despotic Emperors or Kings had I refused to make the reforms demanded by the people at the moment when the people were ripe to accept them, and the result had been revolution upon revolution in every land lexcept the God-blest, land of England. (Cheers.) 'He cams there to ask them to make one more concession to preserve the traditions of the great Whig and Liberal party, which had kept this ceuntry free from civil war and from civil strife for 200 years. He asked them to grant to another section of their fellow citizens the power of suffrage which, was granted to us in 1832, and then again in 1868 and 1885. (Loud cheers.) He appealed be them not to follow the lead of Mr. John ttriebt upon this question, becluse he had stood I aloof and taken but little interest in the new developments and tendencies of our Democratic movements. (Hear, hear.) He had never cared much about the great temper- ance question, or the great education question; and he must , ask them reverentially to pass away frem the advice which 'he had given them • at the present time, and to look to that greater leader and greater statesman who had never stopped in his representation 'of the force of Democratic Reform, William- Ewart Gladstone. (Cbeers.) Mr. Melly spoke with great sarcasm of the fears expressed by the Tories if Home Rule was granted to Ireland. Was he to be told that after cur soldiers fought at Alma, stood upon the heights of Inkerman, put down the Indian Mutiny, and sailed 2,000 miles on the Nile to try and save General Gor- don, was be to be told that as a. nation Eneland did not ' dare to give justice to Ireland--(" No," and cheers)— through fear. ("No," and renicw74 cheers.) Let them be just and fear not. (Loud cheers.) That was ' lat saes the policy, the axiom, the tradition of the Liberal • party. (Cheers.) They told Canada when she was absolutely in armed rebellion that she could have Home Rule, and the Canadians had been most peaceable and loyal sabjects ever since. Australia, toe, had been given the full- est governing powers, and they had never swerved from the policy of giving self-government to the colonies when they were ready to accept it. They were told by some—Mr. Murray, of Belfast, and Sir Gilbert Greenall—whom he stigmatised as cowards—that they dare not and must not do I justice to our Irish citizens in Ireland, because it might be ; giving them a platform and a position in which they could I hinder this powerful country. (Cries of "Shame,"and cheers.) IThere was nothing to fear, and they had only to hold their consciences clear before God. (Cheers.) He knew they I would join Mr. Crosfield--(loud cheers)—in granting that' power to their fellow citizens in Ireland to govern them- selves, with the reservation that if they were false to the I trust which was imposed on them, if they 'did not rise to ! the responsibility to which they bad been called, and if 1 they broke the pledges which had ten given to them, 'they were thirty-five millions strong and the power remained with us to oblige Ireland to do so. tCheers.) Ile would re- fer to one thing that had taken place since he last spoke, and that was the rapprochement, the coming nearet on the part of Lord Hartington to the position of Mr. Gladstone. He saw that Lord Hertingtan now proposed that there should be local government. He proposed settlement by giving some form of solf-government, which was nothing like what was asked for, and which there was notlthe least chalice of Ireland accepting ; but on the part of Lord Har- , tington it showed a more advanced and more friendly spirit, : ande ft In abovetdheet a bra aml nl i dtnnhheni he et sit of the not, (Laugher LihNetctNehaehrweuda: l that the Tory rod aetvetri hhfl peoaetetrnhi formed teayeocatdprthadta. enwenreordtrao aNspov !,I;:othri ILl:looftonfirhthdhate hveieHarting- tonSalisbury— (cheers)—au shouldooai l gicbnhtpolicy ' of paper L'nlie bellnlocomcoienegciaolno,nwgell .settled without force—by reasonable argument by careful discusilon.'llev the coming together of interests, and when they, get into a room to settle that question it .would be set- tled. very like the, Seats Bill was settled. (Hear, hear.) When two or three men, who knew what they wanted and were determined to have it, got into a room 'with three or four people who bad not the least idea of what they wanted, and not any great determination nOt,to have it, somehow or other the man eybo went Into a room- knowing what he wanted generally came out of the room with all that he wanted, and perhaps a little more. (Laughter and loud cheers.) And thus, it might be, the matter would be settled. (Hear, hear.) He Wed to pet these, questions on the highest grounds, but they all cared about their own pockets, they all cared about their own political opinions, and they all bad a pet reform that they vtanted to see careied. He wanted to put to them how much longer that. Irish ques- tion was to be allowed to stand in the way. (Heer. hear.) He was a disciple of Mr. Gladstone, who ever hesitated to argue any matter before a great audience like that from any but the highest and noblest and purest point of view, but at the same time he was not Mr. Gladstone, and he might be allowed to put to them a few questions. They bad done nothing in Parliament since be was there eight or ten years ago. They had devoted their whole mind .and their whole time to the settlement and !re-arrangement of Irish affairs and they had neglected their own. There must be man in that room who cared for the. , temperance question. (Cheers.) There must be electors in that room who wished to see a large, extensive, and compre- hensive measure connected with education and placing the cost of education where it should be, upon the Consolidated Fund, and not upon the rates of the people (Cheers.) And there must be men in that room and the surrounding agri- cultural district wh 3 were interested in reforms connected with the soil they cultivated. (Hear, bear.) GREAT LIBERAL MEETING
AT WARRINGTON.

SPEECHES BY MR. M. CONWAY, M.P., MR, GEO. MELLY, MR. JNO. CROSFIELD, &c. On Tuesday another meeting was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, in support of Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., the Liberal candidate for the borough. The hall was again crowded, and marked enthusiasm prevailed throughout the proceedings. During the period oil waiting political songs were sung by the audience, and on MrlCrosfield and party coming upon the platform they met with a reception of great cordiality. The chair was taken by the presi- dent of the Liberal Association, Mr. J. G. McMin- nies, J.P., who was supported on the platform by Mr. M. Conway, M.P.., Mr. George Melly, X.P. (of Liverpool), Mr. John Crosfield, J.P.lAlderman Bur- gess, J.P., Mr. C. Broadbent, JP., the Rev. R. Pit- cher, 8.A., Mr. F. A. Roberts, Dr. Gornall, Council- lors Brown, Fleming, and W. Thornton, George Walker, William Furness, B. Percival, Thomas Shaw, Robert Evans, and James Unsworth. Mr. H. ROBERTS read letters that had been received apolo- gising for the absence of the writers. The first was from Mr. Z. Armitage. who said that physically he wa3 unable to , take an active part in promoting Mr. Crosfield's return for Warrington, being in the hands of the doctor. But he was anxious to do all that lay in his power to secure a victory . for the good cluee,'which he agreed was the cause of real anion, and would best promote the interests of the United Kingdom. Cutting, Wesleyan minister, wrote saying that the Rev. W. Arthur's appeal to Liberals and Nonconformists, and a letter to a 1 London paper, were unfairly used Ly Tories and seceding Liberals. Sentences of his pamphlet were placarded as the , words of an ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference, and I be was represented as signing his letter as ex-president, and thus Wesleyan votes were being alienated, and many good Methodists were led to believe that he represente-4 the Wes- 1 leyan C.r ference, or that he .spoke the general opinion of the Weeleyan ministry. Mr. Arthur himself would be the first to acknow7edge that he had no authority from the Con- ferenc3 or his brethren to represent the views of the Wes- leyan ministry, and Mr. Cutting protested against such un- fair fighting. Mr. Cutting added that the beat way to meet Catholrcism was to act Justly to Roman Catholics, and to try to win thens,not by coercion, but by kindness. (Cheers) Be bad no fe.ir that a.Doblin Parliament would oppress the Peotestant minaity. and it could not if it sr/aid. The third i letter was from the Rev. (Cheers.) The dimins...isr, who was greeted with loud cheers, said there was only one question practically before the country, because the question of the government of Ireland excluded every other at the I present time. What principally commended the principle of Mr. Gladstone's scheme, to his mind, was its far-reaching boldness in the first place, and secondly because it was accepted by the Irish people. (Hear, hear.) What was the use of any measure too feeble to settle this question and which did not meet the aspirations of the Irish penple ? Lord Hartington offered county reform and 'local I government, a very good thing in itself, and as far as ' it went, both for Great Britain and for Ireland, but it did not meet the wishes of the Irish people. (Hear, hear.) It was giving a stone to those who were asking for bread. (Cheers.) Mr. Chamber- lain, as far as be could understand his views, would give them Parliaments in England, and in Scotland and in Ireland for the management of local matters, and an Imperial Parliament in London for the man- agement of imperial matters, supreme over these 'separate Parliaments. But, gentle- out an apostle from Ulster. / (Laughter, and; men, I have had a little fault found with me by one his§es.) • 'He had been told that a Mr. Murray or two gentlemen on the other side---,-(" Never was posing in Warrington as a great Liberal, and an • mind ")—and with your permission I'll just deal advocate of the so-called Union—paper union as it , with one or two of them. • (Laughter and cheers.) was denominated by Mr. Gladstone. Home Rule Parliament in order not only to push their own fortunes, but the. for- - tunes of their province, when Ireland governed her— self. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The province, of .' Ulster was made the text of Mr: Murray'S 'speech, and he tried to persuade his audience that he was guided only by the possibility of oppression in• taking sides with the Orangemen of Ulster. Now they knew that as regarded the representation of Ulster the Nationalist members were in . the ageend- ant. Thirty-threel representatives were returned from what was called "Protestant" Ulster, but which he should prove was Catholic Ulster. Of these 33 representatives 17 were Nationalists, and inasmuch as they were now in the throes of a . general election, he had no hesitation in predicting that they should wha West Belfast and Derry in the forthcoming elections, and so accentuate that Nationalist majority that they claimed. (Loud cheers.) He had in his hand a little pamphlet issued by one of their organisations, the statistics of which were taken from Government returns. There was ,one small 'portion of a map it con- tained marked darkly. That portion represented that part of Ireland where the Protestants i , were n the majority, and that portion was made up of County Antrim, a portion of County Down, and a , portion of County' Armagh. Only in that portion of Ulster was the Protestant population in the ascen- dant; in the rest of Ireland the Catholics were in he majority, and'yet they were told by•those 'ad- vocates pf the so-called loyal minority that those gen- tlemen were afraid of the Irish Catholics if Home , Rule were granted—that they would not have fair- play, and that oppression would obtain. (Laughter.) And, besides, let them remember that the Protes- tants of Ireland were not confined to. that little portion of Ireland, but were spread throughout the whole country—(hear, hear)—and it was his sin- gular pleasure at the last general election, not merely to have Catholic popular support, for Pro- testant farmers%cante to him—ay, and even Orange- men, for he represented a constituency in which. there was an. important Orange lodge—and ap- plauded the sentiments he gave expression to on the platforms of the constituency, and said—" Mr. Conway, if these are your opinions, I am with you, and will give you my vote." (Cheers.): these men were not tyrannised over by Catholics in any part of /reland (Cheers.), Could they say that the catholic major,- it y oppressed the Protestant minority? (" No.") Why, he believed that in Ireland they were in thess. matters thorou6hly liberal, on equal terms with each other; and were prepared to extend the hand' of fellowship to their fellow Protestants, and not only that, if a Protestant only fell into the line that the welfare of his country demanded, they were pre- pared to give him every chance of proving the man that was in him. (Cheers.), Let him point out that , in Protestant Ulster they did not follow the example set by the rest of Ireland; for they had not a single Catholic representative. But how did it standwith the Nationalists of Ireland? They had in their chief, Mr.. Parnell—(lmit cheers)—a leading 'Pro- testant; they had Protestant representatives in Dr. Tanner, his friend Mr. Abraham, and others. There was a 'neighbour of 'his, a Methodist, adopted as the Nationalist candidate for county, Clare, the county which sent Dan O'Connell to Parliament— and this Methodist is their candidate at the present election. That did not look like a spirit of intoler- ance. ("No.") He thought it looked like a question of fair-play. And if they, looked in the press that 'day they would find'. that, for the seven vacancies which had occurred on their side for one reason or another, they had already adopted as candidates for some of these constituencies Protestant gentlemen who sided with Ireland's aspirations. (Loud cheers.) He had already spoken of the little portion of Ire- land, the majority of the population, of which was' , Protestant, but in that part even there was a good ' minority of Catholic's. There were no less than 188,000 Catholics in a population of half a million of Protestants. Why, Ulster as a whole was Roman Catholic, they might almost say to' the very core, and therefore if they were guided by the logic of facts they would say that the representation of Ulster being mainly Nationalist, and the population of Ulster largely Catholic, and taking into account that Ireland demanded Rome Rule as exemplified by her 85 members, they would say that Mr. Glad - stone's legislation was demanded by the whole of Ireland, and should be an accomplished fact. (Loud cheers.) They were told that the wealth of Ireland was in Ulster, but, as regarded the income tax Der head, in Leinster, jw a 8

no. —iv, ........ ..,ays, . , in a speech, if is reported correctly, that I was the greatest coercionist, for I had ordered the Salvation Army, when I was Mayor of Warrington, to pull down the placards they had put on the wall. I never did any such thing. (Cheers.) I venture to say from this platform that I have as broad religious sympathies as Dr. Mackie, and broader—(cheers and laughter)—but when the Salvation Army came to Warrington, and some of you will remember, they put a flaring placard on the walls in, red letters, headed "Blood and Fire." (Laughter.) You know lam for peace. I did not like that. (Laughter.) The Chief Constable; Mr. Hunt, came to me, I being. the chief magistrate of the town, and he represented to me that the peace of the town was in danger of being disturbed through these placards which were on the walls. Mr. Hunt gave orders himself. I did not give an order to have those placards covered, not pulled down, and I sent for th e „leaders of the Salvation Army to my office to confer with them as to the best thing to do. (Cheers.) Two'of the lady officers came—two of the strongest-minded women I ever saw—(laughter)—and I tell you gentlemen, it took me all my time to hold my own with them. (Re- newed laughter.) I represented to these lady offi- cers that if they went through the streets of War- rington with a brass band, on a Sunday morning, dis- turbing denominations during their hours of wor- ship, I, as chief magistrate of the town, could not allow it. (Cheers.) I think, gentlemen, you will acquit me of doing anything that was kinfair— (cheers) —or anything that was unjust, or anything in the way of coercion—(renewea cheers) —when I persuaded the Salvation Array-not to dis- turb other people during their hours of worship. (Cheers.) I think Dr. Mackie had better-try te find something else out before he begins to attack me. He has been looking back for twenty years, I sup- pose, to see every word .I have spoken—(laughter)— and to find anything that he could complain about, and he says that I once spoke of the great Lord Bea- consfield as a "wolf in sheep's-clothing." It is quite true I did—(laughter and cheers)—and I am not at all ashamed of it. (Cheers.) I Went over to • Hawarden, and saw our great leader. Mr. Gladstone, —(cheers)—and I begged of Mr. Gladstone to save the country froni this "wolf in sheep's clothing." (Cheers.) What did Mr. Disraeli do. in 1867? He jumped Jim Crow. (Laughter.) He resisted every measure for the extension of the franchise to the people before that. He would not listen to any- thing prposed by Mr. Gladstone or by Mr. ,Bright; but he saw that there was a chance of getting into office and retaining office, so he jumps Jim Crow and brings in- a' bill 'that goes beyond both Mr. Glad- stone and Mr. Bright—a measure for giving house- hold suffrage. • "I remember walking up Sankey- street, and I met one of the first Tories in Warring: ton, well respected and deserving of respect, and he,said " I'll never vote "for that man again as long as I live." (Laughter and cheers.) He was so dis- gusted at his abandoning his previous principles. The Tory party are ready to do it again. ((Aeers.) They'll jump Jim Craw if they can get into office— (cheers), and My opinion is that Lord Randolph Churchill—(hisses)—at this present nice. ment has got a bill for Ireland far beyond this bill of William Ewart Gladstone. (Laughter and cheers.) , But the country won't have Lord Ran- dolph Churchill. (Groans and a voice: "Not at any price.") Well, there was a young 'Tory in Warrington, who was speaking the other night, and 'he said that John Crosfield had got a passage in his address about voluntary and undenominational edu- cation, and he said this was a little infant that had just been born, or words to that effect. I .shoard advise this young gentleman—l am old enough to be his father—that he had better be a bit more cautious before he makes insinuatips of that sort, for if he had known all about me during the last twenty years he would not have made so foolish a remark as that. Why, gentlemen, I have been, in , favour of that sort of education ever since I can re- member anything--(cheers)—and as proof —I do not want to boast to you-=-I built a school at Bank Quay myself ten years ago—(cheers)—and five years 'ago I built a wing myself of the People's College, which saved the People's College from being closed. ,I think that-was pretty good proof. (Ldudcheers.) I do not say this in the way Of complaint, gentlemen; understand that I am rather glad that they did it, because I always find that the • attack recoils upon themselves, and it does me good. (Cheers.) It is no use attacking you by telling lies. If they, want to attaelt your character they must say some- thing about you which is true. I hope I have con- vinced you by this that there was no tfuth in this statement 'by Mr. W. J. Burgess. (Laughter • and cheers.) Well, gentlemen, I have been in the town

£lO 68 9d, in Munster £6 (V 7d, and the ,great rich I thriving Ulster came third oil the list with £5 14s. (Laughter, and hear,. hear) What became of the wealth of Ulster? Yet these were figures supplied to the Government, and supplied by them to the pub- lic. (Hear, hear.) The valuation per inhabitant of the provinces showed as follows. In Leinster it was £3 135.5 d, in Munster £2 10S 10d, in Ulster £2 98 11d, and poor Connaught ve2y nearly reached Ulster with _EI 15s. So they woult see that in these. matters Ulster was not only not foremost, but was only third rate. But the advocates of the- prosperity of Ulster chose to ignore these facts,. and Mr. Gos- chen, who sided with them in this matter, when trying to prove that Ulster was really thewealthiest part of Ireland, left out of consideration all source of income except these which came undelesehedule D. This particular schedule, however, was most misleading, and when Mr. Goschen presented his statement to the House, the very- next speaker was able to tear it to pieces aid prove that Mr. Gosehen was wrong iii his calculations. (Cheers.) In the matter of edu- cation, Ulster was anything but to the fore, and to say that Ulster was leading Irelesad in wealth and intelligence was simply to lead them aitraSe (Hear, hear.) They had heard a good deal about llister • threatening, but Ulster had always threatened' when: any reforming legislation was projected, s'o that when they heard of Ulster men drilling by mid- night, armed with revolvers at half-a-crown a, piecel —(loud laughter)—they neednot be afraid that arw ' fearful consequences would ensue. ' The Catholic population could take them up with a pinch of salt and obscure them for ever. (Lourilaughter and. cheers.) Referring to the present position of the Irish question, Mr. Conway said that' if Mr. Glad- stone's bill be not carried the Tories would repeat the tactics of 1867 and bring in another bill. (Hear, hear.)' But they did not wish for a Tory bill; they accepted the bill of Mr. Gladstone. (Prolonged cheering.) They accepted that bill as afinal settle- ment, and they were prepared, under those dream- tances, to-work out Ireland's future asregarded its peace and prospeiity, and they were not prepared to exploit their political influence in the direction of the Tories, on. thesupposition that they were going to jump "Jim Crow "—(laughter)—as one of their speakers had put it. No, they world take Mr, Gladstone as he stood with the weight of 76 years upon Mm, but strong and alert, with the mind like the mind of youth as regarded activity, with the mature judgment of middle age, and the splendour of 50 years' experience in Parliament. (Continued cheering and waving of hats.) They accepted Wm. Ewart Gladstone as their champion. (Renewed cheering.), Their Tory friends said they-were going in for entire separation, but the bill was safeguarded by thirteen conditions, and, even supposing there were no conditions at all; could it be beßeved for a moment that poor little Ireland, with a small pop- ulation, without anyresources as regarded army and I navy, would- be so insane as to pit her five millions ! against thirty-six millions? ("No.") Did they think she would go,bare-breastedion the bayonets of their F hundreds of thousands of soldiers? Did they-think , that, without ships, she would challenge the/salts from the finest war vessels the world had ever seen? ("NC.") Nothing of the kind.. Ireland said she accepted that bill with all its reservations, and Irishmen:would try to prove that it had been the right thing 'toll° for their mother country.'. It was • all nonsense that wee enunciated by the Tdries, and they knew right well that it was all fustian. (Hear, hear.) He. believed that the Conservative candi- date appealecrto-Tory working-men in order that that bill might not come to fruition. We*, he had had some little experience in Parliament, and in the House of-Commons, right opposite to • his place, sat elpven representatives of labour. (Cheers) These men were sent by their fellow working-men toirepresent the' interests of labour, but how were they treated by-the TOries? Every tim, they get upv they were -aliaost howled down by the Tones. '(" Shame.") The- Tory voters should take the trouble to go to. the House of Commons, and get admission to'-the strangers' gallery some night when some of the labour candidates got -up to try to ameliorate the-condition ih which the working people of thern country lived, and they 'Won 1 d see the Tory members howl them down with their voices and decline to give them a hearing. (" Shame.") • It was only the strength of the democratic vote on the Liberal and Irish sides of the House that came to the rescue—(lou(jtheers)— and gave them an opportunity for doing some- thing for, their . class. And yet they were told that. there were. 'Tory working-men in existence!. To hie mind it was surprising that.' men -.,could so demean their intelli- gence, as tp lick the chains that: encircle their, limbs when they ought to tand •up arid shake them- ,off, and stand true to the prin- ciples of liberty. (Loud cheers.) There was a gen- tleman on that- platform who had lived for many years inethe same town as he (Mr. Conway) had spent 'many years in—Mr. John Walker. They hapl spent most of their 3-ears in the town of Blackburn, and in that town there was, strange to say, in this democratic age, a large workinfg--men Tory vote, and the reason that was- adduced for their-being Tory was that they got their bread and butter from cer- tain employers whose politics were Tory. (Laugh- ter). That wae scarcely an intelligenJ reason, be- cause they- gave their labour for their 'hy. There was no favourou either side. (Hear, hear.) So far as he-knew, no- Liberal employer of labour had ever yet made -use of lds position to grind the consciences of his -employes. and make them vote in the direc- tion . in, which he wished. (Hear, hew.) But on the Tory side there was an organisation, a patient persistent, organisation in a great =Weer of manu- factories, and in a great number of establishments in which capital was invested. (Real hear.) They took care that the men who- were pro- , nounced in the direction of Liberalism shoultl be gentl3r weeded out. (Hear, hear.) Those great Tory employers of labour made use of their positionto get votes at elections. (!‘No," and in- terruption.) Who said no. He knew where over- lookers in the mills canvassed in order to swell the vtAe on the Tory side. (Hear, hear.), At the last generalelection the Irish voters voted not with ' friends ; they voted with the intriguers. (Hear, hear, and loud cheers.) He saw- that that 'Nast audiencerecognisedthe tactics of Lord Caniarvon, and-Mr.- Howard Vincent. (Hear, hear.) But this time they voted for the declared friends of the cause of liberty friends who were deter- mined that no Paper Union, should exist, but a- union of hearts and. minds. (Loud cheers:), In cham'pioning Mr.. Crosfleld's cause they were championing the cause of the masses against money, class, and influence. (Loud cheers 4 On Friday night he bereaved Mr. Crosfield would be declared victor, and he would be one of . thefirst to side with Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—and the resultof the Warrington election would en- . courage other constituencies in England, Scotland, and Wales to follow their example -and determine, that Mr. Gladstone should hamea decisive majority, when the elections were over:. (Prolonged cheering , and waving of hats).

were hand and glove With their Irish Mends. They must wort?' shoulder to shoulder togtther, and , then on Friday. night they would have ti- victory. ! (Cheers.) The resolutioA was then nut and carried with great enthusiasm. Mr. CROSFIELD, "c"llo was again cordially cheered, in reply, said :—I thank you, gentlemen, heartily for your kindness in passing that resolution, and ! I can tell you that I feel every confidence that we shall win. (Cheers.) The meeting has got very late and you have all sat there patiently and atten- tively, and I feel proud, gentlemen, that our friend Mr. Conway has had such An audience as he has had to-night. (Cheers.) • It is now nay-pleasure and my duty to, ask you to pass a kearty vote of thanks to ; our vEnerable old leader, Mr. McMinnie3. (Loud ! cheers.) Ido not think that any worthier Liberal member of Parliament ever sain the British House ',Jommons. (Renewed cheers) I arn;., exceedingly ! sorry that his health and strength would not per- mit him to have occupied the phce that I do, but I cm tell yen that I shall follow in his footsteps— (cheers)—andl shall be delighted'to work shoulder to 3houlder with such gentlemen' as Hz.. Conway. (Cheers.) As he has truly said tonight he repre- sents the Irish. democracy; I'll represent the Eng- glish democracy— (cheers) —and togeth erwo will see if we-cannot pass some measure in the-House of Com- mon - that shall do some good for the great democ- racy of Englandi and of Ireland. (Cheers.) I have also to move a vote of thanks to the vititon. rwill include them in this, and I will ask you-to paas-it in ths ole fashioned English way, and e7eryonse. -irho is in favour I. will ask to say "Aye." MT. C. BROADBENT rose tO,propose a resoluticn. They would allow him, he said, to say a word or tno about himself. His absence-irorn he last great met- ing held by the Liberal party in Warrington was. misunderstood by some of his fellow townsmen, and especially by some of his Conservative friends.. It "VMS said that he was going to stand aside in that great contest. He saw no reason whatever to desert his great leader. , (Cheers.) In passing he witaied to pay a compliment on the excellent spirit in which the contest had: been so far conducted. He. believed that scarcely a weird had been spoken that was not fair on either side, and the few objections Mr. Crosfield had mentioned were so • slight Oat he considered they were perhaps hardly worthy-of any charge against their. opponents. He thouglit this was partly to be. attrihnted to the good feeling of the town, but he-also attributed it to the rev,sou that the candidate was se. Well known, so.' rluch re- spected,'that -nothing could be said agaiust him. (Cheers.) Of course their Conservative fri4nds had different opinibns to what they had, but it was least' easy to bear opposition from their own friends. Ho. held the dibsenbient, Liberals in great respect, nisl. thought that they were actuated by the boat motives, and he believed that the gentleman whose name had been mentioned there that night was as conscien- pious 0 any man could be. Ile then proposed, "That this meeting expresses unabated confidence hal Mr. Gladstone, and its hearty approval of his proposal for the Government of Ireland, and pledges itself to use every possible lawful effort to secure the.return of Air. John Crosfield at the forthcoming election." (Cheers.) Mr. Broadbent then mentioned that be met a gentleman at Liverpool, who said that "he was a Conservative, but John Crosfield was one of the best men he knew." He (the speaker) belie-fe4 that in sending Mr. Crosfield Le. Parliament " they Would have a good representative. (Cheers.) IMPORTANT INTERVIEW. On Monday evening a dep-utation of workino-men, re-- presenting the wire, iron, and other industries of the town, met Mr. John Crostield, .7:17.. Liberal candidate :or War- rington, at the residence of Mir. McMinnies, in Bewsey-road to obtein his views on questions chiefly concerning the working-classes.- The gatheriag was not of a political natere in the party sense of the term, the deputation hay- ioe, on behalf of their fellow-workmen, deteemined to ask each candidate's opinion on ceestions affecting trade, with the intention of supporting the one who was most favourable to theoeforms that they desired i Both candidates were com- municated with, end Mr. Henry Greenall, election agent for the Cor.serrative candidate, replied on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greene!), M.P., in a letter dated from the Central Commit- - tee Room, Winmarleigh-streen and addressed to Mr. Thus: Wadsworth. The letter read as fellows : " Sine—Sir •liilbert Greenall has handed me your letter of the 25th inst. I have advised hid, that there can be no ad- vantage under existing circurnstanees in an interview. I may, honoever, say I haye reaeon to know Sir Gilbert is of opinion that amendments and ameliorations in reference to tbe matters you have named are needed." Mr. John Crosfield granted, the- request of the working- men and reccordiogly met the deputation as stated. The following gentlemen attended as the deputation :—Messrs. H. Whitoam, T. Eden, T. Sykese.B,.Edwa.rdscra, T. Wads- worth, A. Hiboll, T. Houghton,. DI nenderson. and Joseph Cotterill. Mr. IV:dreneotrein introducing the deputation, first re- ferred to the question of royalties.- They' desired to know whether Mr. Urosfield would support he Labour representa- tives that might be sent to Parliament ire their endeavours. to reduce these landowners' taxes upon industry. Mr. T. Soiosoas a representative of the Trades Council, said that the royalty rates, they thought, were crippling them as Englishmen, seeing that they were so much higher than the German rates. Mr. Hicoon-said that the plea fore reduction of wages in the wire trade had always been German, competition, and if they could get the royalty rates reduced it wonld no doubt help their trade. . These rates-weighed heavily upon the manufacturers of iron, and upon all descriptions of the hard- ware trade. ' Mr. Joint CRDSFIELD, in reply, seidee ire am much obliged to you, gentlemen, for coming to see me on-this question, because I am quite clear in rnynown mind that that is the right and proper 'course to take. I said on Saturday night that I quite agreed with Mr. Percy in the opinions that he expressed. I think that the royalties ought to be dealt with, and that the. English workman ought to be put in quite as good a position, as far as- royalties are concerned, aS any German workman—(hear, hear)—and I shall hear- tily support the working-men's representatives, or any other members of Parliament, who take up this question in the coining session of Parliament. (Hear,hear.) I understood Mr. Percy tO say that in Germany they did not pay any royalty on coal without the company male's a profit—("Yes, that's it ")—and that the royalty wee 5 per cent on the profits. If we could get our royalties fined at a certain per- centage on the profits made by a company it would be a very great improvement on the present eyetern. (" Yes.") I should be very glad indeed to support it. (Hear, bear.) I think those were two startling caeca that Mr. Percy mentioned, where such enormous sums of money had been paid, and the coal had never heel' got. (Hear. hear.) Mr. WIIITHAZI then-intimated that the next question of the deputation referred to railway tariff,. The railway companies had the home manufacturer in their grip and could deal with himeal they liked,' but for the foreigner they made a special and encouraging rate. They wished to thaw his attention to the matter so that if ony measure was introduced in Partiament that was likely to benefit em- ployers, and must benefit workmen, hoiwould not fail to be in his place, if returned. The other question was as to the payment of members of Parliament. He was not himself certain* of the advieahility of paying all members, but they thought something should be done to make it eaeier for working-men to enter Parliament--(hear, hear)—to represeet their views. He should not -like-Mr.. Croslield to pledge himself to vote • for the payment of members pure and simple, but at the same time they desired to make it easier for Working-men to sit in Parliamentn Mr. Devoe said that they were told by their employers that working-men were the persons to bring the questions of foreign c:impetition and railway rates to the front. So lone; as the railway rates so much favoured the foreigners, so long would the mannfacturere, and, through them, the work- men, be in.a crippled state. Mr. CROSFIELD an eaeily answer you, gentlemen, on these two questions ; as easily as I.conld on the other. I am entirely of opinion that the raihway rates ought to be revised, and that the English inanufactueer ought certainly to be put on as goad terms as any foreigner. I know from what Mr. Carson has told me repeatedly that you are sadly handicapped in Warrington owing to the excessive railway rate. (Hear, lit:.ar.) He has told me repeatedly of large orders that have gone past White Cross Company, owing, he said, entirely to the excessive railway rate, end I have al ways sympathised with him and always said that Parliament ought to interfere to moist the manu- facturers of this country to compete better with foreign inakers. So you you see, that beinn my opinion, you can understand, if I, go to Parliament that I should certainly support an ineiniry into this matter. (Hear, hear.) I sup- pcse it would probably be referred to a Select Committee to obtain information, and then report to the Huse. I am quite of opinion that it will be quickly altered whenever it comes to be Inquired into. Then as regards the payment of members, I think that it would be quite right and fair that the Mayor's expenses should be paid either by the ratepayers or out of the national exchenuer—(hear. hear)—either one or the other. Ido not think it, would be right to pay the candidates' individual expenses, because I ceo see veiy great evil would arise if you attempted to do so. You might have 50 candidates put up at an election if a man had nothing to pay for it. I could not pledge myself to vote for a bill which proposed to pay all candidates' expenses at an elec- tion. I ahould, of course, be prepared to consider any bill that was brought in, but I am clearly of opinion that it , would be right and fair to-throw nhe Mayor's expenses either upon the rates, or else upon the national exchequer. I snail; be inclined to put it on the national exchequer as the fairest thing, because theSe Mayors' expenses are necessary oxe pauses for obtaining a repnasentative of the peope, and it is necessary, for the government of the nation, and therefore I think that the Mayol'a expenses should crone out of the national exchiopeer. Of course I speak to you sea manufacturer who hao,been in boldness for nearly 40,yeare and I know pretty well ,how, railway rates affect business, We know it in our own boa- nese, and I should be very glad indeed to do anything that would assist the industries in Warrington, especiean the iron industries, which form so important a part. (Hear, hear.) Alter Nether conversation, Mr. Crosfield continued : Ph give you a. case Mr. Caron pointed oat to me. He said there was a rate from Warrington to Soothampton for wire that was going to be shipped abroad, and that the r. rate was either dt3 or la) a ton less than the rata for wire r'going to Southampton for home consumption. That ap- pears tome to be a most extraordinary thing. Mr. EDEN : And that 53 a ton would repiessnt, Our wages on mazy a ton that is drawn. CONSERVATIVE 1111,ETING IN WARRINGTON. SPEECH BY SIR R. A. CROSS. On Monday evening, .a well-attended Conservative meeting was held in the Public Hall. Captain Rey- nolds presided, and amongst those on the platform were Sir R. A. Cross (Conservative candidate for the Newton Division), Sir G. Greenall (Conservative candidate for Warrington), Major Litton, Aldermen Davies and Webster, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. J. R. Pick- mere, Mr. p. Greenall, Mr. John White, Sze. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said that he thought it was rather hard lines that they should be brought there that night, about the first fine summer night that they had had this year, in order to bear what their friends had to say about another contested election. He thought they would agree with him that if that question at Home Rule was of so much importance it ought to have been brought before the country last October. (Hear, hear.) He advised teem not to look too much upon the wonderful papers on the walls, beceuse if they believed all that was on these papers their mouths would not be wide enough to receive all the honey that would be dropped into them. (Laugh- ter.) There might be some people so foolish as to open their months, but the honey would never come if Mr. Gladstone had a majority in the next Parliament. (Laugh- ter and cheers.) Sir R. A. CROSS, who was received with loud cheers, said that nothing could be more gratifying to him than in that old town in which he bad lived so many happy years to find that they at all events had not forgotten an old friend. (Hear, hear.) But they were all of them at the present time upon very serious business. They all thought at the time of the last election, when they were for the first time in the history of this country to have a Parliament which would represent every section of the community, that the new Parliament would speak with no uncertain voice as to what the feeling of the country was on questions that might be put before it. But no sooner did the present Prime Minister find that that Parliament was perfectly determined to give that voice, quite irrespective of the person who held ' the high office of First Minister of the Crown, than-he be- gan to change his opinion, and be did not think the Parliament was so good as he had before thought it was. He was prepared to welcome its first vote which turned the Conservative Government out of office, but he did not like its second. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He would put two questions to the Prime Minister. The first was—" Did you mean, at the time of the last election, to bring forward the question of a separate Parliament for Ireland? " If he did, he ought to heye told the country that he meant it. (Hear, hear.) Of course if the question had come suddenly before the country it wae quite right that Parliament should be dissolved and another Parliament elected. But he would ask another question, and the Prima Minister could not get out of the dilemma. It was—" You have said yourself that you did mean that this question of a separate Irish Parliament should conic forward, and you have said that in your speeches you did give the country the necessary warnings; then, I say why are you not content with the voice in which Parliament has answered the ques- tion ?" (Cheers.) He (Sir Richard) did not care on vstich horn of the dilemma the Prime Minister chose to ride ; he was wrong either way. If he meant to bring the question forward he ought to have told the country, and if ha did tell the country he ought to have been satisfied with the voice of that Parliament which had, given such a decisive vote against him. (Hear, hear.) He (Sir Richard) went to the country on that question with the greatest confidence, because there was only one answer that as reasonable ptople , • they could give. (Cheers.) He should like, with all the authority he could give, having consulted with his late col- ! leagues and Prime Minister into the bargain, to give answers ; to two questions that had been put to him elsewhere. The first question which he wanted to answer and to which he ; .ated to give the most positive and absolute denial was one which Mr. Parnell had made no later than Friday last, that be had reason to believe that if the Conservatives got into power after the general election they would have given Ireland a statutory legislature. He wanted to state on his own authority and on that of hie-colleagues that there was not a shadow of foundation for any sucti assertion. (Cheers.) 1 ; He would undertake to say that the notion of giving a state- tory legislature to Ireland was one which never was '•under the consideration of the cabinet, and which the cabinet ; never have considered for a single moment. (Cheers.) This was quite another question to local self-government, such as might have been given to Scotland or England. (Hear, hear.) With regard to Ireland, there was : one thing they were absolutely determined upon, ; and ' that was that nothing should be granted that could be twisted into the germ of a Parliament of any sort or description. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was quite 1 right that that should be known publicly, and he had, therefore, taken the first opportunity he could, after the ; speech by Mr. Parnell on Friday night, to tell them in that hall in Warrington, to his constituents in Newton, and to the whole world, so far as they may care to hear, that there was ; not one shadaw of truth upon which Mil. Parnell could rest the assertions which he so plainly and so shamefully made. (Cheers.) Another question he was asked by one of his constituents was whether the Conservative Govern- ment had in their contemplation, and whether, if they were put into power, be could conceive it possible that they would contemplate the buying out of the Irish landlords ' either with Erklish money or with English credit in any such way as was proposed by the Government measure.. He should like to give as positive a denial to that question I as he had given to the statement of Mr. Parnell. (Loud cheers.) The question of buying out the Irish landlords only arose because of the enormous injustice that was going to be done to them by the Government of Ireland Bill, and • if that Government of Ireland Bill'fell to the ground—as he sincerely hoped it would—never to appear again, there ! was no reason why English taxpayers should be burdened ; with buying out Irish landlords, because they should treat ' the Irish landlords like every other class, with no more favour than they deserved and with strict justice. (Loud cheers.) Sir Richard concluded by moving "That this ; 1 meeting is of opinion that the establishment of a separate ; I Parliament in Dublin, as proposed by Mr. Gladstone, would not only be fraught with disastrous consequences to the British Empire, but would be an injustice towards the loyal portion of the Irish people." (Cheers.) Mr. R. W. MURRAY, of Belfast, who was received with applause, seconded the resolution. He stood there a Loyal- I ist, but he stood there a Liberal also, and let him say that i it was his own proposition that he should come to Warring- ton, and he was invited by no living soul. (Cheers.) When he proposed to come to Warrington, he received encourage- ment, and in supporting Sir Gilbert Greenall he sup- ported his positive declaration against that mischievous diastrous proposition of Mr. Gladstone. His only hope ! of serving the Union was in getting among the Liberals of Warrington, for he heard that there were many Union Liberals. He suggested that he might have an opportunity of speaking to these Union Liberals, but he found it impos- Bible to get up a meeting of that character ; hence he ap- peared on a Conservative platform in order to get the ears of tee Liberals through the press besides those who might be present. (Cheers.) He contended that he represented , the only consistent Liberal party ; they were not the sece- ders. (Hear, hear.) There was one thing he had heard a good deal of since he came to Warrington. He was often asked by Liberals if he had more confidence in Lord Salis- bury than in Mr. Gladstone. His reply was that he had I not, and when asked why he supported the Tory party when the question was Lord Salisbury versus Mr. Gladstone, he replied that the position was not that. (Hear, hear.) So far as Sir Gilbert Greenall was concerned, he had nothing to do with him with regard to that contest except as to the positive pledge he gave the other night to vote against Home etule. He therefore said the question was not Salis- bury versus Gladstone, bet was whether they would accept Mr. Gladstone and Home Rule or would they accept somebody else—possible Lord Hartington—without Home Rule. (Cheers.) He was met constantly with the most delightful prophecies of men in this country that ought to be better informed, but they knew as little of Ireland as the Indians. (Laughter.) Hethad been reading a letter in the papers in Warrington from a minister of his, which contained the wh iosn ludt t enro t i gunsoer aan cset roofs zt the tlerri sn than C's most question personal thonaal urrnionng to he ti‘hi re. dhlesacrrriabyedaaais Mr. hCardo snfieevl de rs ta.ttaßcekfe indulged in a personal attack on the platform and he never would. He would not reply to Mr. Croefield. (Cheers.) Hu Opno nE Rhxo wDdAiviit Ee differently n itnl y su p constitutedpo ug people were. Some the resolution, re- markedpeople thought that Mr. Gladstone ought to be impeached t and there were others who waited upon him with peaches. (Loud laughter.) Sir CrIIBERT GREENALL, who was received with cheers, next spoke. He said they were glad to see Mr. Murray, and he might believe him (Sir Gilbert) to be a true and loyal man to Ireland. He was no Horne Ruler in the bad sense or in any dangerous sense whatever in which that phrase was used. He was for the integrity of the empire. He was as true and as loyal as Mr. Murray was himself. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) • The resolution was then carried. Mr. J. C. PARR moved "That this meeting pledges it- the Newton division of Lancashire and, Sir Gilbert Greenall self to use all legitimate means to return Sir R. A. Cross for as member for the borough of Warrington at the next elec- tion." (Cheers.) Mr. TAYLOR seconded, and Mr. DICKENS supported the proposal, which was carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman closed the proceedings.

THE Asirrall POISONING Cur.—At the Ashton-under- Lyne Police Court, on Wednesday, Mary Ann Britland was charged with causing the death of Mary . Dixon, factory operative, by administering poison to her on the 13th of May last. Mr. Broadbent appeared on behalf of the Trea- sury to prosecute, and Mr. Bromley represented the prisoner. At the commencement of the proceedings Mr. Broadbent stated that as the coroner had not completed his labours, it would be much bettter, both in the interests of the prisoner and the Treasury, if the case were again adjourned. The magistrates, therefore, remanded the prisoner until nezt Tuesday.

two parts like America "—what did the man mean: pinched in the middle F—(langhter)---" it would answer the purpose better?" He did not know that America was divided into two parts, and he did not think any effort of his would divide Ireland into two parts. What the questioner meant he believed was, e• Don't you think it right that the Protes- tants in the North of Ireland should be allowed to separate themselves from the rest of their fellow countrymen ?" (Hear, hear.) He believed that the Protestants of the North of Ireland were far too manly to desire any such thing. (Cheers.) He was perfectly satisfied that if it was settled in the rnglish Parliament that Ireland should have two legislatures, one for the Protestants and one for the Roman Catholics, the'first act of the Protestants would be to join thenaselves to their Roman Catholic fellow-country- men. (Cheers.) I The resolution was carried amid much cheering with only I one dissentient.

Mr. ROBERT &taw, who was received very heartily, moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting ap- proves of the candidature and of the consistent support given by our member, Mr. J. T. Brunner, to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, adopts him as the Liberal candidate at the ensuing electron, and pledges itself to use every legiti- mate means to secure his return to the next Parliament." (Cheers.) Referring to the Irish question, Mr. Shaw said that the real point was whether now they had got the opportunity of voting they desired to do justice to a down- trodden and an oppressed people. They would have to answer that question at the ballot boxes. (Cries of "We shall answer it.") He argued that, inasmuch as 86 members pledged to Home Rule bad been returned to the House of Commons, and that Protestant Ulster had returned 17 mem- bers also pledged to the principle, it was the duty of Eng- land to listen to the voice of the people, and to grant them what they desired. (Cheers.) Mr. W. H. OCBLESTON, who was received with cheers, eecanded the resolution. He believed that Mr. Brunner had conscientiously supported Mr. Gladstone in the Parliament which bad just been dissolved, and he was certain that if he was returned as their member, and they pledged themselves that he would be returned, he would, as in the past, worthily represent that constituency. (Cheers ) Mr. Moore O'Farrell, an Irishmen, supported the resolu- tion in a speech that frequently elicited cheers. The motion was carried unanimously; and Mr. BRUNNER, on rising to reply, was greeted with three ringing cheers. He said be had to thank them for the proof that they were of one mind, and for having declared that that mind was on the side of right and justice. He asked them to join with him in thanking Mr. Handley for presid- ing over the meeting that evening. Mr. Handley deserved well at their hands. He set a good example in many ways. He was not afraid, although a rich min and in high posi- tion, of maintaining his Nonconformity and his Liber dim]. When a man did that he was a man, ard Mr. Handley was such a one. (Cheers.) _

The Rev. W. VAUSE, who was cordially 'received, sp•con- ded the motion proposed by their candidate and tueir future member. (Cheers.) He did not think Mr. Hand- ley had had a difficult task to discharge. He Lad heard of one gentleman who, when he took the chair, bad not only to be chairman, but had also to do the work of a special constable. (Laughter and cheers.) The motion was carried, and the Chairman having re- sponded, the proceedings terminated with the singing of the National Anthem.

During the proceedings the heat of the room became most oppressive and unbearable, and at the instigation of Mr. Brunner, who pointed out the inadequacy of the ven- tilation provided, s,!ver3l window panes were broken. Some relief was thus afforded, and a more comfortable feeling re- sulted.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. T. C. 7.idwards-Moss,.the Conservative candidate for the Widnes Division waslield in the Drill Hall on Tuesday evenimer. The building was well filled, but the unanimity of the meeting was disturbed by the presence of a hostile element that frequently toads its presence known Ny cries and ' shouts of dissent when the various gentlemen were speak- ing. The speakers occasionally retorted upon their oppo- nents, and the proceelings may be dasoribed as' lively. Major Cross presided, and he was supported on the plat- form by the csndidate,Biro'n fi! De Worms,. Rey George Bond, key WriOit Williams, and Messrs T B Boyden, G W Moss, W J' Stewart, E Banner, A Fletcher, Moly- neux Seel, R Lewis, J White, and W T Husband (agent). Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, J:P., wrote declining an invitation ld to jein the Election Committee ofr.Edwards Moss. or to speak at the meeting. He-added that,.as a Unionist, he shorild vote for the Tory candidate. Mr. John Brock wrote to Major Cross declining to,take an active part in in the election. He too concluded, by espressing his intention to vote for Mr. Edwards-Moss.

MR. BIRRELL'S. CANDIDATITRX AT WIDNES. Mr. Birrell has conducted a very vigorous campaign dur- ing the past week, and at each place viaited his reception has been of the most enthueiastic and encouraging descrip- tion. On Monday afternoon be was present at Henglers Circus, Liverpool, to support Mr. Gladstone, and made a short, but admirable speech. The cheers that greeted him showed the esteem in which he, is held by those acquainted with his plucky contest at Walton last rive-ember, and that they &sired tile success in the chemical centre on the 9th int. In the evening of that day he addressed the workers in the Liberal cause at the Central ,Committee-rooms, at iinee, and his words infused ,fresh spirit and enthusiasm in those present. Tuesday night saw him addressing an open air meeting at Woolton, tbe audience being of large proportions. Mr. P.. H. Gossage,.J.P.:. occupied the chair, and Mr. E. K. Muspratt made one of his, thoughtful speeches. A resolution pledging those present to use their best endeavours to return Mr. Birrell at the head of the poll was carried unanimously. Garston was Tisited on Wednes. dive night Here Mr. W. B. Bewring was the chairman, and Mr. Birrell's eloquence was backed up by Mr. E. K. Muspratt. and,Mr: J.eimidley, and others. The unanimity which had cheracterised all the meetings since the contest commenced, was :wain displayed, accompanied with much heartiness:. The Welsh electors met% ia the Central Com- mittee-rooms, Widnes, on Thursday evening. There were about 850. persons present, and the proceedings were con- ducted with the greatest enthnsiarfin. The Rey. E. Jones, of Runcorn, presieed.—Aanetion • expressing confidence in Mr.' Gladstone was unanimoieely.adoptede on the proposi- tfon of Mr. J. Thomas. of Liverpool, seconded by Mr. Ray. —Oa tho proposition of the Rev D. Davies, s•conded by Mr. Wiiliarns,. a resolution to sup- port Mr. Birrell's candidature.. was passed without a dissentiertevote. Mr. Birrell arrived at a late part of the proceedings from Runcorn, where he had been aiding Mr. Brunner, and the reception he met with was of the most flattering description. • MEETINGS- LAST AEGHT. Last night a.meeting was held at Cronton, under the presidency if Mr. Thomas Robinson. Mr. Birrell delivered a long add ress,,and a resolution of support and confidence was passed.. There was aleo held last night a meeting in the Hale Bank Wine WLries, where.aecepitel. ,room had been placed at the dieorsel of- the patty by MT. W. Dainteth. A large audience assembled,.andeolonel Newburn presided. Whilst waiting for the arrival of Mr. Birrell from Crouton, the Chairman delivered aconvincing.speech in favour of Mr. Gladetone's Home Rule scheme, and of the candidature of Mr. Birrell. Mr. BIRRELL, who was.ereeted with enthusiastic cheers. said there were many reforms., dear to most of them, to which they believed they could make out an exceedingly good cause. There was. one reform to which he attacned immense importarice—the reform of the land laws. (Cheers.) The great reform in cennectioa with the land laws which they. desired to see carried oat was the establishment of it registration of titles, so that an acre of land coald be transferred as easily as the share of a ship. (Cheers.) Then there was the temperance cause. He was not-in favour of suppressing public-houses. If there wv a district of 1,000, people and 501 did not want any public-bouees at all and the rernainiteg 499 did, it would be tyranny for the majority to say that the 499 should not have any. piece at all,. They ought simply to provide drinking accommodation for 499 persons who still adhered to what must on. the whole be a disastrous. habit,, that of constantly drinking whether . they were thirsty or not. (Cheers.) Upon the great question, of education his mind had long been made up. It would, be an unjust and Ungenerous thing, if because the state had recently awakened to its responsibilities and had got the purse of the taxpayer behind it, to an unlimited, o. tent, they sheald seek to injure and starve out their de- nomination4l. schools, which had done good work in tb..e past, and was doing a great work in Oe present, and if not interfered with would continue to do. a great work in. the ;uture. (Ceeers.) Mr. Birrell pointed out that none of these questions could he dealt with until the Irish quostion : was settled and out of the way, and went on to ereak of Home Rule in terms similar to those previously repor- ted. (Cheers.) At the close of his address a resolution of confidence and support in Mr. Birrell was unanimously carried on the motion of Mr. Duxbury. NOMINATION AND POLLING. The nomination will be made on Monday, at the Local Board Offices, Alforde Chambers, and the election is fixed for nem' Friday. :he 9th, The arrangements for the polling are similar to those of last November, which were carried out then with such efficiency.

At the moment when the important alectors' conteats are beginning a weighty letter from the Premier on two. vital points of the question at issue is published. It is a'llresed to Mr. Lawson Tait, a candidate for the Bordesley division of Birmingham. Mr. Gladstone, referring to the Carnar- von•Parnell affair, says that Lord Salisbury--aware. as is now clear, of bin Viceroy's views—kept this " dismeraberer " in the Viceroyalty and in the Cabinet, together with other dismembering Ministers, until the general election and the meeting of Parliament, when, though the state of Ireland remained the same, he went over to coercion aud repression. As to Mr. Chamberlain's Irish land purchase proposals, the Premier declares that according to the best judgment, which after having been Finance Minister for thirteen years he confirms, the Government scheme would not haTe cost the ' country one farthing, while Mr. Chimberlain's plan must have cost it many millions of money,
