div.p: SIR W. GUNLIFF E BROOKS AT
LYMIL

On Wednesday evening Sir. W. C. Brooks, Conser- vative candidate. for the Altrimkern Division of Ches- hire, who is the only candidate in the field up to the present, addreesPd a meeting abis supporters, which was held at the Plough Hotel, iymm, and was pre• sided over by IV./r. T. P. Norris. sir. W. C. Bunoxs, who was wsiil received, said that the absorbing question at the present time was now they were to preserve their interests as a nation. To their great sur- prise, Mr. Gladstone. without a wcrat of warning, suddenly brought forward's scheme the direct antithesis of all that he had himself ot er before advocated, and one which his friends themselvies did not hesitate to descrihle as the pro- duction of a man who no longer had a proper judgment. (Cheers.) Ordinary, common-sense people were confronted with a plan. proposed with the -utmost gravity, which had been described by Lord Selborna, late Lord Chancellor, as being the madness of politics. No sooner was it proposed than the moat loyal and discr:raioating, co-workers of Mr. Gladstone him that they coltld not be parties to sub-., mitting such a scheme to the, people. Lord Hartington, ; steady and reliiable,the able and clear Sir Henry James, Mr_ Bright, the,Zirrn friend of the people through thick and thin, i did not hesitate to say that there were principles in the bil to which it yeas impossible the 7 should subscribe, and Mr.l, Gladstone ;hand himself unhappily deserted by his truest;„ his greatcs4-.; and his best frien.ls. -Put he ignored this, and steadily went on with the scheme upon which be had set mind. Mr.. Gladstone said at the bill was dead—dead 14r

the moment, whatever that In.:gbt mean—but through hia• lieutenants Mr. Morley, ha said that the principles of the bill were still living. Mr, Chamberlain hit the eight nail. on the head when he said that the bills were "shamming dead "-Ls( laughter and cheers)—and he (Mr. Brooks) the other day heard a man insbffanchester say "Never mind. they aro.in their coffins, and we'll put Some tails into them.' (Laughter.) Mr. Gladstone was unwilling to say whether he would bring the bills.forward again, but any sensible, straightforward man wonli recognise that be was bocad to . so—they contained, principles he was bound: to bring-,forward. What would be the effect of the proposed bill far the bettergovernment of Ireland. It would be to turn from We.stminstsa the Irish representatives, and to establish in Dublin a distinct and representative Parliunent, but,with only modifiet:, powers. Yet the powers thaF wevdd have were great—the, maintenance of law and order, civil administration, the. appointment and dismiss.al el magistrates and jndges. Who was it to whom they were to commit this great and vital power ? To. the leaders of the National Leaque.r ("Shame.") It was to. such men as Mr. Biggar, who boasted of the power of Odynamite, and of the happy results that he expected hem ,t.lse introduction a Irish dynam;tards ; and as Mr. Healy, jwho said that tbe.most powerful speaking trumpet he knew ;was the mouth of the blundorbcos, and that-the pleasantest ;sound to his ears es an argument was the ra.ttle of the slugs along the roadsid'a. ("Shame') It was to these that they • were asked to cenunit the maintenance of law and order, ,ancrthe power over fellow subjects whom they regarded with the bitterest hatrsd. The late Earl of Beaconstied— (cheers)—kne ar how to maintain law and order; and, thank Gad, there yet remained in the Conservative party many rising men—and many mer,of position—who were willing to emulate the position ad doctrines of the late Lord Beaconsield—(loud cheers)—and who would undertake to maintain that law and order which was the real panacea of the ills of ?eland. (Qheers.) He could not hear of any grievance that the Irish had. When in the House of Com- mons a member, turnina to the body of Irishmen, demanded what their grievance was, and asked what grievance was there that the House of Commons had not shown itself ready and anxious to redress, they- wore silent. They had not a gstievencs. (Cheers.) Bat they had an aspiration. The leaders of the party were anxious to become presidents of the future Irish epublic, and, to secure place and praat, desired one thing crily—seoaration from this country. Mr. Parnell, when challenged with having) at Cincinnati .saisxl :- 44ya shall never be satisfied until the last links are broken' that bind England to Ireland," replied that he could not charge his memory absolutely, bra a report that appeared the next morning did not contain those words. (Laughter.) That might be true, but another rspott coot tined them, and Mr. Parnell could not deny having used them, (Cheers.) 'There was no doubt that what they desired was to maks Ireland a separate nation. Ho could not conceive anything more disastrous, more likely to lead to the misery of I.re- land, and to the disintegration of the Empire, and, holding these opinions, he should, if again returned to the House of Commons, vote against the bill. (Cheers.) On the motion of Mr. ERNEST SWINWICX• seconded by BRABAZON, a resolution was passed expressing cenfi- dance in Sir William Cuuliffe Brooks as a candidate, and pledging the meeting, in the event of a contest, to use every

GREAT LIBERAL MEETING- AT RUNCORN. SPEECHES BY MR. BRUNNER AND MR. BIRRELL.

Runcorn Public Hall was crowded on. Thursday evening with an audience unanimcus and enthusias- tic in favour of Mr. J. T. Brunner, the late M.P. for the division, and "the real Liberal Unionist candi- date.' At Runcorn, as elsewhere throughout the division, Mr. Brunner's reception was most cordial, and in striking contrast to the demenstratinns of his opponent, who even at tinsford and Northwich, where his personal influence might be expected to have the greatest weight, has had to face hostile audiences. On Thursday evening, the half hour previous to the commencement of the proceedings was agreeably passed by the audience singing songs of Liberal sentiment, led by Mr. R. Moore, and aided by a piano manipulated by Miss F. Handley. "Brunner- and -Victory," re-written to suit the altered circumstances, was as great a favour- ite as ever' 'and was sung with much heartiness to the tune of "Wait till the clouds roll by." One verse in "Brunner's Grand March ran Bluff Robert last wore Tory Red, Ha! Ha! Ha' Ha! 'fwas said that he was Liberal bred, Ho! Ho ! Ho ! Ho! P'rhaps next he'll wear the Emerald Green, Or Red and Green with maize between, Bat, howe'er he trim, our Brunner's sure to win. Theon Mr. -Brunner appearing- on the platform he was greeted with a simultaneous enthusiasm that augured well for his cause, and later on rising to a idresss the meeting he was treated to an ovation. He devoted first part of his speech to giving an account of his brief stewardship, and from the patient and intelli• gent manner in which he was listened to, it was evi- &nt that the greatest interest was taken in Mr. Brunner's narration of his labours in "practical poli- tics " His sentiments on Ireland were quite in touch 'with those of his auditors, and he was frequently cheered. Mr. James Handley, J.P., presided, and on the platform, besides the candidate, were Messrs. A. Birrell (candidate for Widnes), R. Shaw, J. T. Gen- nor, P. Spe Osman, S. C. Beckett, W. H. Ockleston, J. R. Frith. J. Brurner, jun.' Joseph Brunner, B. Knive- cos, J. Bridgewater, S. Pope, T. H. Spender, T. Handley, 3 Williams, G. Bellamy, Rev. J. D. Thomas, Rev. W. Vallee, and Mr. W, Handley (secre- tary and agent). The Cuatuaras, who was cordi elly greeted, after a refer- ence to Mr. Brunner's unanimous selectiou by the council as the candidate, geld Mr. Brunner had promised a continu- ance of the genera! support which he bad always given through the last session of Parliament to the principles of Mr. Gledstone's measure for the better government of Ire- land. (Cheers.) It was therefore in the interests of Mr. Gledstone's policy as well as to farther the candidature of their late representative that they were met together that night. (Ilear, hear.) He had no doubt that the meeting woald ratify the choice of the council, and pledge itself to use every lawful effort to secure the triumphant return of their Gladetonian Liberal and the real Unionist candidate, Mr. Brunner. (Cheers, and a voice: "keep your pecker up,'' laughter.) It would not be cast down. (A Voice : "We are sure to win," and cheers.) The issue the voters were called upon to decide was an exceedingly plain and simple one, and should there be any wavers-re present be had little doubt that before the close of the proceedings they would be ftelv persuaded that the principle underly- lag Mr. (ilachtone;a policy, namely, trust in the Irish people, was the only one to bring peace and contentment to Ireland. (Cheers.) It was this want of truet which lay at the root of all tee opposition they had unfortunately to en- counter at this election. (Hear, hear.) The Northwich Division, by returning Mr. Brunner to the House of Com- mons, would share in the happiness which was certain to follow the hmefic.ent seheme of legislation propeunded by Gladstone—(cheers)---and would also hasten on those domestic reforms which they had so long anxiously waitel for, but which had been kept in the background because of the non-settlement of the Irish question. (Cheers.) He hoped they would not lose that golden opportunity of assist- ing their leader in the giant labour he had undertaken in the cause of humanity, and Which they ware fully per- suaded would teicg contentment, happiness, and prosperity to a people hitherto downtrodden and oppressed. (Cheers.) Mr. B. KeriveToN moved "That this meeting recognises in the Home Rule proposals of the Right Hon. W. E. Glad- stone—(cheere)—an earnest and righteous intention to do justice to Ireland—(bear. hear;,—and to maintain and strengthen the unity and integrity of the Einpire—(hear. hear,)—on the basis of conciliation instead of coercion." (Cheers.) Mr. Kniveton pointed out that of all the legis- lative referee which they anticipated so eagerly at the last election, not one bad bsen dealt with in censequence of the Irish question. (Heee,hear.) The 86 followers of Mr. Par- nail had been sent by the people of Ireland to demand Home Rule—(hear, hear,)—and they said, "If you dont% let us mind our own business we will take jolly good care you don't mind yours." (Cheers.) They were all Liberals, but at this moment they said, "We don't care for Conservatism or Liberalism ; our country lies nearest our heart. It has been downtrodden for 86 years, and we are determined now that we have got the power that we will have these wrongs righted before anything else is done." (Cheers.) He said they were in the right of it. (Cheers.) It was the only weapon they had left to fight with, and he heartily wished them success in their struggle. (Hear. hear.) What they were asking for was a restoration of their own Parliament, taken front them in 1800 by force and fraud. Since that period England had tried to govern Ire- land. Had she succeeded? (At this paint Mr. Bin. rail errived, and he was received with prolonged cheering.) Wherever there was good government the popu- lation increased in numbers, in wealth, and in happiness. :In Ireland there was the reverse of this. Her prpulation -and wealth had decreased, and the country, seething wOlt aenreet and disquiet, had again and again been on the bor- ders of civil vra,-. India, and Australia, and CinAda had -improved, but there was this portion of England going from bad to worse unler our benign goverment. (Hear, hear.) Eighty-six years was long enough to try anything, and if it was a failure at the end of that period it was quite time we turned over a new leaf. (Hear, hear.) If the Irish people -could not make Ireland contented and prosperous could • they make it any worse than it had been. Not a bit of it. (Hear, hear.) The country ceuld not get worse, and they 'hoped and believed that it would be better. (Cheers.) Thev were told that if the Home Rule Bill passed. the Methodists and Presbyterians, and Independents, and in fact all the Prottstants, would have to clear out of Ireland. rtey were not to believe it. The day of teligions persecu- tion wee over, and never would return. (Cheers.) It -would not live in the glare of public opinion, and in the face of a free press and open public meetings. 'I hey might as well attempt to carry coal to the moon as revive the days of religious persecution. (Cheers and laughter.) He said this was raising a false issue. This bill was to bring good, and jast,anci wise governm,nt to Ireland, and for nothing else, and if these little " isms" could not exist in Ireland, along with a good and honest Goverpment, then let them go to the wall. (Cheers.) They would have noticed the wonderful figures on the walls, tut there was nothing about the wrongs of Ireland in them. It was all the interests of England. That was a selfish policy—(cheers)—and the -men who advocated it had not hearts as big 39 a horse (Laughter.) They might depend upon it that the lUt'nodisls, Independents, and Presbyterians, aye, all the Thotestants in Ireland, would be quite able to take care of ttemselves. Admitting for the sake of argument that in- tolerance was practised, what would be the result? The persecuted wonld appeal at once to the British House of Commons, and England would respond to the appeal in less than 24 hours, and stamp it out at once. (Cheers.) He did not believe In either separation or religious intelerance. It was all moonshine. They believed this, that it would tend to the unity and integrity of the Empire, because it was a measure of conciliation. It was time they tried some- thing else. Coercion had failed, and justly failed, and it eves for thene, now that they had an ocportunity, 'to shake hands with Ireland over all the wrongs of those 86 years, and like Englishmen do what they could to bring about a better state of things. Mr. Gladstene—(renewed cheers)_ had made an apoeal to the democracy et England—thie was his :vat great effort of securing humanity and right—to help him to settle this great question, and put an end to this long-standing feud between the two peoples. (Cheers.) Mr. PHILIP SPEA/C3IAN, who was warmly received, said be had very great pleasure in seconding the resolntion that had been so very ably moved by their friend, Mr. Janice- ton. (Hear, hear.) He, like thsmselves, had been studying this qeestion for a long time and he had come to the con- clusien that Home Rule for Ireland would be best. (Cheers.) It was made plain, and never se plain, he thought, as on Monday last by the Grand Old Man. (Loud cheers.) He made it plain that all this talk about the separation of the Empire, and its disintegration, was all a bogey. Mr. Glad- stone put the true facts of the case before the country when he said in the British House of Commons that when the franchise was established throughout the length and breadth of the land the throne of England would be more secure than it ever had been, and this Act, which he trusted was about to he given to acland, he believed would consolidate that throne, and make it firmer and riots respected among the nations of the world. (Cheers.) If they had seen the sight that he saw last Monday, and if they had heard the words of truth and soberness that fell from Mr. Gladetone —(cheere)—he did not know who could help but be con- vinced. He knew that there were a great many people who thought differ,ntly from him, and they had perfect right to think as they liked. (Hear, hear.) He thought for himself, and he thoueht they would all admit that the; had sever seen him on a political platform before ; but he felt constrained to came forward and do what he could to help forward the great act of jostice that was now to be gleen to Ireland, end Ireland would have that Act of jus- tice given to her. be trusted, while Mr. Gledetone was in their midst. (Cheers.) Mr. A. BIHRELL, who was received with great enthusi• stem, said if anybody wondered why he was on the platform to support Mr. Brunner when he was busily engaged at Widnes on a little enterprise of his own—(laieglater, and a Voice: "We hope you'll go in ")—his answer was that his sympathies were a great deal wider than the river Mersey, even at high tide. and even wider than St. George's Chan- nel ; and he rejoiced that the enterprise in which they were engaged was one in which they might be proud to take a part. Itavads a policy of pacification and reconciliation, and if it was euccessful the result would be that long cen. turies of disappointment, long centuries of pain and disas- ter might be effaced from men's memories, and in time to

come people would forget the there was ever a time when Irishmen and Englishmen failed to live together in unity. (Cheers.) It was indeed surprising to find that a g.ntle- man living in that part of the country who considered him- self a Liberal bad considered that it was his duty as a Liberal to come forward to oppose the return of Mr. Brun- ner. The policy which Mr. Brunner would support was a policy which he should have supposed all would recognise as one of the most vital articles in the crefd of eve!), , true Liberal. (Applause.) They were told that the pro- posal of Mr. Gladstone was one of violence, and that it was one which must of necessity lead to the disintegration of the Empire. He asked thaw, as reasonable men; to consider for a moment whether that was likely to be the result of that policy. (Cries of "No.") If they were to tell any intelligent foreigner that within 60 miles of their shore there was an island containing some five or six millions of people, crowded with large cities possessed with Universi- ties, inhabited by a religious people, where they found or- dinary crime hardly existent, where they found that the ordinary laws were obeyed with a regularity that he could only wish could be said of other parts of the United Kingdom, to whose people the proposal to grant the power of making the laws to govern themselves and be regulate their own affairs had thrown the whole of that great country into commotion from one end to the other, he was afraid that the Frenchmen would only use the remark that bad been used oftentimes before, that they need be surprised at nothing in an Englishman (Laughter) They found that in America the principle which they were now considerint bad long been recognised as nothing more than the very alphabet of leberalism, as nothing more than the ordinary right which might be granted to persons when they had formed themselves into a homogeneous state. (Hear, hear.) The whole onus lay upon their opponents when they said that Mr. Gladstone was preparing what must of necessity lead to war and bloodshed. He had yet to learn that absolute uniformity was necessary to secure good government. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) It was not I from Protestants in scattered and isolated districts that they heard this cry of despair, but from the people in the North of Ireland. Was there ever greater nonsense talked ? (Cheers.) If they believed that the first act of the Irish Parliament, when they met in the histotic building in Dub- lin, with all the memories of the pest bebind them, with all hopes of the future before them with the eyes of Europe upon them, with all the hopes of their friends, and the evil prognostications of their enemies, would be one of robbery and of plunder; they might have some hesitation, which be thanked God they did not feel in , urging the cause of their Irish brethren. (Cheers.) Alluding to the disesteblishment of the Irish Church, the speaker said that the Anglican Protestant Church in Le- land at the present moment was in a more healthy and prosperous condition than it was at the time when it exis- ted by permission of the State. The old religious differences and distinctions which used to be so bitter between the Presbyterians and the Episcopalians were rapidly dying out and Presbyterians were now content to worship in the 1 Protestant Episcopalian Church. The state of things illus- trated in that small way in the Protestant Church of Ireland they would find in tbe country when restored in some mea- sore to its Parliament. By granting a measure of Home Rule to Ireland they would enlist on the side of the country I Irish intellect and Irish hearts. Irishmen would no longer feel that there was no career for them at heme. They would feel that they had an opportunity I for working out the destiny of their own land 1 under favourable circumstances. (Cheers.) They were told that the bill brought in by Mr. Gladstone must put an end to political union. On the contrary, all they wanted to do , was to bring the Irish to see that their connection with the I British throne and their connection with the United King- dom was of great benefit to themselves. (Cheers.) It was I not likely that they would querrel with their best customer. As soon as they plucked out of the memories of Irishmen their rooted sorrow and showed that they recognised that they were fit to be trusted with the government of their on affairs, all those feelings for separation, if they had ever ex- isted, would disappear. (Cheers) He did not imagine that Ithe electors of that division were going to turn out Mr. I Brunner in favour of his opponent, who was characterised by such chameleon-like political principles. It was per- fectly true that on account of the brevity of Mr. Brunner's Parliamentary life he could not point to a long record of useful labour, but that was not the fault of Mr. Brunner. It was the fault of the Irish question. When this difficulty I had been removed from the political horizon, and when I their Irish friends were conducting their own affairs, then would be Mr. Brunner's opportenity to carry out the wishes of the Liberal party, and to aid in accomplishing those re- forms which they ought long since to have had. He was I quite certain that if they stuck to Mr. Brunner he would be I faithful to them. (Cheers.) I Mr. BauNNEn, who was greeted with prolonged cheers, I said thet he had not the shadow of adouht Piet a fortnight ; hence he was going to be as proud of them as ever he was I last year. (Cheers.) His meetings had been enthusiastic, patient, earnest, and attentive to the last degree. but what about the meetings on the other side ? (Laughter.) Friends of his who had seen them told him that they reminded him of the " shindy " in the pantomime. There had been just as much noise as there had been at his (Mr. Brenner's) vnee inos, and he believed almost as much enthusiasm, but, unluckily for his opponent, the enthusiasm had been on the wrong side. (Laughter.) It appeared that their friends, ! the enemy had come to the conclusion that discussion in public did not suit their book, and they had turned on another tap, •which was the tap of personal influence and talk in private. He was very sorry ,to tell them that influences were being used that he and themselves would not stoop to for a moment— ( heir, heer)—social influences, personal ir,fl oences, trade influences. If he and his hearers could not agree to be politicians, and nothing but politicians, the sooner they par- ted the better. Mr. Brunner claimed to have voted in tha List session perfectly straight. He believed they wan- ted their representative to vote straight, for he believed they were straight themselves, and be did not believe that any man who ran crooked would ever represent them. (A voice "Not long.") They and these who sat with him upon the same platform had been told in that contest that they were swvile fol- lowers of one man. (Cries of "No.") They must follow some man. and it seemed to him that Mr. Chamberlain and his five follewers—(laughter)—ceuld better be described by the word servile than the hundreds who followed the Grand Old Man. (Cheers.) During the last session he voted quite as often against the Government as in their favour, and he meant to stand by that principle. Be was net going to be the slave of any party whip. If the Government seamed to be going Tory, he should not represent the people of that constituency if he followed them. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner said that he always voted on the Crofters Bill with the representatives of the Crofters, and atrainst the re- presentativee of the landlords. Alluding to the Belfast Drainage Bill, he said that he supported Mr. Sexton and the Irish members. He alert voted with the Irish membess against the enfranchisement of the Royal Irish Constabulary, and joined with them in defeating that Bill. Mr. Brunner referred to a Government Bill which provided that the cutting of hedges skirting the highways of the country should be paid for by the public. He, as being responsible for soma five miles of hedges in Cheshire, objected resolutely to the public paving for the lopping of those trees. (Cheers.) He moved an amendment to that Bill with the object of defeating it. The Government, he was surprised to find, supported the Bill, and the Government defeated his amend- ment by 58 votes to 34. He moved another amendment, and this time several of the members who had been talking over the master voted with him, and the Government found only 54 supporters, while he received 50. He tried a third time, when the Government came to him and said, " Mr. Brunner, we think von are right and we are wrong, and we shall support this Bill no further." The result was that although highway authorities had pewee to lop trees and hedges if the proprietor did not do it, they had to charge the proprietors with the cost. (Cheers.) Alluding to his ex- perience of the !rig) members, the speaker said that he had found them to be reasonable and practical, and not by any means so extreme as they were represented. He also spoke of the great interest taken in technical education by rtlr.Parnell. What he asked was the real mainspring to the Government work proposed by Mr. Gladstone? The mainspring was distrust of the Irish people. They as Liberals had no sym- pathy whatever with that distrust. What had the Grand Old Man himself told them? He said that Toryism "is distrust of the people, tempered by fear. (Cheers. Liberalism in trust of the people tempered by prudence." The more he studied the character of the Irish, and the more he studied their circumstances, the more thoroughly did be believe they would manage their own. affairs far more to their advantage that would the English people. The Tories of Great Britain, and those cross-bred politicians —(laughter)—who called themselves Liberal Unionists— ' (" Oh, oh ")—insisted that Irishmen should not be allowed to manage their own affairs, but with the most foolish con- tradiction in the world they would have it that those men who were not able to manage their own effaire should con- tinue to manage Englieh affairs. (Laughter and cheers.) Great Britain governed directly or indhectly one fifth of the human race. There was no spot over tbe world where the English rule bad not prodticed benefit to the people, except Ireland. Ireland was their one failure. To his mind this I was the accepted time to redeem that failure, and to make the thoueht of their great Imperial race a joy to the civilized world. (Loud cheers) At the conclusion of his address Mr. Brunner answered The first was : " Does Mr. Brunner think the Volunteers unworthy of the increased card- tition grant, and why did he vote against it ?" To the first part he did not think the Volunteers unworthy: (Hear, hear.) Ti) the next question of why he voted against the increased capitation grant, he had a little story to tell. Be (Mr. Brunner) was asked to join a deputa- tion of members of the House of Commons who were interested in the Volunteers to meet the Secretary of State for War to aek him to take into his favourable considera- tion the question of increasing the grant to the Velunteers. The condition he (Mr. Brunner) made was that no pressure should be put upon the Government to increase the vises this year, because the finances of the country were in a strained condition. He got that undez taking, but a few days afterwards a Tory member of the house of Commons brongbt forward a resolution demanding,in imperious tones, that the grant should be made immediately. Mr. Gladstone said it was a wrong thing, constitu- tionally, for a private member to propose to increase the taxes upon the country He (Mr. Brunner) angeed with Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) Another question which had been put to him was as follows : "Is it the moon- lighters' that has frightened You into this course or the dynamite round the House?" He had never been frightened into anything, and he did not think he snould he. (A Voice : " Verdin wouldn't frighten you.") Another ques- tion was: "Don't you think if Ireland was divided into

listmataccrs. Having been solicited by a large and influential body of Unionists to contest this Division as a Liberal Unionist, I have pleasure in acceding to that request. My Liberal prin:iples are well known to you all, but all other considerations and objects are in my opinion subservient to, and overehadowed ty, the one great issue now before the isountry; namely, the supremacy of the English Parliament, the maintenance f the IJni6n between Great Britain and Ire- land, and the protection of the Irish Loyalists. The serious effect the measures proposed by Mr. Gladstone will have upon this country and upon Ireland has not yet been realized. If such proposals are carried out, I believe that the wealth and capital invested in Ireland will leave that coun- try, stagnation of trade will follow, by which the latour mar- ket in England will be overwhelmed, to the krest and serious , detriment of our wirking classes. It has often been stated that there is ne intermeiate course between the Government proposals and the policy oi Coercion, yet it must be obvious that the support acoorded to Mr. Glad- stone's Bills undoubtedly meant coercion of the worst charac- ter, namely, the coercion of the Lcyallsts of Ireland. The Protestant communities of Ireland, comprising the Episcopalians, the Presbyterians, the Wesievans. the primative Methodists, apd the New Connexknal Churches, have shown their sense of the injustice sought to be committed by sendemning the Irish Bills. These proposals would never have teas submitted for con- sideration if Mr. Gladstone had been returned to tower with a I sufficiently large Liberal vote to lupport him against the vote of the Irish Party. We are, therefore, undoubtediy yielding to a class of agitators whose only desire is to injure England, land who have been aided in obtaining their present place and power by a system of terrorism and eritme unknown in any other part of Her Majesty's dominions. Their object is nf.st Union. but Separation. I can, therefore, confidently promise that if you shnuld honour me with your confidence I shall strive to the utmost of my power to resist any measures which te,d to destroy the su- premacy of the Imperial Parliament or injure the Union now existing between the two countries. Whilst adopting that course, I shall always be ready to assist in remoymg any real grievance of which the Irish people may have just cause to complain. I would govern Ireland by the same laws as those which govern my fellow-electors in this Division, but we must first maintain law and order, and secure to life and property that value which every civilized State ensures for the commu- nity. I need scarcely add that it will ever be my desire to pro- mote the interests of every industry in this Division, whether agricultural, commercial, or manufacturing, and this as well for employed as employer, so that the depression now unfor- tunately existing may be effectually removed. To this end the establishment of a settled and stabls Govern- ment will best contribute. 6 I am, Gentlemen. Your obedient cervant, NOBERT TEBDI.N. The Brockhurst, Northwich, 21st June, 1888. SATURDAY, 4 JULY 3 1886 • npo THE ELECTORS AND NON-ELECTORS OF TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON PARMA- I -a- THE ALTRINCHAM DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. MENTARY DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCASTER. GENTLEMEN.—Her Majesty has been pleased to appeal to the sense of her people in, the gravest issue of modern times. You are called on to select a policy for dealing with Ireland, on ' which will depend the tranquility—perhaps the safely of the Empire; to say whether that policy Is to be one of prudent concessions and just reforms, the policy of Mr. Gladstone, con- sonant with the best traditions of the Liberal party, or one based on the incoherent projects of our opponents, powerless alike to subdue or conciliate Ireland. white teeming with im- mediate anxieties and future dangers. At this cri,ical juncture, it is the duty of every true Liberal to go forward in support of our principles; and it is on this account that I venture, even at the eleventh hour,, having only just landed from a distant voyage, and though compara- tively a stranger among you, to accept ith gratitude your selection of me, in my absence, to contest your division at the approaching election. We can hardly doubt what the verdict of the country will be, and if you honour me w th your support you will find in me an unflinching defender of the Crown and Constitution, de- termined to preserve through thick and thin, the Unity of the Empire, while co, ceding to Ireland that due measure of Home ltule without Which I believe Unity can no longer be- maintained. But there are many other questions of the utmost impor- tance, such as that of Local Gaverment ana Administration the Reform and Simplification of the Laws connected with the Ownership, Occupation, and Transfer of Land, the advance- ment of our depressed Commercial and Agricultural interests, and, closely connected with these, the Consolidation and Development of our Great Colonial Empire; also, as matter' of special urgency, the amendment and extension of the Em- ployers Liability Acts, and the proposed Legislation, with re- ference to theßegutation of Mines, especially as to the seleo- tion of checkweighmen by the miners themselves. Further, as a Catholic. I warmly support our National 53 stem of De- nominational Education. But, vital and urgent as all these matters are, they are dependent upon and must await the settlement of the Irish Difficulty; till that question is disposea of the legislative arm of England is paralysed. It rests with you. gentlemen, ;Ind with the constituencies of the couttry, by supporting Mr. Gladstone, to restore to Par- liament its freedom of action, without which all further Liberal progress is impossible. I hope to have the honour of laying my views before you in detail on all these subjects, and I remain, in the meanwhile, Your very faithful Servant, GEORGE ERRINGTON. The Hall, Rainhill, June 25th, 1186.

PARLIAMENTARY ELECTION, 1886. -- ITO THE ELECTORS OF THE NEWTON DIVI- SION OF THE COUNTY OF LANCAbTER. GFNTLEMEN, The Parliament which was elected only a few months ago is at once to be dissolved. The programme as to domestic legislation, which was at the time of the last ehetion put before the country by the present Prime Modeler as one of urgent importance (and as to a great portion of which all parties were agreed) has been ruthlessly set aside, and is for all practical purposes indefinitely post- poned, and, to use the language of the Government themselves, they have taken a " totally new departure," and "the fact of the re.ponsible Government of the Queen making such propo- sals as they have done is the gravest and most startling event in the political life of any man among us." The Government proposals are to set up within the United Kingdom a legislative and administrative body for Ireland, ab- solutely independent of the Imperial Parliament. The Govern- ment proposals would deprive the inhabitants of that part of the United Kingdom, whether the majority or the minority, of that which is undoubtedly the birthright of both the one and the other, namely, the protection of the Imperial Parlia- ment. The Government proposals wou:d, if honestly carried out, impose on the taxpayers of Great Britain a financial bur- den of at least £120,000,000, in addition to an annual surrender of revenue to the extent of £1,900,001. Parliament has, as I think, most wisely rejected these proposals by the large majority of 30, and the Prime Minister has appealed to the country. The issue, though very grave, is very clear and simple. Happily, this is so party question. In common with the Con- servative party, I am entirely opposed to the Government !proposals, but on this great Imperial question I have also had the pleasure of finding' myself fighting on the same side with such Liberals as Lord Harting-ton and Mr. Gesehen, and even with such advanced Liberals as Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamber- lain, and with those who agree with them, and who helped to form the majority of 30. The Prime Minister speaks of this large and influen ial num- ber of Members of the Liberal party as "seceders," It is he himself who has seceded. He appealed strongly at the Gen- eral Eleo.tion to the Liberal party that he might have a great majority, in order that he might be independent of the Irish vote. He bad himself publiely stated, while he was hat in office, that he was endeavouring to relieve the people of Ire- land frem a tyrannical yoke; that is to say, from the tyranny of the National League. He now yields to the b'dding of the Irish vote, and seeks to snake the National League the National Government in Ireland. He apparently wilfully misinterprets Lord Salisbury's ianguage. and BO misinterprets Min as having no policy save that of coercion. No one desires coercion; but, as I believe, every true patriot not only desires but insists upon ensuring liberty fri every part of the United !Kingdom; Lib- erty, which used, at all events, to be the watchword of the, Liberal party ; Liberty to carry out our religious views without let or hindranee ; Liberty to work your own honest industry or calling without fear of being coerced by others; Liberty to go your own way with- out fear of loss of life'or limb, of injury to cittle or to crops; without fear of being e'eprived of all the means of freely carry- ing out your own honest trade. To secure these blessings (which in Great Britain we all enjoy) to our fellow subjects in Ireland is the purpose we have in view in refusing cur assent to the Government measures, and in declining to deprive our Irish fellow subjects of the protection of the Imperial Parlia- ment of the United Kingdom, and we are at the same time as strongly convinced that for the preservation of our influ- ence for good abroad, and for the maintenance of our Indian and Co'onial Emoire, it is essential that the heart of the Em- pire should remain whole and undivided; that the three United Kingdoms should remain united, and that the absolute supremacy of the Imperial Parliament should continue unim- paired. This is the only question now before the constituen- cies, and on patriotic grounds, and in no party spirit, I appeal confidently for support to the general body of the electors of the Newton Division. I have the honour to remain, gentlemen, Very faith'ully yours, RICHARD ASSHETON 0R039. ! 12. Warwick-square, S.W. 22nd Jane, 1886.
